In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The scholars said: this word is used only of God, glorified is He, and only in the past tense. Al-Furqan is the Qur'an. It was called al-Furqan because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood through its rulings, or between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. By "His servant" is meant our Prophet (ﷺ). Then He gave the reason for the sending down, "that he may be a warner to the worlds," for warning (nidhara) is the purpose intended by the sending down. By "the worlds" here is meant mankind and the jinn, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to both of them, and no other prophet before him was sent to both of the two species (thaqalan). The word nadhir means "one who warns," i.e., that Muhammad should be a warner, or that the sending down of the Qur'an should be a warning. It is also permissible for nadhir here to be used in the sense of a verbal noun for emphasis (mubalaghah), i.e., that its sending down be a warning, or that Muhammad be a warning. Making the pronoun refer to the Prophet (ﷺ) is preferable, because the issuing of warning is from him in the literal sense (haqiqah), while from the Qur'an it is figurative (majaz), and it is better to take the literal meaning. It is also preferable because he is the nearest antecedent mentioned.

It was also said that it is better for the pronoun to refer to the Criterion, because of His saying, ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾.

Then God, glorified is He, described Himself with four attributes. The first: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, to the exclusion of any other, so He alone disposes of them. It is possible that the other relative clause is an apposition or an explanation of the first relative clause, and the descriptive (wasf) reading is preferable. This also indicates that all things depend on Him for existence and its consequences, including splendour and other things.

The second attribute: ﴿and has not taken a son﴾. This is a refutation of the Christians and Jews.

The third attribute: ﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. This is a refutation of the various groups of polyhteists, including the idolaters, the dualists (thanawiyyah), and the people of hidden shirk.

The fourth attribute: ﴿He created everything﴾ among existing things, ﴿and determined it precisely﴾, i.e., He determined everything He created by His wisdom according to what He willed, and prepared it for what suits it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: He determined everything concerning its term and its provision, so the decrees ran according to what He created. It was also said: by creation here is meant simply bringing into being and originating, without regard to the meaning of determination, although determination is not absent from it in reality. So the meaning is: He brought everything into being and then determined it, lest there be repetition. Then God, glorified is He, explicitly exposed the falsehood of the doctrines of the worshippers of idols.

He said: ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾. The pronoun in ittakhadhu (they have taken) refers to the polytheists, although they have not been previously mentioned, because the negation of a partner indicates them. That is, the polytheists have taken for themselves, passing beyond God, gods ﴿that create nothing﴾. The clause is in the accusative position as a descriptive for gods, i.e., they are not able to create any of things. The masculine rational plural pronoun was used for them rather than for non-rational beings, because among the objects worshipped by the unbelievers are angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah. ﴿While they themselves are created﴾, i.e., God, glorified is He, creates them. It was also said: He expressed the gods with the pronoun for rational beings, following the belief of the unbelievers that they harm and benefit. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿while they themselves are created﴾ is that their worshippers make images of them.

Then, when God, glorified is He, described Himself with overwhelming power, He described the gods of the polytheists with utter helplessness, and said: ﴿and they possess no power to harm or benefit themselves﴾, i.e., they are not able to bring themselves any benefit or to repel any harm from themselves. If they are such that they cannot repel or bring benefit concerning themselves, how could they possess that for those who worship them?

Then He increased the explanation of their helplessness and specified these matters, saying: ﴿and possess no control over death, life, or resurrection﴾, i.e., they are not able to cause the living to die, nor to bring the dead to life, nor to raise them from their graves. When He had finished explaining tawhid and refuting the doctrines of the polytheists, He began to mention the doubts of those who deny prophethood.

Then He mentioned the second doubt, saying: ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients"﴾, i.e., the stories of the former peoples and what they wrote down of reports.

This is what al-Kashshaf says, and Abu Hayyan objected to it.

﴿So it is dictated to him﴾, i.e., those tales are cast upon him after he had them written down, so that he might memorize them from the mouths of those who dictate them to him from that written material, because he is illiterate and cannot read them from the writing himself. God answered this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"﴾, i.e., it is not something that is invented and fabricated through the help of one group and the writing of another from fabricated tales and reports of the ancients. Rather it is a heavenly matter sent down by Him who knows everything, from which nothing among things is hidden. For this reason you were unable to oppose it, and you did not produce a single surah like it. The word "secret" (sirr) is singled out to indicate that what He sent down contains wondrous secrets to which human minds cannot attain. Sirr means the unseen, i.e., He knows the unseen that exists in them both. The clause ﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason for the delay of punishment, i.e., although you deserve to have punishment hastened for what you do of lying against His messenger and wronging him, He does not hasten punishment upon you for that, because He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in the dominion. He created everything and determined it precisely.﴾ ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, while they themselves are created, and they possess no power to harm or benefit themselves, and possess no control over death, life, or resurrection.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it." Indeed they have committed injustice and falsehood.﴾ ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and which are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful."﴾

God, glorified is He, speaks in this surah about tawhid (the oneness of God) because it is the most ancient and most important matter, then about prophethood (nubuwwa) because it is the intermediary, then about the return (ma'ad) because it is the conclusion.

The root of tabaraka (blessed is) is derived from barakah (blessing), which is growth and increase, whether sensory or intellectual. Al-Zajjaj said: tabaraka is of the form tafa''ala, from barakah. He said: the meaning of barakah is abundance of every good thing. Al-Farra' said: tabaraka and taqaddasa (sanctified) are synonymous in Arabic, and both mean greatness. It was also said that the meaning is: "His bounty is blessed," i.e., it increased and abounded. It was also said that the meaning is: it endured and remained (p. 1032). Al-Nahhas said: this is the most preferable meaning in the language, and the derivation is from barak al-shay' when a thing became firm, and from it comes barak al-jamal, meaning it lay down and settled.

The view of al-Farra' has been objected to on the ground that taqdis (sanctification) comes from purity, and this has nothing to do with it. The scholars said: this word is used only of God, glorified is He, and only in the past tense. Al-Furqan is the Qur'an. It was called al-Furqan because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood through its rulings, or between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. By "His servant" is meant our Prophet (ﷺ). Then He gave the reason for the sending down, "that he may be a warner to the worlds," for warning (nidhara) is the purpose intended by the sending down. What is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ), or the Criterion. By "the worlds" here is meant mankind and the jinn, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to both of them, and no other prophet before him was sent to both of the two species (thaqalan). The word nadhir means "one who warns," i.e., that Muhammad should be a warner, or that the sending down of the Qur'an should be a warning. It is also permissible for nadhir here to be used in the sense of a verbal noun for emphasis (mubalaghah), i.e., that its sending down be a warning, or that Muhammad be a warning. Making the pronoun refer to the Prophet (ﷺ) is preferable, because the issuing of warning is from him in the literal sense (haqiqah), while from the Qur'an it is figurative (majaz), and it is better to take the literal meaning. It is also preferable because he is the nearest antecedent mentioned.

It was also said that it is better for the pronoun to refer to the Criterion, because of His saying, ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾.

Then God, glorified is He, described Himself with four attributes. The first: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, to the exclusion of any other, so He alone disposes of them. It is possible that the other relative clause is an apposition or an explanation of the first relative clause, and the descriptive (wasf) reading is preferable. This also indicates that all things depend on Him for existence and its consequences, including splendour and other things.

The second attribute: ﴿and has not taken a son﴾. This is a refutation of the Christians and Jews.

The third attribute: ﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. This is a refutation of the various groups of polyhteists, including the idolaters, the dualists (thanawiyyah), and the people of hidden shirk.

The fourth attribute: ﴿He created everything﴾ among existing things, ﴿and determined it precisely﴾, i.e., He determined everything He created by His wisdom according to what He willed, and prepared it for what suits it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: He determined everything concerning its term and its provision, so the decrees ran according to what He created. It was also said: by creation here is meant simply bringing into being and originating, without regard to the meaning of determination, although determination is not absent from it in reality. So the meaning is: He brought everything into being and then determined it, lest there be repetition. Then God, glorified is He, explicitly exposed the falsehood of the doctrines of the worshippers of idols.

He said: ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾. The pronoun in ittakhadhu (they have taken) refers to the polytheists, although they have not been previously mentioned, because the negation of a partner indicates them. That is, the polytheists have taken for themselves, passing beyond God, gods ﴿that create nothing﴾. The clause is in the accusative position as a descriptive for gods, i.e., they are not able to create any of things. The masculine rational plural pronoun was used for them rather than for non-rational beings, because among the objects worshipped by the unbelievers are angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah. ﴿While they themselves are created﴾, i.e., God, glorified is He, creates them. It was also said: He expressed the gods with the pronoun for rational beings, following the belief of the unbelievers that they harm and benefit. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿while they themselves are created﴾ is that their worshippers make images of them.

Then, when God, glorified is He, described Himself with overwhelming power, He described the gods of the polytheists with utter helplessness, and said: ﴿and they possess no power to harm or benefit themselves﴾, i.e., they are not able to bring themselves any benefit or to repel any harm from themselves. He mentioned harm first because repelling it is more important than bringing benefit. If they are such that they cannot repel or bring benefit concerning themselves, how could they possess that for those who worship them?

Then He increased the explanation of their helplessness and specified these matters, saying: ﴿and possess no control over death, life, or resurrection﴾, i.e., they are not able to cause the living to die, nor to bring the dead to life, nor to raise them from their graves. Because nushur (resurrection) means life after death. One says: Allah anshara al-mawta, "God raised the dead," and they were raised (nushiru). From it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Until people say at what they see: 'How strange, the dead one who rises!'"

When He had finished explaining tawhid and refuting the doctrines of the polytheists, He began to mention the doubts of those who deny prophethood.

The first doubt is what He related of them in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication"﴾, i.e., a lie, which he invented, i.e., which Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated. The demonstrative "this" refers to the Qur'an. ﴿and other people have helped him with it﴾, i.e., in the fabrication, ﴿other people﴾, meaning, as they intended, from among the Jews.

It was said that they were: Abu Fukayhah Yasar, a client of al-Hadrami; 'Addas, a client of Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza; and Jabr, a client of Ibn 'Amir. These three were Jews. The discussion of something like this has already passed in al-Nahl.

As for it being falsehood on their part, it is evident, because they have lied in this statement.

Then He mentioned the second doubt, saying: ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients"﴾, i.e., the stories of the former peoples and what they wrote down of reports.

This is what al-Kashshaf says, and Abu Hayyan objected to it.

﴿So it is dictated to him﴾, i.e., those tales are cast upon him after he had them written down, so that he might memorize them from the mouths of those who dictate them to him from that written material, because he is illiterate and cannot read them from the writing himself. It is also permissible that the meaning of iktatabaha is: he intended its writing, ﴿so it is dictated to him﴾, because one says umliyat 'alayhi, "it was dictated to him," so he writes ﴿morning and evening﴾, i.e., at dawn and at dusk. It is as if they said: these people teach Muhammad at both ends of the day. It was also said: the meaning of bukratan wa-asilan is always, at all times.

God answered this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"﴾, i.e., it is not something that is invented and fabricated through the help of one group and the writing of another from fabricated tales and reports of the ancients. Rather it is a heavenly matter sent down by Him who knows everything, from which nothing among things is hidden. For this reason you were unable to oppose it, and you did not produce a single surah like it. The word "secret" (sirr) is singled out to indicate that what He sent down contains wondrous secrets to which human minds cannot attain. Sirr means the unseen, i.e., He knows the unseen that exists in them both. The clause ﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason for the delay of punishment, i.e., although you deserve to have punishment hastened for what you do of lying against His messenger and wronging him, He does not hasten punishment upon you for that, because He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

Then He mentioned the second doubt, saying: ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients"﴾, i.e., the stories of the former peoples and what they wrote down of reports.

Al-Zajjaj said: the singular of asatir is ustura, like ahadith and uhdutha. Others said: asatir is the plural of asfar, like aqawil and aqwal. Ikkatabaha, i.e., istaktabaha (had it written down) or wrote it down for himself. The position of iktatabaha is in the accusative as a circumstantial of asatir, or its position is in the nominative as a second predicate, because asatir is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "these are the tales of the ancients which he had written down." It is also permissible for asatir to be the subject and iktatabaha its predicate. It is also permissible that the meaning of iktatabaha is "gathered them from books," which is gathering, not writing with a pen. The first is preferable.

Talhah read iktutiba (it was written down for him), in the passive, and the meaning is: a scribe wrote it for him, because he was illiterate and could not write. Then the lam was removed, so the verb reached the pronoun and became iktatabaha iyyahu, then he made the verb refer to the pronoun which is iyyahu, and so it became a hidden nominative after having been an explicit accusative. This is what al-Kashshaf says, and Abu Hayyan objected to it.

﴿So it is dictated to him﴾, i.e., those tales are cast upon him after he had them written down, so that he might memorize them from the mouths of those who dictate them to him from that written material, because he is illiterate and cannot read them from the writing himself. It is also permissible that the meaning of iktatabaha is: he intended its writing, ﴿so it is dictated to him﴾, because one says umliyat 'alayhi, "it was dictated to him," so he writes ﴿morning and evening﴾, i.e., at dawn and at dusk. It is as if they said: these people teach Muhammad at both ends of the day. It was also said: the meaning of bukratan wa-asilan is always, at all times.

God answered this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"﴾, i.e., it is not something that is invented and fabricated through the help of one group and the writing of another from fabricated tales and reports of the ancients. Rather it is a heavenly matter sent down by Him who knows everything, from which nothing among things is hidden. For this reason you were unable to oppose it, and you did not produce a single surah like it. The word "secret" (sirr) is singled out to indicate that what He sent down contains wondrous secrets to which human minds cannot attain. Sirr means the unseen, i.e., He knows the unseen that exists in them both. The clause ﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason for the delay of punishment, i.e., although you deserve to have punishment hastened for what you do of lying against His messenger and wronging him, He does not hasten punishment upon you for that, because He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Tabaraka" is taking part (tafāʿala) from al-barakah (blessing).

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And others helped him in it﴾, that he said: "They are Jews." ﴿Then they have come with injustice and falsehood﴾, that he said: "Lies."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, that he said: "It is the Qur'an, in which is its lawful and its unlawful, its legislations and its religion, and by which Allah distinguished between truth and falsehood." ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾, that he said: "Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a warner from Allah, to warn people of the might of Allah and His punishments upon those who passed before you." ﴿And He created every thing and determined it with precise measure﴾, that he said: "He made clear for every thing of His creation its right condition, and made that according to a known measure." ﴿And they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾, that he said: "They are the idols that are worshipped besides Allah." ﴿They create nothing, and they are created﴾: He is Allah, the Creator, the Provider, whereas these idols are created and create nothing, neither harm nor benefit, and do not possess death, life, or resurrection, meaning raising (of the dead). ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾: this is the saying of the polytheists of the Arabs. ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾: that is, lying. ﴿He has invented it, and others have helped him in it﴾: that is, in this narration and matter of his. ﴿Others have helped him, and they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients"﴾: the lies and stories of the ancients.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 7–16 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had finished mentioning what they criticised the Qur'an for, He mentioned what they criticised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for, and said: ﴿And they say, "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ In this indication (the demonstrative "this") there is a belittling of the one being pointed at, who is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They called him "Messenger" in mockery and derision. ﴿He eats food and walks in the markets﴾ meaning: what is the matter with him that he eats food as we eat, and moves about in the markets seeking a livelihood as we do? They claimed that he ought to have been an angel, free of need for food and earning.

Here, ma (what) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the interrogation is for disapproval (istinkar). Alternatively, ma is the predicate of the subject, "this Messenger." The clause "he eats" (ya'kulu) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning of the statement is completed by it, as in His saying: ﴿So what is the matter with them, turning away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. The disapproval is directed at the cause while the effect is established, namely eating and walking, but they deemed that effect unlikely because its cause was absent in their view, in mockery and derision.

The meaning: if what he claims of prophethood is true, then what is the matter with him that his condition does not differ from ours? ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾ They asked that the Prophet (ﷺ) be accompanied by an angel who would support and assist him. They descended from the proposal that the Messenger (ﷺ) be an angel free of eating and earning, to the proposal that an angel be with him to confirm him and bear witness to his messengership.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read fa-yakuna with the accusative, as it is the answer to the exhortation (tahdid). It was also read as fa-yakunu with the nominative, as coordinated with unzila; coordinating it with the past tense is permissible because what is meant by it is the future.

﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾ is coordinated with unzila, and it is not permissible to coordinate it with fa-yakuna. The meaning: or why is a treasure not thrown down to him? They descended from the level of an angel's descent with him, to the proposal that a treasure be with him, thrown down to him from the sky so that he would be free of seeking provision. ﴿Or he have a garden from which he may eat﴾ The majority read takun with the feminine ta'; al-A'mash and Qatadah read yakun with the masculine ya', because the feminine gender of "garden" (jannah) is not real. Hamzah, Ali and Khalaf read na'kulu with the nun; the rest read ya'kulu with the ya', meaning: a garden from whose fruits we eat, or he alone eats from it, so that he would have a distinction over us by his eating from his own garden.

Al-Nahhas said: both readings are good, though the reading with the ya' is clearer, because the Prophet (ﷺ) alone was previously mentioned, so the return of the pronoun to him is evident.

﴿And the wrongdoers say, "You follow nothing but a man bewitched."﴾ What is meant by "the wrongdoers" here are those who made the earlier statements. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun along with the description of wrongdoing in order to record this against them. That is: you follow only a man whose mind is overcome by magic. It was said: "dha sihr" means one who has a windpipe (ri'ah), i.e., a human being who has a windpipe, not an angel. The explanation of the like of this has already been given in (the commentary on) Subhan.

﴿Look how they strike for you the parables﴾ so that they might thereby reach your denial. The "parables" (amthal) are rare sayings and strange proposals; these are what they mentioned here. They have strayed from the right course, so they find no way to it and have reached nothing of it. Rather, they came with these false statements, which would not proceed from even the least intelligent of the sensible and the least discerning. For this reason He said: ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾, meaning they find no path among the paths to discredit the prophethood of this Prophet.

﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ meaning: abundant is the good of Him who, if He wills, will give you in this world, in advance, good better than that which they proposed.

Then He explained the good, saying: ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, so "gardens" is a substitute (badal) for "good." ﴿And will give you palaces﴾ is coordinated with the position of "will give" (ja'ala), which is the jussive, and the majority read with the jussive. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read yaj'alu with the nominative, as a resumptive clause (isti'naf). It is established in the science of i'rab that when the conditional verb is in the past tense, its answer may be jussive or nominative, so ja'ala here may be in a jussive or nominative position, and what is coordinated with it may be jussive or nominative. It was also read with the accusative. It was read with the assimilation of the lam of laka into the lam of yaj'al because of the meeting of two identical letters, and read without assimilation because the two words are separate. The qasr is a house of stone, because its occupant is shut off from being reached; it was said to be a house of clay, and houses of wool and hair.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from rebuking them with what He related of their speech, which does not proceed from the intelligent.

﴿Nay, but they deny the Hour﴾ meaning: nay, they came with something more astonishing than all of that, namely their denial of the Hour. For this reason they do not benefit from the proofs, nor do they reflect upon them. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He has prepared for those who deny the Hour, saying: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾, meaning a fire kindled and blazing. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: nay, they deny the Hour, while the state is that "We have prepared." Abu Muslim said: "a'tadna" means: We made it ready and prepared for them.

﴿When it sees them from a far place, they will hear its raging and roaring.﴾ This conditional clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "a blaze," because it is feminine in meaning as fire. It was said: the meaning of "when it sees them" is: when it appears to them and becomes visible to the viewer at a distance. It was said: the meaning is: when its keepers see them. It was said: the seeing from it is real, and likewise the raging and roaring; there is no barrier to Allah, glory be to Him, making it perceive in this way.

The meaning of "from a far place" is that it sees them while it is far from them; it was said that between it and them is a distance of five hundred years. The meaning of raging is that it has a sound indicating rage against the disbelievers, or that its boiling produces a sound resembling the sound of one who is enraged. Zafir (roaring) is the sound heard from the inside of the chest.

Al-Zajjaj said: what is meant is the hearing of that which indicates anger, namely the sound; that is, they heard from it a sound resembling the sound of one enraged.

Qutrub said: he meant "they knew its rage and heard its roaring," as the poet said:
"Girding on a sword and a spear"
meaning: and carrying a spear. It was said: the meaning is: they heard in it rage and roaring for the tormented, as He said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ [Hud: 106]. The two prepositions (fi and li) are close in meaning; you say: "do this in Allah" and "for Allah."

﴿And when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, bound together﴾ The place is described as narrow to indicate the increase of severity and the utmost of affliction upon them. The accusative of "bound together" (muqarranin) is a circumstantial state: when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, while their hands are bound to their necks with chains, shackled with iron. It was said: "bound" means tied at the wrists. It was said: they were bound together with the devils, meaning each one of them was bound to his devil. The discussion of the like of this has already been given in Surah Ibrahim.

﴿They will call out there for destruction﴾, i.e., in that narrow place, "thubur," meaning ruin. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "we were ruined with ruin." It was said: it is accusative as an object of purpose, and the meaning is that they wish for ruin there and call out for it because of the affliction that has befallen them.

Then they are answered with His saying: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾ That is, this statement is said to them, and the one saying it to them is the angels, meaning: give up calling for a single destruction, for what you are in of ruin is greater and more severe than that. Thus said al-Zajjaj. ﴿But call out for many destructions﴾: "thubur" is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many, therefore it is not made plural. Similar is: "I struck him a great blow" and "he sat a long sitting." The multiplicity here is according to the multiplicity of the calls connected to it, not according to its multiplicity in itself, for it is one thing. The meaning: do not call down ruin upon yourselves once, but call for it in many supplications, for what you are in of punishment is more severe than that, because of its long duration and its endlessness. It was said: this is an illustration and depiction of their condition by the condition of one to whom that is said without any speech actually being spoken. It was said: the meaning is that you have fallen into what your ruin is not single in, but is many, because the punishment has kinds. The more preferable view is that what is meant by this answer to them is to indicate the eternity of their punishment and to despair them of attaining the destruction they wish for, which would deliver them from what they are in.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, rebuked them with a severe rebuke through the tongue of His Messenger, saying: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the God-fearing?"﴾ The indication with His saying "that" is to the blaze characterised by those great attributes; that is: is that blaze better, or the Garden of Eternity? In the attribution of "the Garden" to "eternity" is an indication of the permanence of its bliss and the non-cessation of it. The meaning of "which has been promised to the God-fearing" is: which was promised to the God-fearing. The use of the word "better" here, though there is no good at all in the Fire, is because the Arabs do say this; among it is what Sibawayh related from them, that they say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" It was also said: this is not of the category of comparison, but is like your saying: "he has good."

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good view, as the poet said:
"Would you satirise him, when you are not his equal? So your evil and your good are both a ransom."

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿It is for them a reward and a destination﴾, meaning: that Garden is for the God-fearing a reward for their deeds and a destination to which they arrive.

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, meaning: whatever they wish of bliss and kinds of delights, as in His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31]. The accusative of "abiding" is a circumstantial state, and the reality of the meaning of eternity has already been established. ﴿It has been upon your Lord a promise to be asked for﴾, meaning: what they wish was a promise. It was said: eternity was the promise. It was said: the promise indicated by His saying "were promised to the God-fearing." The meaning of "a promise to be asked for" is: a promise that is established, to be requested and sought, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]. It was said: the angels ask the Garden for them, as in His saying: ﴿And admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them﴾. It was said: what is meant is an obligatory promise even if it is not asked for.

(p-1035) Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Zamʿah ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-ʿAs ibn Wail, Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj gathered together. Some of them said to others: "Send to Muhammad, speak with him and dispute with him, so that you may be excused from him." So they sent to him: "The nobles of your people have gathered for you so that they may speak with you." He said: "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them, and they said: 'O Muhammad, we sent for you so that we might give you an excuse [to stop]. If you have only brought this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you some of our wealth; and if you seek nobility, we will make you our lord; and if you desire kingship, we will make you king.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What I have is not what you say. I have not brought you this seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah has sent me to you as a messenger, has revealed to me a Book, and has commanded me to be for you a bringer of good news and a warner. So I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and given you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter; and if you reject it from me, I will be patient over the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you.'

They said: 'O Muhammad, if you will not accept anything from us of what we have offered you,' or they said: 'If you will not do this, then ask for yourself and ask your Lord to send an angel with you to confirm what you say and to answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to make for you gardens and palaces of gold and silver that will make you independent of what we see you seeking, for you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may recognize your merit and rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'I will not do that. I am not one who asks his Lord for this, and I was not sent to you with this, but Allah has sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And they say, 'What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?'﴾ and ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others: will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]," meaning: I made some of you a trial for others so that you would be patient; and had I wished, I would have made the world available to My messengers, and they would not oppose Me, I would have done so.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khaythamah, who said: "It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If you wish, we will give you from the treasures of the earth and its keys what has not been given to any prophet before you, nor will we give it to anyone after you, and that will not diminish from what you have with Allah anything; and if you wish, we will gather it for you in the Hereafter.' He said: 'Gather it for me in the Hereafter.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through Khalid ibn Duraik from a man among the Companions, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says about me what I did not say, or claims to belong to other than his parents, or claims affiliation to other than his patrons, let him take his seat in the Fire between the two eyes of Hell." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, does Hell have two eyes?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard Allah say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾?"

Adam ibn Abi Iyas in his tafsir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾ that he said: "From a distance of a hundred years. That is when Hell is brought, led by seventy thousand halters, each halter pulled by seventy thousand angels. If it were left, it would reach every righteous and wicked person. ﴿They hear from it a raging and roaring﴾; it breathes one breath after which no drop of tears remains without appearing, then it breathes a second time, and hearts are torn from their places and hearts reach the throats."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Yahya ibn Usayd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Allah's words: ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place therein, bound together﴾, and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will be forced into the Fire as a peg is forced into a wall."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿They will cry out there for destruction﴾ that he said: "Woe," and concerning ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction﴾, that he said: "Do not call out today for one woe."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth [narrated it].

Al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to be clothed in his garment of Fire is Iblis. He places it upon his brows and drags it behind him, and his offspring after him, crying out, 'Woe to me!' and they say, 'Woe to them!' until he stands before the people and says, 'Woe to me!' and they say, 'Woe to them!' Then it is said to them: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾"

The chain of Ahmad is thus: "ʿAffan narrated to us from Humayd ibn Salamah from ʿAli ibn Zayd from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)..." and so he mentioned it.

Regarding ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an there is a well-known discussion.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿A promise binding on your Lord, one to be requested﴾ that he said: "Ask of what I promised you, and you will be given it."

The qasr is a house of stone, because its occupant is shut off from being reached; it was said to be a house of clay, and houses of wool and hair.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from rebuking them with what He related of their speech, which does not proceed from the intelligent.

﴿Nay, but they deny the Hour﴾ meaning: nay, they came with something more astonishing than all of that, namely their denial of the Hour. For this reason they do not benefit from the proofs, nor do they reflect upon them. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He has prepared for those who deny the Hour, saying: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾, meaning a fire kindled and blazing. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: nay, they deny the Hour, while the state is that "We have prepared." Abu Muslim said: "a'tadna" means: We made it ready and prepared for them.

﴿When it sees them from a far place, they will hear its raging and roaring.﴾ This conditional clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "a blaze," because it is feminine in meaning as fire. It was said: the meaning of "when it sees them" is: when it appears to them and becomes visible to the viewer at a distance. It was said: the meaning is: when its keepers see them. It was said: the seeing from it is real, and likewise the raging and roaring; there is no barrier to Allah, glory be to Him, making it perceive in this way.

The meaning of "from a far place" is that it sees them while it is far from them; it was said that between it and them is a distance of five hundred years. The meaning of raging is that it has a sound indicating rage against the disbelievers, or that its boiling produces a sound resembling the sound of one who is enraged. Zafir (roaring) is the sound heard from the inside of the chest.

Al-Zajjaj said: what is meant is the hearing of that which indicates anger, namely the sound; that is, they heard from it a sound resembling the sound of one enraged.

Qutrub said: he meant "they knew its rage and heard its roaring," as the poet said:
"Girding on a sword and a spear"
meaning: and carrying a spear. It was said: the meaning is: they heard in it rage and roaring for the tormented, as He said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ [Hud: 106]. The two prepositions (fi and li) are close in meaning; you say: "do this in Allah" and "for Allah."

﴿And when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, bound together﴾ The place is described as narrow to indicate the increase of severity and the utmost of affliction upon them. The accusative of "bound together" (muqarranin) is a circumstantial state: when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, while their hands are bound to their necks with chains, shackled with iron. It was said: "bound" means tied at the wrists. It was said: they were bound together with the devils, meaning each one of them was bound to his devil. The discussion of the like of this has already been given in Surah Ibrahim.

﴿They will call out there for destruction﴾, i.e., in that narrow place, "thubur," meaning ruin. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "we were ruined with ruin." It was said: it is accusative as an object of purpose, and the meaning is that they wish for ruin there and call out for it because of the affliction that has befallen them.

Then they are answered with His saying: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾ That is, this statement is said to them, and the one saying it to them is the angels, meaning: give up calling for a single destruction, for what you are in of ruin is greater and more severe than that. Thus said al-Zajjaj. ﴿But call out for many destructions﴾: "thubur" is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many, therefore it is not made plural. Similar is: "I struck him a great blow" and "he sat a long sitting." The multiplicity here is according to the multiplicity of the calls connected to it, not according to its multiplicity in itself, for it is one thing. The meaning: do not call down ruin upon yourselves once, but call for it in many supplications, for what you are in of punishment is more severe than that, because of its long duration and its endlessness. It was said: this is an illustration and depiction of their condition by the condition of one to whom that is said without any speech actually being spoken. It was said: the meaning is that you have fallen into what your ruin is not single in, but is many, because the punishment has kinds. The more preferable view is that what is meant by this answer to them is to indicate the eternity of their punishment and to despair them of attaining the destruction they wish for, which would deliver them from what they are in.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, rebuked them with a severe rebuke through the tongue of His Messenger, saying: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the God-fearing?"﴾ The indication with His saying "that" is to the blaze characterised by those great attributes; that is: is that blaze better, or the Garden of Eternity? In the attribution of "the Garden" to "eternity" is an indication of the permanence of its bliss and the non-cessation of it. The meaning of "which has been promised to the God-fearing" is: which was promised to the God-fearing. The use of the word "better" here, though there is no good at all in the Fire, is because the Arabs do say this; among it is what Sibawayh related from them, that they say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" It was also said: this is not of the category of comparison, but is like your saying: "he has good."

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good view, as the poet said:
"Would you satirise him, when you are not his equal? So your evil and your good are both a ransom."

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿It is for them a reward and a destination﴾, meaning: that Garden is for the God-fearing a reward for their deeds and a destination to which they arrive.

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, meaning: whatever they wish of bliss and kinds of delights, as in His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31]. The accusative of "abiding" is a circumstantial state, and the reality of the meaning of eternity has already been established. ﴿It has been upon your Lord a promise to be asked for﴾, meaning: what they wish was a promise. It was said: eternity was the promise. It was said: the promise indicated by His saying "were promised to the God-fearing." The meaning of "a promise to be asked for" is: a promise that is established, to be requested and sought, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]. It was said: the angels ask the Garden for them, as in His saying: ﴿And admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them﴾. It was said: what is meant is an obligatory promise even if it is not asked for.

(p-1035) Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Zamʿah ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-ʿAs ibn Wail, Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj gathered together. Some of them said to others: "Send to Muhammad, speak with him and dispute with him, so that you may be excused from him." So they sent to him: "The nobles of your people have gathered for you so that they may speak with you." He said: "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them, and they said: 'O Muhammad, we sent for you so that we might give you an excuse [to stop]. If you have only brought this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you some of our wealth; and if you seek nobility, we will make you our lord; and if you desire kingship, we will make you king.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What I have is not what you say. I have not brought you this seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah has sent me to you as a messenger, has revealed to me a Book, and has commanded me to be for you a bringer of good news and a warner. So I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and given you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter; and if you reject it from me, I will be patient over the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you.'

They said: 'O Muhammad, if you will not accept anything from us of what we have offered you,' or they said: 'If you will not do this, then ask for yourself and ask your Lord to send an angel with you to confirm what you say and to answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to make for you gardens and palaces of gold and silver that will make you independent of what we see you seeking, for you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may recognize your merit and rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'I will not do that. I am not one who asks his Lord for this, and I was not sent to you with this, but Allah has sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And they say, 'What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?'﴾ and ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others: will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]," meaning: I made some of you a trial for others so that you would be patient; and had I wished, I would have made the world available to My messengers, and they would not oppose Me, I would have done so.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khaythamah, who said: "It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If you wish, we will give you from the treasures of the earth and its keys what has not been given to any prophet before you, nor will we give it to anyone after you, and that will not diminish from what you have with Allah anything; and if you wish, we will gather it for you in the Hereafter.' He said: 'Gather it for me in the Hereafter.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through Khalid ibn Duraik from a man among the Companions, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says about me what I did not say, or claims to belong to other than his parents, or claims affiliation to other than his patrons, let him take his seat in the Fire between the two eyes of Hell." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, does Hell have two eyes?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard Allah say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾?"

Adam ibn Abi Iyas in his tafsir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾ that he said: "From a distance of a hundred years. That is when Hell is brought, led by seventy thousand halters, each halter pulled by seventy thousand angels. If it were left, it would reach every righteous and wicked person. ﴿They hear from it a raging and roaring﴾; it breathes one breath after which no drop of tears remains without appearing, then it breathes a second time, and hearts are torn from their places and hearts reach the throats."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Yahya ibn Usayd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Allah's words: ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place therein, bound together﴾, and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will be forced into the Fire as a peg is forced into a wall."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿They will cry out there for destruction﴾ that he said: "Woe," and concerning ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction﴾, that he said: "Do not call out today for one woe."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth [narrated it].

Al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to be clothed in his garment of Fire is Iblis. He places it upon his brows and drags it behind him, and his offspring after him, crying out, 'Woe to me!' and they say, 'Woe to them!' until he stands before the people and says, 'Woe to me!' and they say, 'Woe to them!' Then it is said to them: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾"

The chain of Ahmad is thus: "ʿAffan narrated to us from Humayd ibn Salamah from ʿAli ibn Zayd from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)..." and so he mentioned it.

Regarding ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an there is a well-known discussion.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿A promise binding on your Lord, one to be requested﴾ that he said: "Ask of what I promised you, and you will be given it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 7–16 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had finished mentioning what they criticised the Qur'an for, He mentioned what they criticised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for, and said: ﴿And they say, "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ In this indication (the demonstrative "this") there is a belittling of the one being pointed at, who is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They called him "Messenger" in mockery and derision. ﴿He eats food and walks in the markets﴾ meaning: what is the matter with him that he eats food as we eat, and moves about in the markets seeking a livelihood as we do? They claimed that he ought to have been an angel, free of need for food and earning.

Here, ma (what) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the interrogation is for disapproval (istinkar). Alternatively, ma is the predicate of the subject, "this Messenger." The clause "he eats" (ya'kulu) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning of the statement is completed by it, as in His saying: ﴿So what is the matter with them, turning away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. The disapproval is directed at the cause while the effect is established, namely eating and walking, but they deemed that effect unlikely because its cause was absent in their view, in mockery and derision.

The meaning: if what he claims of prophethood is true, then what is the matter with him that his condition does not differ from ours? ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾ They asked that the Prophet (ﷺ) be accompanied by an angel who would support and assist him. They descended from the proposal that the Messenger (ﷺ) be an angel free of eating and earning, to the proposal that an angel be with him to confirm him and bear witness to his messengership.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read fa-yakuna with the accusative, as it is the answer to the exhortation (tahdid). It was also read as fa-yakunu with the nominative, as coordinated with unzila; coordinating it with the past tense is permissible because what is meant by it is the future.

﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾ is coordinated with unzila, and it is not permissible to coordinate it with fa-yakuna. The meaning: or why is a treasure not thrown down to him? They descended from the level of an angel's descent with him, to the proposal that a treasure be with him, thrown down to him from the sky so that he would be free of seeking provision. ﴿Or he have a garden from which he may eat﴾ The majority read takun with the feminine ta'; al-A'mash and Qatadah read yakun with the masculine ya', because the feminine gender of "garden" (jannah) is not real. Hamzah, Ali and Khalaf read na'kulu with the nun; the rest read ya'kulu with the ya', meaning: a garden from whose fruits we eat, or he alone eats from it, so that he would have a distinction over us by his eating from his own garden.

Al-Nahhas said: both readings are good, though the reading with the ya' is clearer, because the Prophet (ﷺ) alone was previously mentioned, so the return of the pronoun to him is evident.

﴿And the wrongdoers say, "You follow nothing but a man bewitched."﴾ What is meant by "the wrongdoers" here are those who made the earlier statements. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun along with the description of wrongdoing in order to record this against them. That is: you follow only a man whose mind is overcome by magic. It was said: "dha sihr" means one who has a windpipe (ri'ah), i.e., a human being who has a windpipe, not an angel. The explanation of the like of this has already been given in (the commentary on) Subhan.

﴿Look how they strike for you the parables﴾ so that they might thereby reach your denial. The "parables" (amthal) are rare sayings and strange proposals; these are what they mentioned here. They have strayed from the right course, so they find no way to it and have reached nothing of it. Rather, they came with these false statements, which would not proceed from even the least intelligent of the sensible and the least discerning. For this reason He said: ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾, meaning they find no path among the paths to discredit the prophethood of this Prophet.

﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ meaning: abundant is the good of Him who, if He wills, will give you in this world, in advance, good better than that which they proposed.

Then He explained the good, saying: ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, so "gardens" is a substitute (badal) for "good." ﴿And will give you palaces﴾ is coordinated with the position of "will give" (ja'ala), which is the jussive, and the majority read with the jussive. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read yaj'alu with the nominative, as a resumptive clause (isti'naf). It is established in the science of i'rab that when the conditional verb is in the past tense, its answer may be jussive or nominative, so ja'ala here may be in a jussive or nominative position, and what is coordinated with it may be jussive or nominative. It was also read with the accusative. It was read with the assimilation of the lam of laka into the lam of yaj'al because of the meeting of two identical letters, and read without assimilation because the two words are separate. The qasr is a house of stone, because its occupant is shut off from being reached; it was said to be a house of clay, and houses of wool and hair.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from rebuking them with what He related of their speech, which does not proceed from the intelligent.

﴿Nay, but they deny the Hour﴾ meaning: nay, they came with something more astonishing than all of that, namely their denial of the Hour. For this reason they do not benefit from the proofs, nor do they reflect upon them. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He has prepared for those who deny the Hour, saying: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾, meaning a fire kindled and blazing. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: nay, they deny the Hour, while the state is that "We have prepared." Abu Muslim said: "a'tadna" means: We made it ready and prepared for them.

﴿When it sees them from a far place, they will hear its raging and roaring.﴾ This conditional clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "a blaze," because it is feminine in meaning as fire. It was said: the meaning of "when it sees them" is: when it appears to them and becomes visible to the viewer at a distance. It was said: the meaning is: when its keepers see them. It was said: the seeing from it is real, and likewise the raging and roaring; there is no barrier to Allah, glory be to Him, making it perceive in this way.

The meaning of "from a far place" is that it sees them while it is far from them; it was said that between it and them is a distance of five hundred years. The meaning of raging is that it has a sound indicating rage against the disbelievers, or that its boiling produces a sound resembling the sound of one who is enraged. Zafir (roaring) is the sound heard from the inside of the chest.

Al-Zajjaj said: what is meant is the hearing of that which indicates anger, namely the sound; that is, they heard from it a sound resembling the sound of one enraged.

Qutrub said: he meant "they knew its rage and heard its roaring," as the poet said:
"Girding on a sword and a spear"
meaning: and carrying a spear. It was said: the meaning is: they heard in it rage and roaring for the tormented, as He said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ [Hud: 106]. The two prepositions (fi and li) are close in meaning; you say: "do this in Allah" and "for Allah."

﴿And when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, bound together﴾ The place is described as narrow to indicate the increase of severity and the utmost of affliction upon them. The accusative of "bound together" (muqarranin) is a circumstantial state: when they are thrown into a narrow place of it, while their hands are bound to their necks with chains, shackled with iron. It was said: "bound" means tied at the wrists. It was said: they were bound together with the devils, meaning each one of them was bound to his devil. The discussion of the like of this has already been given in Surah Ibrahim.

﴿They will call out there for destruction﴾, i.e., in that narrow place, "thubur," meaning ruin. Al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "we were ruined with ruin." It was said: it is accusative as an object of purpose, and the meaning is that they wish for ruin there and call out for it because of the affliction that has befallen them.

Then they are answered with His saying: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾ That is, this statement is said to them, and the one saying it to them is the angels, meaning: give up calling for a single destruction, for what you are in of ruin is greater and more severe than that. Thus said al-Zajjaj. ﴿But call out for many destructions﴾: "thubur" is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many, therefore it is not made plural. Similar is: "I struck him a great blow" and "he sat a long sitting." The multiplicity here is according to the multiplicity of the calls connected to it, not according to its multiplicity in itself, for it is one thing. The meaning: do not call down ruin upon yourselves once, but call for it in many supplications, for what you are in of punishment is more severe than that, because of its long duration and its endlessness. It was said: this is an illustration and depiction of their condition by the condition of one to whom that is said without any speech actually being spoken. It was said: the meaning is that you have fallen into what your ruin is not single in, but is many, because the punishment has kinds. The more preferable view is that what is meant by this answer to them is to indicate the eternity of their punishment and to despair them of attaining the destruction they wish for, which would deliver them from what they are in.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, rebuked them with a severe rebuke through the tongue of His Messenger, saying: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the God-fearing?"﴾ The indication with His saying "that" is to the blaze characterised by those great attributes; that is: is that blaze better, or the Garden of Eternity? In the attribution of "the Garden" to "eternity" is an indication of the permanence of its bliss and the non-cessation of it. The meaning of "which has been promised to the God-fearing" is: which was promised to the God-fearing. The use of the word "better" here, though there is no good at all in the Fire, is because the Arabs do say this; among it is what Sibawayh related from them, that they say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" It was also said: this is not of the category of comparison, but is like your saying: "he has good."

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good view, as the poet said:
"Would you satirise him, when you are not his equal? So your evil and your good are both a ransom."

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿It is for them a reward and a destination﴾, meaning: that Garden is for the God-fearing a reward for their deeds and a destination to which they arrive.

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, meaning: whatever they wish of bliss and kinds of delights, as in His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31]. The accusative of "abiding" is a circumstantial state, and the reality of the meaning of eternity has already been established. ﴿It has been upon your Lord a promise to be asked for﴾, meaning: what they wish was a promise. It was said: eternity was the promise. It was said: the promise indicated by His saying "were promised to the God-fearing." The meaning of "a promise to be asked for" is: a promise that is established, to be requested and sought, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]. It was said: the angels ask the Garden for them, as in His saying: ﴿And admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them﴾. It was said: what is meant is an obligatory promise even if it is not asked for.

(p-1035) Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Zamʿah ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-ʿAs ibn Wail, Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj gathered together. Some of them said to others: "Send to Muhammad, speak with him and dispute with him, so that you may be excused from him." So they sent to him: "The nobles of your people have gathered for you so that they may speak with you." He said: "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them, and they said: 'O Muhammad, we sent for you so that we might give you an excuse [to stop]. If you have only brought this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you some of our wealth; and if you seek nobility, we will make you our lord; and if you desire kingship, we will make you king.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What I have is not what you say. I have not brought you this seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah has sent me to you as a messenger, has revealed to me a Book, and has commanded me to be for you a bringer of good news and a warner. So I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and given you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter; and if you reject it from me, I will be patient over the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you.'

They said: 'O Muhammad, if you will not accept anything from us of what we have offered you,' or they said: 'If you will not do this, then ask for yourself and ask your Lord to send an angel with you to confirm what you say and to answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to make for you gardens and palaces of gold and silver that will make you independent of what we see you seeking, for you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may recognize your merit and rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'I will not do that. I am not one who asks his Lord for this, and I was not sent to you with this, but Allah has sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And they say, 'What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?'﴾ and ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others: will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]," meaning: I made some of you a trial for others so that you would be patient; and had I wished, I would have made the world available to My messengers, and they would not oppose Me, I would have done so.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khaythamah, who said: "It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If you wish, we will give you from the treasures of the earth and its keys what has not been given to any prophet before you, nor will we give it to anyone after you, and that will not diminish from what you have with Allah anything; and if you wish, we will gather it for you in the Hereafter.' He said: 'Gather it for me in the Hereafter.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through Khalid ibn Duraik from a man among the Companions, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says about me what I did not say, or claims to belong to other than his parents, or claims affiliation to other than his patrons, let him take his seat in the Fire between the two eyes of Hell."
