This is a phrase they used to say when meeting an enemy or when a calamity attacked, placing it in the position of seeking refuge. It is said to a man: "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies: "*ḥijran maḥjūran*," meaning: "Forbidden to you is to approach me."

It has also been said that this is the speech of the angels, meaning: they say to the disbelievers, "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that any of you enter Paradise." From this is the words of the poet:

*Ala aṣbaḥat Asmā'u ḥijran muḥarramā*
*wa aṣbaḥtu min adnā ḥumūmatihā ḥamā'*

Meaning: "Asma' has become utterly forbidden, and I have become, from the nearest of her kin, a protector." Another said:

*Ḥannat ilā al-nakhlati al-quṣwā fa qultu lahā*
*ḥijrun ḥarāmun illā tilka al-dahārīsu*

Sibawayh mentioned, in the chapter on verbal nouns in the accusative governed by verbs whose display is omitted, this expression and counted it among them. (p. 1038)

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ This is another threat. They used to do deeds that had the appearance of good: maintaining family ties, relieving the distressed, feeding the hungry, and the like. Nothing prevented their reward for these except the disbelief they were upon. Their state and deeds are therefore likened to the state of a people who opposed their ruler and disobeyed him, so he turned to what they had of goods and destroyed it, leaving nothing of it. Otherwise there is no "turning" (*qudūm*) here in the literal sense.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of *qadimna* is "we intended and aimed," as one says: "So-and-so turned to a matter" when he aimed at it or intended it. From it is the poet's saying:

*Wa qadima al-khawārijul-ḍallālu*
*ilā ʿibādi rabbihim faqālū*
*Inna dimā'akum lanā ḥalālu*

Meaning: "The misguided Kharijites turned toward the servants of their Lord and said: Indeed your blood is lawful for us."

It has also been said that it is the "coming" of the angels, which He reported about Himself, exalted is He. *Al-habā'* (dust motes) has the singular *habā'a*, and the plural *ahbā'*. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-habā'* is the dust that the wind raises, as if it were smoke. Al-Zajjaj said: it is what enters through a window together with the sunlight, resembling dust. Al-Azhari said the same. *Al-manthūr* is the scattered. The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) rendered their deeds void until they became like scattered dust. He did not suffice with likening their deeds to dust, but described it further as scattered and dispersed. It has also been said that *al-habā'* is the dry leaves of trees that the winds blow about; it has been said that it is spilled water; and it has been said that it is ashes. The first is what is established in the Arabic language and transmitted by those who know it.

Then He (glory be to Him) distinguished the state of the righteous from the state of the wicked, saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾ That is, they are more excellent in dwelling in Paradise, and better in a place of *qayla* (midday rest). *Mustaqarran* is in the accusative of specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Azhari said: *al-qaylūla* among the Arabs is resting at midday when the heat intensifies, even if there is no day with it. Al-Nahhas said: the Kufans permit the construction "honey is sweeter than vinegar."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿and the Day He gathers them﴾ (the verse), that he said: "Jesus, Ezra and the angels." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿a people lost﴾ that he said: "Destroyed."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿and whoever of you does wrong﴾ that he said: "It is shirk." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj who said: "He associates partners." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾, that he said: the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) were in this condition: they ate food and walked in the markets. ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾: he said, "a trial." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from al-Hasan concerning ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ that he said: The poor man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me rich like so-and-so," the sick man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me healthy like so-and-so," and the blind man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me seeing like so-and-so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿and they have transgressed with great transgression﴾ that he said: "The severity of disbelief." Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ that he said: "The Day of Resurrection." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Atiyyah al-Awfi. Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "A protection and a seeking of refuge; the angels say it." In another wording he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that good news be on that day for anyone except the believers." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Atiyyah al-Awfi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that we give you good news with what we give good news to the pious." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatadah concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that both said: "It is a phrase the Arabs used to say; when a man was struck by hardship he would say: *ḥajran maḥjūran*, forbidden, utterly forbidden."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ that he said: "We will intend what they did of good, of those whose deeds are not accepted in this world." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His words ﴿scattered dust﴾ that he said: "*al-habā'* is the ray of sunlight that comes out of a window." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*al-habā'* is what flies off from fire when it blazes; sparks fly from it, and when it falls, it is nothing." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him: "It is what the wind blows away and scatters." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "It is spilled water."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him concerning ﴿better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest﴾ that he said: "In the upper chambers of Paradise." Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The day of Resurrection will not end until these and those take their midday rest." Then he recited: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾

**The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied as "and mention" (wa-dhkur). The linking of the reminder to "the Day," although the intended meaning is what occurs on it, is for emphasis and affirmation, as has passed many times.

Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Duri read ﴿yahshuruhum﴾ with the yā' (third person). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it because of the earlier words ﴿was upon your Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 16]. (p-1036) The rest read it with the nūn (first person plural), in exaltation (of Allah). Al-A'raj alone read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ with a kasra on the shīn throughout the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, because ﴿yafil﴾ with a kasra on the 'ayn in the transitive verb is more analogical than ﴿yaful﴾ with a ḍamma." Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying that the ḍamma and the kasra are equal, except that when one of them becomes well known it is followed.

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is coordinated with the object of ﴿nahshur﴾. The non-rational (ghayr al-'uqalā') forms, such as idols and images and the like, were given precedence over the rational beings, such as the angels, the jinn, and the Messiah. This is to indicate that they all share in being unfit to be gods, or because those who worship what has no intellect are more numerous than those who worship rational beings among them, so the non-rational form was given precedence in consideration of the number of those who worship it.

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: the intended meaning is the angels, mankind, the jinn, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, as evidenced by their address and their reply later on.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning is only the idols. Even though they do not hear or speak, Allah, glory be to Him, will make them on the Day of Resurrection hearing and speaking. ﴿Then He will say: "Did you lead astray these servants of Mine, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Kathir, and Hafs read ﴿fa-naqūlu﴾ with the nūn. The rest read it with the yā'. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the yā' reading, as he preferred it in ﴿yahshuruhum﴾, and so did Abu Hatim.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿a-antum aḍlaltum﴾ is for reproach and rebuke.

The meaning is: Was their straying due to you and your calling them to worship you? Or did they stray from the path of truth by themselves, through not reflecting on what leads to the truth and not contemplating what leads to the right course?

The clause ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You"﴾ is a new clause (mustaʼnafa), an answer to an implied question. The meaning of "Glory be to You" (subḥānaka) is an expression of wonder at what was said to them, because they are angels or infallible prophets, or lifeless things that do not understand; that is, "exalting You (above such things)." ﴿It was not fitting for us to take any protectors besides You﴾: that is, it was not valid or proper for us to take protectors besides You and then worship them. So how could we call Your servants to worship us, when we ourselves worship none but You? The word walī (protector) is used for the follower as it is used for the one followed. This is the meaning of the verse according to the reading of the majority, ﴿nattakhidh﴾ in the active voice.

Al-Ḥasan and Abu Ja'far read ﴿nuttakhadh﴾ in the passive voice, meaning: it was not fitting for us that the polytheists take us as protectors besides You.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: this reading is not permissible; even if it were sound, the second ﴿min﴾ would have been dropped.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this reading is not permissible, because Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned ﴿min﴾ twice, and if it were as he read, He would have said: "that we take protectors besides You." It was also said that the second ﴿min﴾ is superfluous.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related from them that after this answer they mentioned the reason the polytheists abandoned faith. He said: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance.﴾ In this there is an indication that they themselves were the ones who strayed from the path, and that others did not lead them astray. The meaning is: "We did not lead them astray, but You, O Lord, gave them and their fathers enjoyment through blessings, widened their provision for them, and prolonged their lives for them, until they became heedless of Your remembrance, forgot Your admonition, and forgot to reflect upon Your Book, to consider the wonders of Your creation and the marvels of Your creatures."

Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari read ﴿yunbagha﴾ in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: Sibawayh claimed that it is a dialect.

It was also said: the intended meaning of "forgetting the remembrance" here is abandoning gratitude.

﴿And they were a people doomed﴾: that is, those who associated others with You and worshipped other than You, in Your eternal decree, were a people doomed (būr), that is, destroyed. It is derived from al-bawār, which is destruction. It is said: "a man is bā'ir and a people are būr," the same for singular and plural, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) applied to the few and the many. It is also permissible that it be the plural of bā'ir. It was also said: al-bawār is corruption. It is said: "his merchandise went bad" (bārat), that is, it spoiled, and "a bā'ir matter" means a corrupt matter, and this is the dialect of the Azd.

It was also said: the meaning is "there is no good in them," derived from the barrenness of the land (bawār al-arḍ), which is its being left idle from crops, so there is no good in it. It was also said: al-bawār is slump, as in "the commodity went slack" (bārat al-silʿa) when it became unsold.

﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: Allah said, when the worshipped ones disassociate themselves, addressing the polytheists who worshipped other than Allah: "So they have indeed denied you," that is, the worshipped ones have denied you in what you say, that is, in your saying that they are gods. ﴿So they cannot avert﴾: that is, the gods cannot avert (ṣarf), that is, repel the punishment from you by any means. It was also said: "by a stratagem" (ḥīla). ﴿Nor help﴾: that is, nor can they help you. It was also said: the meaning is: these disbelievers, when the worshipped ones denied them, cannot avert the punishment with which Allah punishes them, nor (can they obtain) help from Allah. This interpretation is sound according to the reading of whoever read ﴿tastaṭīʿūn﴾ with the yā' of the second person, which is the reading of Hafs; the rest read it with the yā' of the third person.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: "So they have indeed denied you, O believers, these disbelievers, in what Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) brought." On this view, the meaning of "in what you say" is "what you say of the truth."

Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning is: they cannot avert from you any turning away from the truth to which Allah has guided you, nor (can they help) themselves against what descends upon them of punishment for their denial of you.

The majority read ﴿mā taqūlūn﴾ with the second-person tā'. Al-Farra' reported that it is permissible to read ﴿fa-qad kadhabūkum﴾ with the verb unstressed (kadhabūkum), "in what they say" (bi-mā yaqūlūn), meaning: they denied you in their saying. Likewise Mujahid and al-Bazzi read with the third-person yā'.

﴿And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great punishment.﴾ This is a threat to every wrongdoer, and those who are in the context fall under it first and foremost. The great punishment is the punishment of the Fire. It was also read ﴿yudhiqhu﴾ with the yā'. This verse and similar verses are restricted to the absence of repentance.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, returned to addressing His Messenger, clarifying the falsehood of what came before in their saying: "He eats food and walks in the markets." So He said: ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the clause that comes after ﴿illā﴾ is an attribute of a deleted noun, and the meaning is: "We did not send before you any one of the messengers except eating and walking," and the noun was deleted because ﴿of the messengers﴾ is evidence for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 164], meaning: "there is none of us but one (who has)." Al-Farra' said it has no place in the grammatical structure; it is only a relative clause (ṣila) for a deleted relative pronoun which is the object, and the estimated meaning is: "except (that) they," so the pronoun in "they" and what follows it refers to the estimated noun. A similar example is His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71], meaning: "except one who will come to it." Al-Kisa'i read in this way.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, because the relative "man" (man) cannot be deleted. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the estimated meaning is: "except while they," so the deleted element in his view is the waw.

The majority read ﴿illā innahum﴾ with a kasra on inna, because of the presence of the lām in its predicate, as established in the science of grammar, and this is agreed upon among them.

Al-Naḥḥas said: "However, 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad that he said: 'It is permissible with this inna to have a fatḥa even if the lām follows it,' and I think it is a mistake."

The majority read ﴿yamshūna﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā', a sukūn on the mīm, and a light shīn. 'Ali, Ibn 'Awf, and Ibn Mas'ud read it with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the mīm, and a ḍamma on the doubled shīn. It has the same meaning as the first reading. The poet said:

"I walk among the watering-places of the waters, and I guard against she-camels that are hard to handle and riding them."

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"From it the beasts of prey of the tribe remain subdued, and the sick-people do not walk in its valley."

﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others.﴾ This address is general to mankind. Allah, glory be to Him, has made some of His servants a trial for others. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, and it was said: the intended meaning of the first "some" is the disbelievers of the nations, and of the second "some" the messengers. The meaning of "trial" (fitna) is testing and affliction. The first is preferable, because some people are tested by others and afflicted by them. The sick person says: "Why was I not made like the healthy?" and so does everyone who has an affliction. The healthy person is tested by the sick, so he does not become impatient with him or belittle him. The rich is tested by the poor, so he consoles him. The poor is tested by the rich, so he envies him. Something similar to this is like it.

It was also said: the intended meaning of the verse is that when a nobleman wanted to accept Islam and saw a lowly man had accepted it before him, he was too proud and said: "I will not accept it after him, so that he will have precedence and superiority over me." So he remains in his disbelief. That is the testing of some of them by others. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

There is no basis for restricting the verse to this, for even if these were the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl), the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Then, after the report that Allah has made some a trial for others, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, and there is an ellipsis in the speech, the estimated meaning being "or will you not be patient?" That is: will you be patient with what you see of this severe condition and this great affliction?

It was said: the position of this interrogative sentence here is the position of His saying ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾ in His saying ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Then He promised those who are patient with His saying ﴿and your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, that is, Seeing of everyone who is patient and everyone who is not patient, so that He recompenses each of them with what they deserve.

It was also said: the meaning of "will you be patient?" is: "be patient," like His saying ﴿so will you then desist?﴾, that is, "desist."

﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us said﴾: this statement is among their doubts by which they cast doubt on prophethood. The clause is coordinated with ﴿And they said: "What is this messenger?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. That is: the polytheists who did not care about meeting Allah said, as in the saying of the poet:

"By your life, I do not hope, if I am a Muslim, on whatever side I fall in Allah's way."

That is, "I do not care." It was also said: the meaning is "they do not fear the meeting with their Lord," as in the saying of the poet:

"When the bee stings him, he does not hope for its sting, and it opposes him in the house of Nawb, the workers."

That is: he did not fear. This is the dialect of Tihama. Al-Farra' said: "hope" (rajā') was put in the place of "fear." It was also said: they do not aspire to it. And from it is the saying of the poet:

"Does a people who killed Husayn hope for the intercession of his grandfather on the Day of Reckoning?"

But carrying the word on its real meaning is preferable. The meaning is: they do not aspire to meet what We promised for obedience of reward. It is known that whoever does not hope for reward does not fear punishment.

﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us?﴾: that is, "why were they not sent down upon us, so that they would inform us that Muhammad is truthful?" Or "why were they not sent down upon us as messengers whom Allah sends?" ﴿Or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ face to face, so that He informs us that Muhammad is a messenger.

Then He (glory be to Him) answered their objection, saying: ﴿Indeed, they have grown arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾ That is, they concealed arrogance toward the truth and obstinacy in their hearts, as in His words: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain.﴾ *Utuww* means exceeding the limit in rebellion and reaching its furthest extent. Describing it as "greatness" is because the utterance of this shameful statement that they made is at the extreme of greatness and magnitude. They were not content with sending a human; they asked for angels to be sent to them. Rather, they went further, to the point of choosing between this and speaking with Allah (glory be to Him) and seeing Him in this world, without any interpreter (*turjuman*) between them and Him. These base people have reached a level in their own estimation that is too lowly, too meager and too vile to be counted among those who belong to it, or among those who are prepared for it. Likewise is the one who does not know his own worth and does not stop at his limit. Whoever his own self does not know the worth of, sees from others what he does not see.

The accusative of ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ is governed by a verb omitted in the sense: "and mention the Day they see the angels," a seeing that is not in the manner they asked for and not in the form they proposed, but in another manner, namely the Day of their appearance to them at death or at the gathering. It is also permissible that the accusative of this time expression is governed by what is indicated by His words: ﴿No good news that day for the criminals,﴾ meaning: they will be denied good news on the day they see, or no good news will exist for them in it. Thus Allah (glory be to Him) informs that the time at which they see the angels, which is the time of death or the Day of Resurrection, Allah has deprived them of good news.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The criminals in this place are those who committed disbelief in Allah." ﴿And they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier.﴾ That is, the disbelievers, upon seeing the angels, will say "*ḥijran maḥjūran*" (a barrier, a forbidding barrier). This is a phrase they used to say when meeting an enemy or when a calamity attacked, placing it in the position of seeking refuge. It is said to a man: "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies: "*ḥijran maḥjūran*," meaning: "Forbidden to you is to approach me."

It has also been said that this is the speech of the angels, meaning: they say to the disbelievers, "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that any of you enter Paradise." From this is the words of the poet:

*Ala aṣbaḥat Asmā'u ḥijran muḥarramā*
*wa aṣbaḥtu min adnā ḥumūmatihā ḥamā'*

Meaning: "Asma' has become utterly forbidden, and I have become, from the nearest of her kin, a protector." Another said:

*Ḥannat ilā al-nakhlati al-quṣwā fa qultu lahā*
*ḥijrun ḥarāmun illā tilka al-dahārīsu*

Sibawayh mentioned, in the chapter on verbal nouns in the accusative governed by verbs whose display is omitted, this expression and counted it among them. (p. 1038)

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ This is another threat. They used to do deeds that had the appearance of good: maintaining family ties, relieving the distressed, feeding the hungry, and the like. Nothing prevented their reward for these except the disbelief they were upon. Their state and deeds are therefore likened to the state of a people who opposed their ruler and disobeyed him, so he turned to what they had of goods and destroyed it, leaving nothing of it. Otherwise there is no "turning" (*qudūm*) here in the literal sense.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of *qadimna* is "we intended and aimed," as one says: "So-and-so turned to a matter" when he aimed at it or intended it. From it is the poet's saying:

*Wa qadima al-khawārijul-ḍallālu*
*ilā ʿibādi rabbihim faqālū*
*Inna dimā'akum lanā ḥalālu*

Meaning: "The misguided Kharijites turned toward the servants of their Lord and said: Indeed your blood is lawful for us."

It has also been said that it is the "coming" of the angels, which He reported about Himself, exalted is He. *Al-habā'* (dust motes) has the singular *habā'a*, and the plural *ahbā'*. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-habā'* is the dust that the wind raises, as if it were smoke. Al-Zajjaj said: it is what enters through a window together with the sunlight, resembling dust. Al-Azhari said the same. *Al-manthūr* is the scattered. The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) rendered their deeds void until they became like scattered dust. He did not suffice with likening their deeds to dust, but described it further as scattered and dispersed. It has also been said that *al-habā'* is the dry leaves of trees that the winds blow about; it has been said that it is spilled water; and it has been said that it is ashes. The first is what is established in the Arabic language and transmitted by those who know it.

In another wording he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that good news be on that day for anyone except the believers." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Atiyyah al-Awfi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that we give you good news with what we give good news to the pious." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatadah concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that both said: "It is a phrase the Arabs used to say; when a man was struck by hardship he would say: *ḥajran maḥjūran*, forbidden, utterly forbidden."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ that he said: "We will intend what they did of good, of those whose deeds are not accepted in this world." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His words ﴿scattered dust﴾ that he said: "*al-habā'* is the ray of sunlight that comes out of a window." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*al-habā'* is what flies off from fire when it blazes; sparks fly from it, and when it falls, it is nothing." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him: "It is what the wind blows away and scatters." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "It is spilled water."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him concerning ﴿better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest﴾ that he said: "In the upper chambers of Paradise." Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The day of Resurrection will not end until these and those take their midday rest." Then he recited: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾

**The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied as "and mention" (wa-dhkur). The linking of the reminder to "the Day," although the intended meaning is what occurs on it, is for emphasis and affirmation, as has passed many times.

Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Duri read ﴿yahshuruhum﴾ with the yā' (third person). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it because of the earlier words ﴿was upon your Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 16]. (p-1036) The rest read it with the nūn (first person plural), in exaltation (of Allah). Al-A'raj alone read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ with a kasra on the shīn throughout the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, because ﴿yafil﴾ with a kasra on the 'ayn in the transitive verb is more analogical than ﴿yaful﴾ with a ḍamma." Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying that the ḍamma and the kasra are equal, except that when one of them becomes well known it is followed.

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is coordinated with the object of ﴿nahshur﴾. The non-rational (ghayr al-'uqalā') forms, such as idols and images and the like, were given precedence over the rational beings, such as the angels, the jinn, and the Messiah. This is to indicate that they all share in being unfit to be gods, or because those who worship what has no intellect are more numerous than those who worship rational beings among them, so the non-rational form was given precedence in consideration of the number of those who worship it.

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: the intended meaning is the angels, mankind, the jinn, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, as evidenced by their address and their reply later on.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning is only the idols. Even though they do not hear or speak, Allah, glory be to Him, will make them on the Day of Resurrection hearing and speaking. ﴿Then He will say: "Did you lead astray these servants of Mine, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Kathir, and Hafs read ﴿fa-naqūlu﴾ with the nūn. The rest read it with the yā'. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the yā' reading, as he preferred it in ﴿yahshuruhum﴾, and so did Abu Hatim.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿a-antum aḍlaltum﴾ is for reproach and rebuke.

The meaning is: Was their straying due to you and your calling them to worship you? Or did they stray from the path of truth by themselves, through not reflecting on what leads to the truth and not contemplating what leads to the right course?

The clause ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You"﴾ is a new clause (mustaʼnafa), an answer to an implied question. The meaning of "Glory be to You" (subḥānaka) is an expression of wonder at what was said to them, because they are angels or infallible prophets, or lifeless things that do not understand; that is, "exalting You (above such things)." ﴿It was not fitting for us to take any protectors besides You﴾: that is, it was not valid or proper for us to take protectors besides You and then worship them. So how could we call Your servants to worship us, when we ourselves worship none but You? The word walī (protector) is used for the follower as it is used for the one followed. This is the meaning of the verse according to the reading of the majority, ﴿nattakhidh﴾ in the active voice.

Al-Ḥasan and Abu Ja'far read ﴿nuttakhadh﴾ in the passive voice, meaning: it was not fitting for us that the polytheists take us as protectors besides You.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: this reading is not permissible; even if it were sound, the second ﴿min﴾ would have been dropped.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this reading is not permissible, because Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned ﴿min﴾ twice, and if it were as he read, He would have said: "that we take protectors besides You." It was also said that the second ﴿min﴾ is superfluous.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related from them that after this answer they mentioned the reason the polytheists abandoned faith. He said: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance.﴾ In this there is an indication that they themselves were the ones who strayed from the path, and that others did not lead them astray. The meaning is: "We did not lead them astray, but You, O Lord, gave them and their fathers enjoyment through blessings, widened their provision for them, and prolonged their lives for them, until they became heedless of Your remembrance, forgot Your admonition, and forgot to reflect upon Your Book, to consider the wonders of Your creation and the marvels of Your creatures."

Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari read ﴿yunbagha﴾ in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: Sibawayh claimed that it is a dialect.

It was also said: the intended meaning of "forgetting the remembrance" here is abandoning gratitude.

﴿And they were a people doomed﴾: that is, those who associated others with You and worshipped other than You, in Your eternal decree, were a people doomed (būr), that is, destroyed. It is derived from al-bawār, which is destruction. It is said: "a man is bā'ir and a people are būr," the same for singular and plural, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) applied to the few and the many. It is also permissible that it be the plural of bā'ir. It was also said: al-bawār is corruption. It is said: "his merchandise went bad" (bārat), that is, it spoiled, and "a bā'ir matter" means a corrupt matter, and this is the dialect of the Azd.

It was also said: the meaning is "there is no good in them," derived from the barrenness of the land (bawār al-arḍ), which is its being left idle from crops, so there is no good in it. It was also said: al-bawār is slump, as in "the commodity went slack" (bārat al-silʿa) when it became unsold.

﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: Allah said, when the worshipped ones disassociate themselves, addressing the polytheists who worshipped other than Allah: "So they have indeed denied you," that is, the worshipped ones have denied you in what you say, that is, in your saying that they are gods. ﴿So they cannot avert﴾: that is, the gods cannot avert (ṣarf), that is, repel the punishment from you by any means. It was also said: "by a stratagem" (ḥīla). ﴿Nor help﴾: that is, nor can they help you. It was also said: the meaning is: these disbelievers, when the worshipped ones denied them, cannot avert the punishment with which Allah punishes them, nor (can they obtain) help from Allah. This interpretation is sound according to the reading of whoever read ﴿tastaṭīʿūn﴾ with the yā' of the second person, which is the reading of Hafs; the rest read it with the yā' of the third person.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: "So they have indeed denied you, O believers, these disbelievers, in what Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) brought." On this view, the meaning of "in what you say" is "what you say of the truth."

Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning is: they cannot avert from you any turning away from the truth to which Allah has guided you, nor (can they help) themselves against what descends upon them of punishment for their denial of you.

The majority read ﴿mā taqūlūn﴾ with the second-person tā'. Al-Farra' reported that it is permissible to read ﴿fa-qad kadhabūkum﴾ with the verb unstressed (kadhabūkum), "in what they say" (bi-mā yaqūlūn), meaning: they denied you in their saying. Likewise Mujahid and al-Bazzi read with the third-person yā'.

﴿And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great punishment.﴾ This is a threat to every wrongdoer, and those who are in the context fall under it first and foremost. The great punishment is the punishment of the Fire. It was also read ﴿yudhiqhu﴾ with the yā'. This verse and similar verses are restricted to the absence of repentance.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, returned to addressing His Messenger, clarifying the falsehood of what came before in their saying: "He eats food and walks in the markets." So He said: ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the clause that comes after ﴿illā﴾ is an attribute of a deleted noun, and the meaning is: "We did not send before you any one of the messengers except eating and walking," and the noun was deleted because ﴿of the messengers﴾ is evidence for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 164], meaning: "there is none of us but one (who has)." Al-Farra' said it has no place in the grammatical structure; it is only a relative clause (ṣila) for a deleted relative pronoun which is the object, and the estimated meaning is: "except (that) they," so the pronoun in "they" and what follows it refers to the estimated noun. A similar example is His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71], meaning: "except one who will come to it." Al-Kisa'i read in this way.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, because the relative "man" (man) cannot be deleted. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the estimated meaning is: "except while they," so the deleted element in his view is the waw.

The majority read ﴿illā innahum﴾ with a kasra on inna, because of the presence of the lām in its predicate, as established in the science of grammar, and this is agreed upon among them.

Al-Naḥḥas said: "However, 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad that he said: 'It is permissible with this inna to have a fatḥa even if the lām follows it,' and I think it is a mistake."

The majority read ﴿yamshūna﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā', a sukūn on the mīm, and a light shīn. 'Ali, Ibn 'Awf, and Ibn Mas'ud read it with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the mīm, and a ḍamma on the doubled shīn. It has the same meaning as the first reading. The poet said:

"I walk among the watering-places of the waters, and I guard against she-camels that are hard to handle and riding them."

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"From it the beasts of prey of the tribe remain subdued, and the sick-people do not walk in its valley."

﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others.﴾ This address is general to mankind. Allah, glory be to Him, has made some of His servants a trial for others. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, and it was said: the intended meaning of the first "some" is the disbelievers of the nations, and of the second "some" the messengers. The meaning of "trial" (fitna) is testing and affliction. The first is preferable, because some people are tested by others and afflicted by them. The sick person says: "Why was I not made like the healthy?" and so does everyone who has an affliction. The healthy person is tested by the sick, so he does not become impatient with him or belittle him. The rich is tested by the poor, so he consoles him. The poor is tested by the rich, so he envies him. Something similar to this is like it.

It was also said: the intended meaning of the verse is that when a nobleman wanted to accept Islam and saw a lowly man had accepted it before him, he was too proud and said: "I will not accept it after him, so that he will have precedence and superiority over me." So he remains in his disbelief. That is the testing of some of them by others. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

There is no basis for restricting the verse to this, for even if these were the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl), the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Then, after the report that Allah has made some a trial for others, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, and there is an ellipsis in the speech, the estimated meaning being "or will you not be patient?" That is: will you be patient with what you see of this severe condition and this great affliction?

It was said: the position of this interrogative sentence here is the position of His saying ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾ in His saying ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Then He promised those who are patient with His saying ﴿and your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, that is, Seeing of everyone who is patient and everyone who is not patient, so that He recompenses each of them with what they deserve.

It was also said: the meaning of "will you be patient?" is: "be patient," like His saying ﴿so will you then desist?﴾, that is, "desist."

﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us said﴾: this statement is among their doubts by which they cast doubt on prophethood. The clause is coordinated with ﴿And they said: "What is this messenger?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. That is: the polytheists who did not care about meeting Allah said, as in the saying of the poet:

"By your life, I do not hope, if I am a Muslim, on whatever side I fall in Allah's way."

That is, "I do not care." It was also said: the meaning is "they do not fear the meeting with their Lord," as in the saying of the poet:

"When the bee stings him, he does not hope for its sting, and it opposes him in the house of Nawb, the workers."

That is: he did not fear. This is the dialect of Tihama. Al-Farra' said: "hope" (rajā') was put in the place of "fear." It was also said: they do not aspire to it. And from it is the saying of the poet:

"Does a people who killed Husayn hope for the intercession of his grandfather on the Day of Reckoning?"

But carrying the word on its real meaning is preferable. The meaning is: they do not aspire to meet what We promised for obedience of reward. It is known that whoever does not hope for reward does not fear punishment.

﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us?﴾: that is, "why were they not sent down upon us, so that they would inform us that Muhammad is truthful?" Or "why were they not sent down upon us as messengers whom Allah sends?" ﴿Or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ face to face, so that He informs us that Muhammad is a messenger.

Then He (glory be to Him) answered their objection, saying: ﴿Indeed, they have grown arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾ That is, they concealed arrogance toward the truth and obstinacy in their hearts, as in His words: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain.﴾ *Utuww* means exceeding the limit in rebellion and reaching its furthest extent. Describing it as "greatness" is because the utterance of this shameful statement that they made is at the extreme of greatness and magnitude. They were not content with sending a human; they asked for angels to be sent to them. Rather, they went further, to the point of choosing between this and speaking with Allah (glory be to Him) and seeing Him in this world, without any interpreter (*turjuman*) between them and Him. These base people have reached a level in their own estimation that is too lowly, too meager and too vile to be counted among those who belong to it, or among those who are prepared for it. Likewise is the one who does not know his own worth and does not stop at his limit. Whoever his own self does not know the worth of, sees from others what he does not see.

The accusative of ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ is governed by a verb omitted in the sense: "and mention the Day they see the angels," a seeing that is not in the manner they asked for and not in the form they proposed, but in another manner, namely the Day of their appearance to them at death or at the gathering. It is also permissible that the accusative of this time expression is governed by what is indicated by His words: ﴿No good news that day for the criminals,﴾ meaning: they will be denied good news on the day they see, or no good news will exist for them in it. Thus Allah (glory be to Him) informs that the time at which they see the angels, which is the time of death or the Day of Resurrection, Allah has deprived them of good news.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The criminals in this place are those who committed disbelief in Allah." ﴿And they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier.﴾ That is, the disbelievers, upon seeing the angels, will say "*ḥijran maḥjūran*" (a barrier, a forbidding barrier). This is a phrase they used to say when meeting an enemy or when a calamity attacked, placing it in the position of seeking refuge. It is said to a man: "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies: "*ḥijran maḥjūran*," meaning: "Forbidden to you is to approach me."

It has also been said that this is the speech of the angels, meaning: they say to the disbelievers, "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that any of you enter Paradise." From this is the words of the poet:

*Ala aṣbaḥat Asmā'u ḥijran muḥarramā*
*wa aṣbaḥtu min adnā ḥumūmatihā ḥamā'*

Meaning: "Asma' has become utterly forbidden, and I have become, from the nearest of her kin, a protector." Another said:

*Ḥannat ilā al-nakhlati al-quṣwā fa qultu lahā*
*ḥijrun ḥarāmun illā tilka al-dahārīsu*

Sibawayh mentioned, in the chapter on verbal nouns in the accusative governed by verbs whose display is omitted, this expression and counted it among them. (p. 1038)

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ This is another threat. They used to do deeds that had the appearance of good: maintaining family ties, relieving the distressed, feeding the hungry, and the like. Nothing prevented their reward for these except the disbelief they were upon. Their state and deeds are therefore likened to the state of a people who opposed their ruler and disobeyed him, so he turned to what they had of goods and destroyed it, leaving nothing of it. Otherwise there is no "turning" (*qudūm*) here in the literal sense.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of *qadimna* is "we intended and aimed," as one says: "So-and-so turned to a matter" when he aimed at it or intended it. From it is the poet's saying:

*Wa qadima al-khawārijul-ḍallālu*
*ilā ʿibādi rabbihim faqālū*
*Inna dimā'akum lanā ḥalālu*

Meaning: "The misguided Kharijites turned toward the servants of their Lord and said: Indeed your blood is lawful for us."

It has also been said that it is the "coming" of the angels, which He reported about Himself, exalted is He. *Al-habā'* (dust motes) has the singular *habā'a*, and the plural *ahbā'*. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-habā'* is the dust that the wind raises, as if it were smoke. Al-Zajjaj said: it is what enters through a window together with the sunlight, resembling dust. Al-Azhari said the same. *Al-manthūr* is the scattered. The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) rendered their deeds void until they became like scattered dust. He did not suffice with likening their deeds to dust, but described it further as scattered and dispersed. It has also been said that *al-habā'* is the dry leaves of trees that the winds blow about; it has been said that it is spilled water; and it has been said that it is ashes. The first is what is established in the Arabic language and transmitted by those who know it.

Then He (glory be to Him) distinguished the state of the righteous from the state of the wicked, saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾ That is, they are more excellent in dwelling in Paradise, and better in a place of *qayla* (midday rest). *Mustaqarran* is in the accusative of specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Azhari said: *al-qaylūla* among the Arabs is resting at midday when the heat intensifies, even if there is no day with it. Al-Nahhas said: the Kufans permit the construction "honey is sweeter than vinegar."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿and the Day He gathers them﴾ (the verse), that he said: "Jesus, Ezra and the angels." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿a people lost﴾ that he said: "Destroyed."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿and whoever of you does wrong﴾ that he said: "It is shirk." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj who said: "He associates partners." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾, that he said: the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) were in this condition: they ate food and walked in the markets. ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾: he said, "a trial." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from al-Hasan concerning ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ that he said: The poor man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me rich like so-and-so," the sick man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me healthy like so-and-so," and the blind man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me seeing like so-and-so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿and they have transgressed with great transgression﴾ that he said: "The severity of disbelief." Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ that he said: "The Day of Resurrection." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Atiyyah al-Awfi. Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "A protection and a seeking of refuge; the angels say it." In another wording he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that good news be on that day for anyone except the believers." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Atiyyah al-Awfi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that we give you good news with what we give good news to the pious." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatadah concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that both said: "It is a phrase the Arabs used to say; when a man was struck by hardship he would say: *ḥajran maḥjūran*, forbidden, utterly forbidden."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ that he said: "We will intend what they did of good, of those whose deeds are not accepted in this world." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His words ﴿scattered dust﴾ that he said: "*al-habā'* is the ray of sunlight that comes out of a window." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*al-habā'* is what flies off from fire when it blazes; sparks fly from it, and when it falls, it is nothing." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him: "It is what the wind blows away and scatters." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "It is spilled water."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him concerning ﴿better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest﴾ that he said: "In the upper chambers of Paradise." Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The day of Resurrection will not end until these and those take their midday rest." Then he recited: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is coordinated with the object of ﴿nahshur﴾. The non-rational (ghayr al-'uqalā') forms, such as idols and images and the like, were given precedence over the rational beings, such as the angels, the jinn, and the Messiah. This is to indicate that they all share in being unfit to be gods, or because those who worship what has no intellect are more numerous than those who worship rational beings among them, so the non-rational form was given precedence in consideration of the number of those who worship it.

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: the intended meaning is the angels, mankind, the jinn, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, as evidenced by their address and their reply later on.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning is only the idols. Even though they do not hear or speak, Allah, glory be to Him, will make them on the Day of Resurrection hearing and speaking. ﴿Then He will say: "Did you lead astray these servants of Mine, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Kathir, and Hafs read ﴿fa-naqūlu﴾ with the nūn. The rest read it with the yā'. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the yā' reading, as he preferred it in ﴿yahshuruhum﴾, and so did Abu Hatim.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿a-antum aḍlaltum﴾ is for reproach and rebuke.

The meaning is: Was their straying due to you and your calling them to worship you? Or did they stray from the path of truth by themselves, through not reflecting on what leads to the truth and not contemplating what leads to the right course?

The clause ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You"﴾ is a new clause (mustaʼnafa), an answer to an implied question. The meaning of "Glory be to You" (subḥānaka) is an expression of wonder at what was said to them, because they are angels or infallible prophets, or lifeless things that do not understand; that is, "exalting You (above such things)." ﴿It was not fitting for us to take any protectors besides You﴾: that is, it was not valid or proper for us to take protectors besides You and then worship them. So how could we call Your servants to worship us, when we ourselves worship none but You? The word walī (protector) is used for the follower as it is used for the one followed. This is the meaning of the verse according to the reading of the majority, ﴿nattakhidh﴾ in the active voice.

Al-Ḥasan and Abu Ja'far read ﴿nuttakhadh﴾ in the passive voice, meaning: it was not fitting for us that the polytheists take us as protectors besides You.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: this reading is not permissible; even if it were sound, the second ﴿min﴾ would have been dropped.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this reading is not permissible, because Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned ﴿min﴾ twice, and if it were as he read, He would have said: "that we take protectors besides You." It was also said that the second ﴿min﴾ is superfluous.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related from them that after this answer they mentioned the reason the polytheists abandoned faith. He said: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance.﴾ In this there is an indication that they themselves were the ones who strayed from the path, and that others did not lead them astray. The meaning is: "We did not lead them astray, but You, O Lord, gave them and their fathers enjoyment through blessings, widened their provision for them, and prolonged their lives for them, until they became heedless of Your remembrance, forgot Your admonition, and forgot to reflect upon Your Book, to consider the wonders of Your creation and the marvels of Your creatures."

Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari read ﴿yunbagha﴾ in the passive voice. Ibn Khalawayh said: Sibawayh claimed that it is a dialect.

It was also said: the intended meaning of "forgetting the remembrance" here is abandoning gratitude.

﴿And they were a people doomed﴾: that is, those who associated others with You and worshipped other than You, in Your eternal decree, were a people doomed (būr), that is, destroyed. It is derived from al-bawār, which is destruction. It is said: "a man is bā'ir and a people are būr," the same for singular and plural, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) applied to the few and the many. It is also permissible that it be the plural of bā'ir. It was also said: al-bawār is corruption. It is said: "his merchandise went bad" (bārat), that is, it spoiled, and "a bā'ir matter" means a corrupt matter, and this is the dialect of the Azd.

It was also said: the meaning is "there is no good in them," derived from the barrenness of the land (bawār al-arḍ), which is its being left idle from crops, so there is no good in it. It was also said: al-bawār is slump, as in "the commodity went slack" (bārat al-silʿa) when it became unsold.

﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: Allah said, when the worshipped ones disassociate themselves, addressing the polytheists who worshipped other than Allah: "So they have indeed denied you," that is, the worshipped ones have denied you in what you say, that is, in your saying that they are gods. ﴿So they cannot avert﴾: that is, the gods cannot avert (ṣarf), that is, repel the punishment from you by any means. It was also said: "by a stratagem" (ḥīla). ﴿Nor help﴾: that is, nor can they help you. It was also said: the meaning is: these disbelievers, when the worshipped ones denied them, cannot avert the punishment with which Allah punishes them, nor (can they obtain) help from Allah. This interpretation is sound according to the reading of whoever read ﴿tastaṭīʿūn﴾ with the yā' of the second person, which is the reading of Hafs; the rest read it with the yā' of the third person.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: "So they have indeed denied you, O believers, these disbelievers, in what Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) brought." On this view, the meaning of "in what you say" is "what you say of the truth."

Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning is: they cannot avert from you any turning away from the truth to which Allah has guided you, nor (can they help) themselves against what descends upon them of punishment for their denial of you.

The majority read ﴿mā taqūlūn﴾ with the second-person tā'. Al-Farra' reported that it is permissible to read ﴿fa-qad kadhabūkum﴾ with the verb unstressed (kadhabūkum), "in what they say" (bi-mā yaqūlūn), meaning: they denied you in their saying. Likewise Mujahid and al-Bazzi read with the third-person yā'.

﴿And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great punishment.﴾ This is a threat to every wrongdoer, and those who are in the context fall under it first and foremost. The great punishment is the punishment of the Fire. It was also read ﴿yudhiqhu﴾ with the yā'. This verse and similar verses are restricted to the absence of repentance.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, returned to addressing His Messenger, clarifying the falsehood of what came before in their saying: "He eats food and walks in the markets." So He said: ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the clause that comes after ﴿illā﴾ is an attribute of a deleted noun, and the meaning is: "We did not send before you any one of the messengers except eating and walking," and the noun was deleted because ﴿of the messengers﴾ is evidence for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 164], meaning: "there is none of us but one (who has)." Al-Farra' said it has no place in the grammatical structure; it is only a relative clause (ṣila) for a deleted relative pronoun which is the object, and the estimated meaning is: "except (that) they," so the pronoun in "they" and what follows it refers to the estimated noun. A similar example is His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71], meaning: "except one who will come to it." Al-Kisa'i read in this way.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, because the relative "man" (man) cannot be deleted. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the estimated meaning is: "except while they," so the deleted element in his view is the waw.

The majority read ﴿illā innahum﴾ with a kasra on inna, because of the presence of the lām in its predicate, as established in the science of grammar, and this is agreed upon among them.

Al-Naḥḥas said: "However, 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad that he said: 'It is permissible with this inna to have a fatḥa even if the lām follows it,' and I think it is a mistake."

The majority read ﴿yamshūna﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā', a sukūn on the mīm, and a light shīn. 'Ali, Ibn 'Awf, and Ibn Mas'ud read it with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the mīm, and a ḍamma on the doubled shīn. It has the same meaning as the first reading. The poet said:

"I walk among the watering-places of the waters, and I guard against she-camels that are hard to handle and riding them."

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"From it the beasts of prey of the tribe remain subdued, and the sick-people do not walk in its valley."

﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others.﴾ This address is general to mankind. Allah, glory be to Him, has made some of His servants a trial for others. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, and it was said: the intended meaning of the first "some" is the disbelievers of the nations, and of the second "some" the messengers. The meaning of "trial" (fitna) is testing and affliction. The first is preferable, because some people are tested by others and afflicted by them. The sick person says: "Why was I not made like the healthy?" and so does everyone who has an affliction. The healthy person is tested by the sick, so he does not become impatient with him or belittle him. The rich is tested by the poor, so he consoles him. The poor is tested by the rich, so he envies him. Something similar to this is like it.

It was also said: the intended meaning of the verse is that when a nobleman wanted to accept Islam and saw a lowly man had accepted it before him, he was too proud and said: "I will not accept it after him, so that he will have precedence and superiority over me." So he remains in his disbelief. That is the testing of some of them by others. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

There is no basis for restricting the verse to this, for even if these were the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl), the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Then, after the report that Allah has made some a trial for others, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, and there is an ellipsis in the speech, the estimated meaning being "or will you not be patient?" That is: will you be patient with what you see of this severe condition and this great affliction?

It was said: the position of this interrogative sentence here is the position of His saying ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾ in His saying ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Then He promised those who are patient with His saying ﴿and your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, that is, Seeing of everyone who is patient and everyone who is not patient, so that He recompenses each of them with what they deserve.

It was also said: the meaning of "will you be patient?" is: "be patient," like His saying ﴿so will you then desist?﴾, that is, "desist."

﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us said﴾: this statement is among their doubts by which they cast doubt on prophethood. The clause is coordinated with ﴿And they said: "What is this messenger?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. That is: the polytheists who did not care about meeting Allah said, as in the saying of the poet:

"By your life, I do not hope, if I am a Muslim, on whatever side I fall in Allah's way."

That is, "I do not care." It was also said: the meaning is "they do not fear the meeting with their Lord," as in the saying of the poet:

"When the bee stings him, he does not hope for its sting, and it opposes him in the house of Nawb, the workers."

That is: he did not fear. This is the dialect of Tihama. Al-Farra' said: "hope" (rajā') was put in the place of "fear." It was also said: they do not aspire to it. And from it is the saying of the poet:

"Does a people who killed Husayn hope for the intercession of his grandfather on the Day of Reckoning?"

But carrying the word on its real meaning is preferable. The meaning is: they do not aspire to meet what We promised for obedience of reward. It is known that whoever does not hope for reward does not fear punishment.

﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us?﴾: that is, "why were they not sent down upon us, so that they would inform us that Muhammad is truthful?" Or "why were they not sent down upon us as messengers whom Allah sends?" ﴿Or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ face to face, so that He informs us that Muhammad is a messenger.

Then He (glory be to Him) answered their objection, saying: ﴿Indeed, they have grown arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾ That is, they concealed arrogance toward the truth and obstinacy in their hearts, as in His words: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain.﴾ *Utuww* means exceeding the limit in rebellion and reaching its furthest extent. Describing it as "greatness" is because the utterance of this shameful statement that they made is at the extreme of greatness and magnitude. They were not content with sending a human; they asked for angels to be sent to them. Rather, they went further, to the point of choosing between this and speaking with Allah (glory be to Him) and seeing Him in this world, without any interpreter (*turjuman*) between them and Him. These base people have reached a level in their own estimation that is too lowly, too meager and too vile to be counted among those who belong to it, or among those who are prepared for it. Likewise is the one who does not know his own worth and does not stop at his limit. Whoever his own self does not know the worth of, sees from others what he does not see.

The accusative of ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ is governed by a verb omitted in the sense: "and mention the Day they see the angels," a seeing that is not in the manner they asked for and not in the form they proposed, but in another manner, namely the Day of their appearance to them at death or at the gathering. It is also permissible that the accusative of this time expression is governed by what is indicated by His words: ﴿No good news that day for the criminals,﴾ meaning: they will be denied good news on the day they see, or no good news will exist for them in it. Thus Allah (glory be to Him) informs that the time at which they see the angels, which is the time of death or the Day of Resurrection, Allah has deprived them of good news.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The criminals in this place are those who committed disbelief in Allah." ﴿And they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier.﴾ That is, the disbelievers, upon seeing the angels, will say "*ḥijran maḥjūran*" (a barrier, a forbidding barrier). This is a phrase they used to say when meeting an enemy or when a calamity attacked, placing it in the position of seeking refuge. It is said to a man: "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies: "*ḥijran maḥjūran*," meaning: "Forbidden to you is to approach me."

It has also been said that this is the speech of the angels, meaning: they say to the disbelievers, "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that any of you enter Paradise." From this is the words of the poet:

*Ala aṣbaḥat Asmā'u ḥijran muḥarramā*
*wa aṣbaḥtu min adnā ḥumūmatihā ḥamā'*

Meaning: "Asma' has become utterly forbidden, and I have become, from the nearest of her kin, a protector." Another said:

*Ḥannat ilā al-nakhlati al-quṣwā fa qultu lahā*
*ḥijrun ḥarāmun illā tilka al-dahārīsu*

Sibawayh mentioned, in the chapter on verbal nouns in the accusative governed by verbs whose display is omitted, this expression and counted it among them. (p. 1038)

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ This is another threat. They used to do deeds that had the appearance of good: maintaining family ties, relieving the distressed, feeding the hungry, and the like. Nothing prevented their reward for these except the disbelief they were upon. Their state and deeds are therefore likened to the state of a people who opposed their ruler and disobeyed him, so he turned to what they had of goods and destroyed it, leaving nothing of it. Otherwise there is no "turning" (*qudūm*) here in the literal sense.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of *qadimna* is "we intended and aimed," as one says: "So-and-so turned to a matter" when he aimed at it or intended it. From it is the poet's saying:

*Wa qadima al-khawārijul-ḍallālu*
*ilā ʿibādi rabbihim faqālū*
*Inna dimā'akum lanā ḥalālu*

Meaning: "The misguided Kharijites turned toward the servants of their Lord and said: Indeed your blood is lawful for us."

It has also been said that it is the "coming" of the angels, which He reported about Himself, exalted is He. *Al-habā'* (dust motes) has the singular *habā'a*, and the plural *ahbā'*. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-habā'* is the dust that the wind raises, as if it were smoke. Al-Zajjaj said: it is what enters through a window together with the sunlight, resembling dust. Al-Azhari said the same. *Al-manthūr* is the scattered. The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) rendered their deeds void until they became like scattered dust. He did not suffice with likening their deeds to dust, but described it further as scattered and dispersed. It has also been said that *al-habā'* is the dry leaves of trees that the winds blow about; it has been said that it is spilled water; and it has been said that it is ashes. The first is what is established in the Arabic language and transmitted by those who know it.

Then He (glory be to Him) distinguished the state of the righteous from the state of the wicked, saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾ That is, they are more excellent in dwelling in Paradise, and better in a place of *qayla* (midday rest). *Mustaqarran* is in the accusative of specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Azhari said: *al-qaylūla* among the Arabs is resting at midday when the heat intensifies, even if there is no day with it. Al-Nahhas said: the Kufans permit the construction "honey is sweeter than vinegar."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿and the Day He gathers them﴾ (the verse), that he said: "Jesus, Ezra and the angels." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿a people lost﴾ that he said: "Destroyed."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿and whoever of you does wrong﴾ that he said: "It is shirk." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj who said: "He associates partners." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾, that he said: the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) were in this condition: they ate food and walked in the markets. ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾: he said, "a trial." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from al-Hasan concerning ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ that he said: The poor man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me rich like so-and-so," the sick man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me healthy like so-and-so," and the blind man says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me seeing like so-and-so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿and they have transgressed with great transgression﴾ that he said: "The severity of disbelief." Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿the Day they see the angels﴾ that he said: "The Day of Resurrection." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Atiyyah al-Awfi. Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "A protection and a seeking of refuge; the angels say it." In another wording he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that good news be on that day for anyone except the believers." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Atiyyah al-Awfi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that he said: "Forbidden, utterly forbidden, that we give you good news with what we give good news to the pious." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatadah concerning ﴿and they will say: a barrier, a forbidding barrier﴾ that both said: "It is a phrase the Arabs used to say; when a man was struck by hardship he would say: *ḥajran maḥjūran*, forbidden, utterly forbidden."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ that he said: "We will intend what they did of good, of those whose deeds are not accepted in this world." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His words ﴿scattered dust﴾ that he said: "*al-habā'* is the ray of sunlight that comes out of a window." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*al-habā'* is what flies off from fire when it blazes; sparks fly from it, and when it falls, it is nothing." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him: "It is what the wind blows away and scatters." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "It is spilled water."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him concerning ﴿better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest﴾ that he said: "In the upper chambers of Paradise." Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The day of Resurrection will not end until these and those take their midday rest." Then he recited: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their midday rest.﴾

**The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied as "and mention" (wa-dhkur). The linking of the reminder to "the Day," although the intended meaning is what occurs on it, is for emphasis and affirmation, as has passed many times.

Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Duri read ﴿yahshuruhum﴾ with the yā' (third person). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it because of the earlier words ﴿was upon your Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 16]. (p-1036) The rest read it with the nūn (first person plural), in exaltation (of Allah). Al-A'raj alone read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ with a kasra on the shīn throughout the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, because ﴿yafil﴾ with a kasra on the 'ayn in the transitive verb is more analogical than ﴿yaful﴾ with a ḍamma." Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying that the ḍamma and the kasra are equal, except that when one of them becomes well known it is followed.

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is coordinated with the object of ﴿nahshur﴾. The non-rational (ghayr al-'uqalā') forms, such as idols and images and the like, were given precedence over the rational beings, such as the angels, the jinn, and the Messiah. This is to indicate that they all share in being unfit to be gods, or because those who worship what has no intellect are more numerous than those who worship rational beings among them, so the non-rational form was given precedence in consideration of the number of those who worship it.

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: the intended meaning is the angels, mankind, the jinn, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, as evidenced by their address and their reply later on.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning is only the idols. Even though they do not hear or speak, Allah, glory be to Him, will make them on the Day of Resurrection hearing and speaking. ﴿Then He will say: "Did you lead astray these servants of Mine, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Kathir, and Hafs read ﴿fa-naqūlu﴾ with the nūn. The rest read it with the yā'. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the yā' reading, as he preferred it in ﴿yahshuruhum﴾, and so did Abu Hatim.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿a-antum aḍlaltum﴾ is for reproach and rebuke.

The meaning is: Was their straying due to you and your calling them to worship you? Or did they stray from the path of truth by themselves, through not reflecting on what leads to the truth and not contemplating what leads to the right course?

The clause ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You"﴾ is a new clause (mustaʼnafa), an answer to an implied question. The meaning of "Glory be to You" (subḥānaka) is an expression of wonder at what was said to them, because they are angels or infallible prophets, or lifeless things that do not understand; that is, "exalting You (above such things)." ﴿It was not fitting for us to take any protectors besides You﴾: that is, it was not valid or proper for us to take protectors besides You and then worship them. So how could we call Your servants to worship us, when we ourselves worship none but You? The word walī (protector) is used for the follower as it is used for the one followed. This is the meaning of the verse according to the reading of the majority, ﴿nattakhidh﴾ in the active voice.

Al-Ḥasan and Abu Ja'far read ﴿nuttakhadh﴾ in the passive voice, meaning: it was not fitting for us that the polytheists take us as protectors besides You.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: this reading is not permissible; even if it were sound, the second ﴿min﴾ would have been dropped.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this reading is not permissible, because Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned ﴿min﴾ twice, and if it were as he read, He would have said: "that we take protectors besides You." It was also said that the second ﴿min﴾ is superfluous.
