It is also related from him that he read *tanazzalati al-malāʾikatu* (تَنَزَّلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ). Other readings have been transmitted as irregular (*shādhdh*).

The emphasis on this verb with the verbal noun ﴿تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("a descent") indicates that this descent is of a strange kind and of a wondrous manner. The scholars said: "This is a descent of good pleasure and mercy, not a descent of wrath and punishment."

**[Verse] "Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful"** (﴿المُلْكُ يَوْمَئِذٍ الحَقُّ لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾). *Al-mulk* (المُلْكُ) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) is an adjective of it, and *li-l-raḥmān* (لِلرَّحْمَنِ) is the predicate (*khabar*). This is what al-Zajjāj said. That is: the enduring sovereignty that does not cease belongs to the Most Merciful on that day, because sovereignty that passes away and ends is not sovereignty in reality. The benefit of restricting it by the time expression is that this sovereignty belongs to Him, glorified is He, exclusively on this day. As for the other days of the world, others have a sovereignty in appearance even if it is not real.

It was also said that the predicate of the subject is the time expression (*al-ẓarf*), and *al-ḥaqq* is an adjective of *al-mulk*. The meaning is: the enduring sovereignty belonging to the Most Merciful is exclusive on this day.

﴿وكانَ يَوْمًا عَلى الكافِرِينَ عَسِيرًا﴾ ("and it is a difficult day for the disbelievers"). That is: this day, although sovereignty on it belongs to Allah alone, is severe for the disbelievers, because of what befalls them on it and the punishment they receive after the reckoning is established. As for the believers, it is easy and not difficult, because of the honour and the great glad tidings they receive on it.

**[Verse] "And the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands"** (﴿ويَوْمَ يَعَضُّ الظّالِمُ عَلى يَدَيْهِ﴾). The time expression is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning "remember" (*wa-dhkur*), just as the first time expression, namely "the day the sky is split open," is governed by this same omitted verb. The apparent meaning is that the biting here is literal, and there is no obstacle to that nor any reason to interpret it otherwise.

It was also said that it is a metaphor for rage and regret. The intended "wrongdoer" is every wrongdoer who comes to that place and arrives at that station. The fact that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion does not preclude this. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion.

**[Verse] "He says, 'Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger'"** (﴿يَقُولُ يالَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا﴾). *Yaqūlu* (يَقُولُ) is in a position of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The content of the speech is: "Oh, I wish..." (*yā laytanī*). The addressee is omitted: "O people, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger." *Sabīlan* (سَبِيلًا) means a path, which is the path of truth; he would have walked on it until he was freed from these misleading matters. The intended meaning is following the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he brought.

**[Verse] "Oh woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend"** (﴿ياوَيْلَتى لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أتَّخِذْ فُلانًا خَلِيلًا﴾). This is a supplication against himself, invoking woe and perdition, for having taken as a close friend a disbeliever who misled him in the world. *Fulān* (فُلانٌ) is a substitute term for proper names.

Al-Naysābūrī said: Some scholars of the Arabic language claimed that the use of *fulān* is not established in eloquent speech except as a quotation. One does not say "So-and-so came to me," but one says "Zayd said: So-and-so came to me," because it is the name of the word which is the name-marker. Thus it occurs in the speech of Allah. It was said that *fulān* is a substitute for the proper name of a male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for the proper name of a female who has intellect. It was also said that it is a substitute for an indefinite male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for an indefinite female who has intellect. As for *al-fulān* and *al-fulānah*, they are substitutes for non-rational beings. *Fulu* (فُلُ) is restricted to the vocative except in cases of necessity, as in the words of the poet:

*"Fī lajjatin amsik fulānan ʿan Fulī"*
("In a deep sea, hold back so-and-so from such-and-such.")

And his saying:

*"Ḥaddithānī ʿan fulānin wa-Fulī"*
("Tell me about so-and-so and such-and-such.")

*Fulu* is not a shortened form (*murakhkhamah*) of *fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Abū Ḥayyān claimed that Ibn ʿUṣfūr and Ibn Mālik both made *fulān* a substitute for the proper name of one who has intellect.

Al-Ḥasan read *yā wayltī* (يا ويْلَتِي) with a clear *yā* (ي), and al-Dūrī read it with *imālah* (the vowel-raising of *alif*). Abū ʿAlī said: Abandoning *imālah* is better, because the original of this word is *yā*, then the *kasrah* was changed to a *fatḥah* and the *yā* to a *tā* (ت), fleeing from the *yā*. So whoever uses *imālah* returns to what was fled from.

**[Verse] "He has led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me"** (﴿لَقَدْ أضَلَّنِي عَنِ الذِّكْرِ بَعْدَ إذْ جاءَنِي﴾). That is: by Allah, this one whom I took as a close friend has indeed led me astray from the Qur'an, or from the admonition, or from the word of testimony, or from all of these, after it had come to me, and I had come under its influence and been able to receive it.

**[Verse] "And Satan is ever a deserter of man"** (﴿وكانَ الشَّيْطانُ لِلْإنْسانِ خَذُولًا﴾). *Al-khadhl* (الخَذْلُ) is abandoning help. From it comes the deserting (*khudhlān*) of Iblīs toward the polytheists, since they take him as an ally, then he abandons them when they call on him for help. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. It is possible that it is part of the speech of Allah, or part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that he called his friend "Satan" after having made him one who misleads. Or it is possible that by "Satan" he means Iblīs, because he is the one who made him patient toward keeping company with misleaders.

**[Verse] "And the Messenger says, 'My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned'"** (﴿وقالَ الرَّسُولُ يارَبِّ إنَّ قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا هَذا القُرْآنَ مَهْجُورًا﴾). This is conjoined to ﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("And those who do not expect to meet Us say") [al-Furqān: 21]. The meaning is: my people have taken this Qur'an, which I brought to them, which You commanded me to convey and sent me with, as something abandoned, left aside. They did not believe in it, nor did they accept it in any way.

It was also said that it derives from *hajara* (هَجَرَ), meaning to talk nonsense (*hadhā*). The meaning would then be that they took it as nonsensical talk and delirium. It was also said that the meaning of *mahjūran* (مَهْجُورًا) is "abandoned in it" (*mahjūran fīhi*), and then the preposition was omitted. Their abandonment of it is their saying: "It is sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients." This statement is what the Messenger (ﷺ) will say on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that it is a quotation of his saying (ﷺ) in the world.

**[Verse] "And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals"** (﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾). (p-1040) This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, has made for every one of the prophets who call to Allah an enemy from among the criminals of his people who opposes him. So do not despair, O Muhammad, for this is the practice of the prophets before you. Be patient as they were patient.

**[Verse] "And your Lord is sufficient as a guide and a helper"** (﴿وكَفى بِرَبِّكَ هادِيًا ونَصِيرًا﴾). The exegetes said: the *bāʾ* is superfluous (*zāʾidah*), meaning "Your Lord is sufficient." *Naṣīran* (نَصِيرًا) and *hādiyan* (هادِيًا) are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*), or as specifications (*tamyīz*). That is: He guides His servants to the interests of religion and of the world, and He helps them against their enemies.

**[Verse] "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"** (﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ القُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً واحِدَةً﴾). This is among their proposals and their obstinate demands. That is: Why did Allah not send down this Qur'an to us in one single installment, not divided into portions?

There is disagreement about who said this statement. It was said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was said that they are the Jews, who said: "Why did you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down?" This is a false claim and an untenable assertion, because those books were also sent down in portions, just as the Qur'an was, but they are obstinate, or ignorant, not knowing the manner in which the books of Allah, glorified is He, were sent down to His prophets.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it"). That is: We sent down the Qur'an in this way, in portions. The *kāf* (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is an indication of what is understood from their speech. That is: like that dispersed sending down which they criticized and proposed the opposite of, We sent it down so that We might strengthen your heart by this manner of sending down. For sending it down in portions, installment by installment, according to events, is closer to your memorizing it and your understanding of its meanings, and that is among the greatest causes of strengthening. The *lām* (ل) is connected to the omitted verb which we have assumed.

Abū Ḥātim said: Al-Akhfash said that it is the answer to an omitted oath. He said: This is a weak opinion. ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read *li-yuthabbita* (لِيُثَبِّتَ) with the third-person masculine, meaning Allah, glorified is He. It was also said that this word, namely *kadhālika* (كَذَلِكَ), is part of the speech of the polytheists, and the meaning is "like that," i.e., like the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. Thus one pauses at His saying "like that," then one begins with His saying ﴿لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("that We may strengthen your heart by it"), with the meaning: We sent it down to you in portions for this purpose. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is better and more excellent. Al-Naḥḥās said: The sending down of the Qur'an in installments was among the signs of prophethood, because they did not ask him about anything without being answered about it, and this could only come from a prophet. So that was a strengthening of his heart and of their hearts.

**[Verse] "And We have arranged it in gradual arrangement"** (﴿ورَتَّلْناهُ تَرْتِيلًا﴾). This is conjoined to the omitted verb. That is: thus We sent it down and arranged it in arrangement (*tartīlan*). The meaning of *tartīl* (التَّرْتِيل) is that one verse follows another. This was said by al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. It was also said that the meaning is that He made it clear with clarification. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās. Mujāhid said: some of it following some of it. Al-Suddī said: We distinguished it with distinction. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I know of *tartīl* only as verification and clarification.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned that they are refuted at every time, and their claim is rejected in every way and in every state. He said:

**[Verse] "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation"** (﴿ولا يَأْتُونَكَ بِمَثَلٍ إلّا جِئْناكَ بِالحَقِّ وأحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا﴾). That is: the polytheists do not come to you, O Muhammad, with any example (*mathal*) of their examples, among which are their obstinate proposals, except that We come to you, in response to their example, with the true answer, established, which nullifies what they brought of the example, crushes it, and repels it.

Thus the intended meaning of "example" here is the question and the proposal, and the intended meaning of "truth" is its answer, which cuts off its pretext, nullifies its doubt, and eradicates its root.

The meaning of *aḥsana tafsīran* (أحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا) is: We bring you the best explanation. So *aḥsana tafsīran* is conjoined to *al-ḥaqq*. The exception in His saying ﴿إلّا جِئْناكَ﴾ ("except that We bring you") is an incomplete exception (*mufarragh*), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. That is: they do not come to you with any example except in a state of Our coming to you with that.

Then He threatened these ignorant people and blamed them, saying:

**[Verse] "Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell"** (﴿الَّذِينَ يُحْشَرُونَ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ إلى جَهَنَّمَ﴾). That is: they will be gathered while upon their faces. The relative clause (*al-mawṣūl*) is the subject, and its predicate is *ulāʾika* (أُولَئِكَ, "those"). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who..." It is permissible to put it in the accusative as a dispraise.

The meaning of "gathered upon their faces" is that they will be dragged upon them to Hell.

**[Verse] "Those are worse in place"** (﴿أُولَئِكَ شَرٌّ مَكانًا﴾). That is: worse in station and in final destination.

**[Verse] "And more astray in way"** (﴿وأضَلُّ سَبِيلًا﴾). That is: more mistaken in path. That is because they have already become people of the Fire.

The exegesis of a verse like this has already been given in Surat Subḥān (al-Isrāʾ). It has been said that this is connected to His saying: ﴿أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا وأحْسَنُ مَقِيلًا﴾ ("The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place and finer in place of repose") [al-Furqān: 24].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verse 25–34 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾. He said: Allah will gather the creation on the Day of Resurrection in one plain: the jinn, the humans, the animals, the beasts of prey, the birds, and all of creation. Then the lowest heaven will be split open, and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those on the earth of jinn, humans and all of creation. They will surround the jinn, the humans and all of creation. The people of the earth will say: "Is our Lord among you?" They will say: "No." Then the second heaven will be split open, and the same will be mentioned, and so on for each heaven until the seventh heaven. In each heaven there will be more than in the heaven before it. Then our Lord will descend in a shade of clouds, and around Him will be the Karubiyyun (the cherubim), who are more numerous than the inhabitants of the seven heavens, and the humans, and the jinn, and all of creation. They have horns like the joints of cucumbers, and they are beneath the Throne. They have a loud sound of glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), and sanctification of Allah, the Exalted. The distance between the sole of the foot of one of them and his ankle is a five-hundred-year journey; from his knee to his thigh is a five-hundred-year journey; from his thigh to his collarbone is a five-hundred-year journey; and what is above that is a five-hundred-year journey.

Its chain according to Ibn Jarir is thus: He said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, al-Hajjaj ibn Mubarak ibn Fudala narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, that he heard Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it with a chain thus: He said: Muhammad ibn ʿAmmar ibn al-Harith Mamul narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn Zayd, with it.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il narrated it with a chain. al-Suyuti said: it is sahih (sound) through the route of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: that Abu Muʿayt used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah without harming him, and he was a forbearing man. But the rest of the Quraysh, when they sat with him, would harm him. Abu Muʿayt had a close friend who was absent from him in Syria. The Quraysh said: "Abu Muʿayt has become a Sabian (has left his religion)." His friend arrived from Syria at night and said to his wife: "What has Muhammad done of what he was upon?" She said: "He has become more intense in his affair." He said: "What has my friend Abu Muʿayt done?" She said: "He has become a Sabian." So he spent a night of ill omen. When morning came, Abu Muʿayt came to him and greeted him, but he did not return the greeting. He said: "Why do you not return my greeting?" He said: "How can I return your greeting when you have turned away?" He said: "Has Quraysh really done this?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what will relieve their hearts if I do it?" He said: "Go to him in his gathering, spit in his face, and insult him with the most vile insult you know." He did so, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not respond except by wiping his face of the spittle. Then he turned to him and said: "If I find you outside the mountains of Makkah, I will strike your neck, patiently (ṣabran)." When the Day of Badr came and his companions went out, he refused to go out. His companions said to him: "Come out with us." He said: "This man promised me that if he found me outside the mountains of Makkah, he would strike my neck patiently." They said: "You have a red camel that cannot be overtaken; if there is defeat, you can fly on it." So he went out with them. When Allah defeated the polytheists and his camel carried him over rough ground, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took him captive, along with seventy men from Quraysh. Abu Muʿayt was brought before him, and he said: "Will you kill me from among these?" He said: "Yes, for what you spat in my face." So Allah revealed concerning Abu Muʿayt: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾ up to His words: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾.

Abu Nuʿaym narrated this story through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned that the friend of Abu Muʿayt was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾, that he said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, and they are the two friends in Hell."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, that he said: "The enemy of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Abu Jahl, and the enemy of Musa was Qarun, and Qarun was the cousin of Musa."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The polytheists said: "If Muhammad were a prophet as he claims, why would his Lord not send down the Qur'an all at once? It descends upon him one verse or two verses, one surah or two surahs." So Allah revealed in answer to what they said on His Prophet: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ up to ﴿and most misguided in way﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ that he said: "So that We may firm up your heart with it and bind your heart." ﴿And We have recited it in measured recitation﴾: he said: "We have made it come in installments (tarsil), one thing after another." ﴿And they bring you no example except that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾: he said: "If We had sent down the Qur'an all at once, then they asked you, you would not have had an answer for them. But We hold it back from you, so when they ask you, you answer."

(p-1039)

**[Verse] "And the day the sky is split open with clouds"** (﴿ويَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السَّماءُ بِالغَمامِ﴾). Here Allah, glorified is He, describes some of the events of the Day of Resurrection. *Tashaqqaq* means to split open or to be opened up. ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Waththáb, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr read *tashaqqaq* with a light *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ). Its underlying form is *tatashaqqaq* (تَتَشَقَّقُ). The rest read it with a doubled *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ), by assimilation (*idghām*). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second. The meaning of "split open with the clouds" is that the sky splits open to release the clouds.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "The sky splits open while clouds are over it, just as you say: 'The prince rode out with his weapons (*bi-silāḥihi*),' meaning, 'with his weapons upon him,' and 'He went out in his clothes (*bi-thiyābihi*),' meaning, 'with his clothes upon him.'" The basis of what he said is that *bāʾ* (ب) and *ʿan* (عن) are interchangeable, as when you say: "I shot with the bow (*bi-l-qaws*)" and "I shot from the bow (*ʿan al-qaws*)."

It is related that the sky splits open to release a thin white cloud. It was also said that the sky splits open with the cloud that lies between it and the people.

The meaning is that the clouds split open when the sky splits open. It was also said that the sky splits open for the descent of the angels, as Allah, glorified is He, says after this: ﴿ونُزِّلَ المَلائِكَةُ تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("and the angels are sent down, a descent"). It was also said that the *bāʾ* in *bi-l-ghamām* (بِالغَمامِ) is causal (*sababiyyah*), meaning "because of the cloud," i.e., because of its emerging from it, as if the cloud were that by which the sky is split open. It was also said that the *bāʾ* is connected to an omitted element, meaning "accompanied by the cloud" (*mutalabbisah bi-l-ghamām*).

Ibn Kathīr read ﴿ونُنْزِلُ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ ("and We send down the angels") with a light *zāy*, from *al-inzāl* (الإنزال), with a *nūn* after it, a silent *nūn*, and a light *zāy* with a *kasrah*, as the imperfect of *anzala*. *Al-malāʾikata* (الملائكة) is in the accusative as the object.

The remaining canonical readers read ﴿ونُزِّلَ﴾ ("and [the angels] are sent down") with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn* and a *kasrah* on the doubled *zāy*, as a past passive. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read *nazzala* (نَزَّلَ) with doubling, as a past active, whose subject is Allah, glorified is He. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read *anzala al-malāʾikata* (أنْزَلَ المَلائِكَةَ). It is also related from him that he read *tanazzalati al-malāʾikatu* (تَنَزَّلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ). Other readings have been transmitted as irregular (*shādhdh*).

The emphasis on this verb with the verbal noun ﴿تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("a descent") indicates that this descent is of a strange kind and of a wondrous manner. The scholars said: "This is a descent of good pleasure and mercy, not a descent of wrath and punishment."

**[Verse] "Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful"** (﴿المُلْكُ يَوْمَئِذٍ الحَقُّ لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾). *Al-mulk* (المُلْكُ) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) is an adjective of it, and *li-l-raḥmān* (لِلرَّحْمَنِ) is the predicate (*khabar*). This is what al-Zajjāj said. That is: the enduring sovereignty that does not cease belongs to the Most Merciful on that day, because sovereignty that passes away and ends is not sovereignty in reality. The benefit of restricting it by the time expression is that this sovereignty belongs to Him, glorified is He, exclusively on this day. As for the other days of the world, others have a sovereignty in appearance even if it is not real.

It was also said that the predicate of the subject is the time expression (*al-ẓarf*), and *al-ḥaqq* is an adjective of *al-mulk*. The meaning is: the enduring sovereignty belonging to the Most Merciful is exclusive on this day.

﴿وكانَ يَوْمًا عَلى الكافِرِينَ عَسِيرًا﴾ ("and it is a difficult day for the disbelievers"). That is: this day, although sovereignty on it belongs to Allah alone, is severe for the disbelievers, because of what befalls them on it and the punishment they receive after the reckoning is established. As for the believers, it is easy and not difficult, because of the honour and the great glad tidings they receive on it.

**[Verse] "And the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands"** (﴿ويَوْمَ يَعَضُّ الظّالِمُ عَلى يَدَيْهِ﴾). The time expression is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning "remember" (*wa-dhkur*), just as the first time expression, namely "the day the sky is split open," is governed by this same omitted verb. The apparent meaning is that the biting here is literal, and there is no obstacle to that nor any reason to interpret it otherwise.

It was also said that it is a metaphor for rage and regret. The intended "wrongdoer" is every wrongdoer who comes to that place and arrives at that station. The fact that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion does not preclude this. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion.

**[Verse] "He says, 'Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger'"** (﴿يَقُولُ يالَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا﴾). *Yaqūlu* (يَقُولُ) is in a position of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The content of the speech is: "Oh, I wish..." (*yā laytanī*). The addressee is omitted: "O people, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger." *Sabīlan* (سَبِيلًا) means a path, which is the path of truth; he would have walked on it until he was freed from these misleading matters. The intended meaning is following the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he brought.

**[Verse] "Oh woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend"** (﴿ياوَيْلَتى لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أتَّخِذْ فُلانًا خَلِيلًا﴾). This is a supplication against himself, invoking woe and perdition, for having taken as a close friend a disbeliever who misled him in the world. *Fulān* (فُلانٌ) is a substitute term for proper names.

Al-Naysābūrī said: Some scholars of the Arabic language claimed that the use of *fulān* is not established in eloquent speech except as a quotation. One does not say "So-and-so came to me," but one says "Zayd said: So-and-so came to me," because it is the name of the word which is the name-marker. Thus it occurs in the speech of Allah. It was said that *fulān* is a substitute for the proper name of a male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for the proper name of a female who has intellect. It was also said that it is a substitute for an indefinite male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for an indefinite female who has intellect. As for *al-fulān* and *al-fulānah*, they are substitutes for non-rational beings. *Fulu* (فُلُ) is restricted to the vocative except in cases of necessity, as in the words of the poet:

*"Fī lajjatin amsik fulānan ʿan Fulī"*
("In a deep sea, hold back so-and-so from such-and-such.")

And his saying:

*"Ḥaddithānī ʿan fulānin wa-Fulī"*
("Tell me about so-and-so and such-and-such.")

*Fulu* is not a shortened form (*murakhkhamah*) of *fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Abū Ḥayyān claimed that Ibn ʿUṣfūr and Ibn Mālik both made *fulān* a substitute for the proper name of one who has intellect.

Al-Ḥasan read *yā wayltī* (يا ويْلَتِي) with a clear *yā* (ي), and al-Dūrī read it with *imālah* (the vowel-raising of *alif*). Abū ʿAlī said: Abandoning *imālah* is better, because the original of this word is *yā*, then the *kasrah* was changed to a *fatḥah* and the *yā* to a *tā* (ت), fleeing from the *yā*. So whoever uses *imālah* returns to what was fled from.

**[Verse] "He has led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me"** (﴿لَقَدْ أضَلَّنِي عَنِ الذِّكْرِ بَعْدَ إذْ جاءَنِي﴾). That is: by Allah, this one whom I took as a close friend has indeed led me astray from the Qur'an, or from the admonition, or from the word of testimony, or from all of these, after it had come to me, and I had come under its influence and been able to receive it.

**[Verse] "And Satan is ever a deserter of man"** (﴿وكانَ الشَّيْطانُ لِلْإنْسانِ خَذُولًا﴾). *Al-khadhl* (الخَذْلُ) is abandoning help. From it comes the deserting (*khudhlān*) of Iblīs toward the polytheists, since they take him as an ally, then he abandons them when they call on him for help. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. It is possible that it is part of the speech of Allah, or part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that he called his friend "Satan" after having made him one who misleads. Or it is possible that by "Satan" he means Iblīs, because he is the one who made him patient toward keeping company with misleaders.

**[Verse] "And the Messenger says, 'My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned'"** (﴿وقالَ الرَّسُولُ يارَبِّ إنَّ قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا هَذا القُرْآنَ مَهْجُورًا﴾). This is conjoined to ﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("And those who do not expect to meet Us say") [al-Furqān: 21]. The meaning is: my people have taken this Qur'an, which I brought to them, which You commanded me to convey and sent me with, as something abandoned, left aside. They did not believe in it, nor did they accept it in any way.

It was also said that it derives from *hajara* (هَجَرَ), meaning to talk nonsense (*hadhā*). The meaning would then be that they took it as nonsensical talk and delirium. It was also said that the meaning of *mahjūran* (مَهْجُورًا) is "abandoned in it" (*mahjūran fīhi*), and then the preposition was omitted. Their abandonment of it is their saying: "It is sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients." This statement is what the Messenger (ﷺ) will say on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that it is a quotation of his saying (ﷺ) in the world.

**[Verse] "And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals"** (﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾). (p-1040) This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, has made for every one of the prophets who call to Allah an enemy from among the criminals of his people who opposes him. So do not despair, O Muhammad, for this is the practice of the prophets before you. Be patient as they were patient.

**[Verse] "And your Lord is sufficient as a guide and a helper"** (﴿وكَفى بِرَبِّكَ هادِيًا ونَصِيرًا﴾). The exegetes said: the *bāʾ* is superfluous (*zāʾidah*), meaning "Your Lord is sufficient." *Naṣīran* (نَصِيرًا) and *hādiyan* (هادِيًا) are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*), or as specifications (*tamyīz*). That is: He guides His servants to the interests of religion and of the world, and He helps them against their enemies.

**[Verse] "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"** (﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ القُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً واحِدَةً﴾). This is among their proposals and their obstinate demands. That is: Why did Allah not send down this Qur'an to us in one single installment, not divided into portions?

There is disagreement about who said this statement. It was said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was said that they are the Jews, who said: "Why did you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down?" This is a false claim and an untenable assertion, because those books were also sent down in portions, just as the Qur'an was, but they are obstinate, or ignorant, not knowing the manner in which the books of Allah, glorified is He, were sent down to His prophets.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it"). That is: We sent down the Qur'an in this way, in portions. The *kāf* (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is an indication of what is understood from their speech. That is: like that dispersed sending down which they criticized and proposed the opposite of, We sent it down so that We might strengthen your heart by this manner of sending down. For sending it down in portions, installment by installment, according to events, is closer to your memorizing it and your understanding of its meanings, and that is among the greatest causes of strengthening. The *lām* (ل) is connected to the omitted verb which we have assumed.

Abū Ḥātim said: Al-Akhfash said that it is the answer to an omitted oath. He said: This is a weak opinion. ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read *li-yuthabbita* (لِيُثَبِّتَ) with the third-person masculine, meaning Allah, glorified is He. It was also said that this word, namely *kadhālika* (كَذَلِكَ), is part of the speech of the polytheists, and the meaning is "like that," i.e., like the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. Thus one pauses at His saying "like that," then one begins with His saying ﴿لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("that We may strengthen your heart by it"), with the meaning: We sent it down to you in portions for this purpose. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is better and more excellent. Al-Naḥḥās said: The sending down of the Qur'an in installments was among the signs of prophethood, because they did not ask him about anything without being answered about it, and this could only come from a prophet. So that was a strengthening of his heart and of their hearts.

**[Verse] "And We have arranged it in gradual arrangement"** (﴿ورَتَّلْناهُ تَرْتِيلًا﴾). This is conjoined to the omitted verb. That is: thus We sent it down and arranged it in arrangement (*tartīlan*). The meaning of *tartīl* (التَّرْتِيل) is that one verse follows another. This was said by al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. It was also said that the meaning is that He made it clear with clarification. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās. Mujāhid said: some of it following some of it. Al-Suddī said: We distinguished it with distinction. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I know of *tartīl* only as verification and clarification.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned that they are refuted at every time, and their claim is rejected in every way and in every state. He said:

**[Verse] "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation"** (﴿ولا يَأْتُونَكَ بِمَثَلٍ إلّا جِئْناكَ بِالحَقِّ وأحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا﴾). That is: the polytheists do not come to you, O Muhammad, with any example (*mathal*) of their examples, among which are their obstinate proposals, except that We come to you, in response to their example, with the true answer, established, which nullifies what they brought of the example, crushes it, and repels it.

Thus the intended meaning of "example" here is the question and the proposal, and the intended meaning of "truth" is its answer, which cuts off its pretext, nullifies its doubt, and eradicates its root.

The meaning of *aḥsana tafsīran* (أحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا) is: We bring you the best explanation. So *aḥsana tafsīran* is conjoined to *al-ḥaqq*. The exception in His saying ﴿إلّا جِئْناكَ﴾ ("except that We bring you") is an incomplete exception (*mufarragh*), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. That is: they do not come to you with any example except in a state of Our coming to you with that.

Then He threatened these ignorant people and blamed them, saying:

**[Verse] "Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell"** (﴿الَّذِينَ يُحْشَرُونَ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ إلى جَهَنَّمَ﴾). That is: they will be gathered while upon their faces. The relative clause (*al-mawṣūl*) is the subject, and its predicate is *ulāʾika* (أُولَئِكَ, "those"). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who..." It is permissible to put it in the accusative as a dispraise.

The meaning of "gathered upon their faces" is that they will be dragged upon them to Hell.

**[Verse] "Those are worse in place"** (﴿أُولَئِكَ شَرٌّ مَكانًا﴾). That is: worse in station and in final destination.

**[Verse] "And more astray in way"** (﴿وأضَلُّ سَبِيلًا﴾). That is: more mistaken in path. That is because they have already become people of the Fire.

The exegesis of a verse like this has already been given in Surat Subḥān (al-Isrāʾ). It has been said that this is connected to His saying: ﴿أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا وأحْسَنُ مَقِيلًا﴾ ("The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place and finer in place of repose") [al-Furqān: 24].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verse 25–34 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾. He said: Allah will gather the creation on the Day of Resurrection in one plain: the jinn, the humans, the animals, the beasts of prey, the birds, and all of creation. Then the lowest heaven will be split open, and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those on the earth of jinn, humans and all of creation. They will surround the jinn, the humans and all of creation. The people of the earth will say: "Is our Lord among you?" They will say: "No." Then the second heaven will be split open, and the same will be mentioned, and so on for each heaven until the seventh heaven. In each heaven there will be more than in the heaven before it. Then our Lord will descend in a shade of clouds, and around Him will be the Karubiyyun (the cherubim), who are more numerous than the inhabitants of the seven heavens, and the humans, and the jinn, and all of creation. They have horns like the joints of cucumbers, and they are beneath the Throne. They have a loud sound of glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), and sanctification of Allah, the Exalted. The distance between the sole of the foot of one of them and his ankle is a five-hundred-year journey; from his knee to his thigh is a five-hundred-year journey; from his thigh to his collarbone is a five-hundred-year journey; and what is above that is a five-hundred-year journey.

Its chain according to Ibn Jarir is thus: He said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, al-Hajjaj ibn Mubarak ibn Fudala narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, that he heard Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it with a chain thus: He said: Muhammad ibn ʿAmmar ibn al-Harith Mamul narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn Zayd, with it.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il narrated it with a chain. al-Suyuti said: it is sahih (sound) through the route of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: that Abu Muʿayt used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah without harming him, and he was a forbearing man. But the rest of the Quraysh, when they sat with him, would harm him. Abu Muʿayt had a close friend who was absent from him in Syria. The Quraysh said: "Abu Muʿayt has become a Sabian (has left his religion)." His friend arrived from Syria at night and said to his wife: "What has Muhammad done of what he was upon?" She said: "He has become more intense in his affair." He said: "What has my friend Abu Muʿayt done?" She said: "He has become a Sabian." So he spent a night of ill omen. When morning came, Abu Muʿayt came to him and greeted him, but he did not return the greeting. He said: "Why do you not return my greeting?" He said: "How can I return your greeting when you have turned away?" He said: "Has Quraysh really done this?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what will relieve their hearts if I do it?" He said: "Go to him in his gathering, spit in his face, and insult him with the most vile insult you know." He did so, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not respond except by wiping his face of the spittle. Then he turned to him and said: "If I find you outside the mountains of Makkah, I will strike your neck, patiently (ṣabran)." When the Day of Badr came and his companions went out, he refused to go out. His companions said to him: "Come out with us." He said: "This man promised me that if he found me outside the mountains of Makkah, he would strike my neck patiently." They said: "You have a red camel that cannot be overtaken; if there is defeat, you can fly on it." So he went out with them. When Allah defeated the polytheists and his camel carried him over rough ground, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took him captive, along with seventy men from Quraysh. Abu Muʿayt was brought before him, and he said: "Will you kill me from among these?" He said: "Yes, for what you spat in my face." So Allah revealed concerning Abu Muʿayt: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾ up to His words: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾.

Abu Nuʿaym narrated this story through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned that the friend of Abu Muʿayt was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾, that he said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, and they are the two friends in Hell."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, that he said: "The enemy of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Abu Jahl, and the enemy of Musa was Qarun, and Qarun was the cousin of Musa."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The polytheists said: "If Muhammad were a prophet as he claims, why would his Lord not send down the Qur'an all at once? It descends upon him one verse or two verses, one surah or two surahs." So Allah revealed in answer to what they said on His Prophet: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ up to ﴿and most misguided in way﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ that he said: "So that We may firm up your heart with it and bind your heart." ﴿And We have recited it in measured recitation﴾: he said: "We have made it come in installments (tarsil), one thing after another." ﴿And they bring you no example except that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾: he said: "If We had sent down the Qur'an all at once, then they asked you, you would not have had an answer for them. But We hold it back from you, so when they ask you, you answer."

(p-1039)

**[Verse] "And the day the sky is split open with clouds"** (﴿ويَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السَّماءُ بِالغَمامِ﴾). Here Allah, glorified is He, describes some of the events of the Day of Resurrection. *Tashaqqaq* means to split open or to be opened up. ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Waththáb, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr read *tashaqqaq* with a light *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ). Its underlying form is *tatashaqqaq* (تَتَشَقَّقُ). The rest read it with a doubled *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ), by assimilation (*idghām*). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second. The meaning of "split open with the clouds" is that the sky splits open to release the clouds.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "The sky splits open while clouds are over it, just as you say: 'The prince rode out with his weapons (*bi-silāḥihi*),' meaning, 'with his weapons upon him,' and 'He went out in his clothes (*bi-thiyābihi*),' meaning, 'with his clothes upon him.'" The basis of what he said is that *bāʾ* (ب) and *ʿan* (عن) are interchangeable, as when you say: "I shot with the bow (*bi-l-qaws*)" and "I shot from the bow (*ʿan al-qaws*)."

It is related that the sky splits open to release a thin white cloud. It was also said that the sky splits open with the cloud that lies between it and the people.

The meaning is that the clouds split open when the sky splits open. It was also said that the sky splits open for the descent of the angels, as Allah, glorified is He, says after this: ﴿ونُزِّلَ المَلائِكَةُ تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("and the angels are sent down, a descent"). It was also said that the *bāʾ* in *bi-l-ghamām* (بِالغَمامِ) is causal (*sababiyyah*), meaning "because of the cloud," i.e., because of its emerging from it, as if the cloud were that by which the sky is split open. It was also said that the *bāʾ* is connected to an omitted element, meaning "accompanied by the cloud" (*mutalabbisah bi-l-ghamām*).

Ibn Kathīr read ﴿ونُنْزِلُ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ ("and We send down the angels") with a light *zāy*, from *al-inzāl* (الإنزال), with a *nūn* after it, a silent *nūn*, and a light *zāy* with a *kasrah*, as the imperfect of *anzala*. *Al-malāʾikata* (الملائكة) is in the accusative as the object.

The remaining canonical readers read ﴿ونُزِّلَ﴾ ("and [the angels] are sent down") with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn* and a *kasrah* on the doubled *zāy*, as a past passive. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read *nazzala* (نَزَّلَ) with doubling, as a past active, whose subject is Allah, glorified is He. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read *anzala al-malāʾikata* (أنْزَلَ المَلائِكَةَ). It is also related from him that he read *tanazzalati al-malāʾikatu* (تَنَزَّلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ). Other readings have been transmitted as irregular (*shādhdh*).

The emphasis on this verb with the verbal noun ﴿تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("a descent") indicates that this descent is of a strange kind and of a wondrous manner. The scholars said: "This is a descent of good pleasure and mercy, not a descent of wrath and punishment."

**[Verse] "Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful"** (﴿المُلْكُ يَوْمَئِذٍ الحَقُّ لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾). *Al-mulk* (المُلْكُ) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) is an adjective of it, and *li-l-raḥmān* (لِلرَّحْمَنِ) is the predicate (*khabar*). This is what al-Zajjāj said. That is: the enduring sovereignty that does not cease belongs to the Most Merciful on that day, because sovereignty that passes away and ends is not sovereignty in reality. The benefit of restricting it by the time expression is that this sovereignty belongs to Him, glorified is He, exclusively on this day. As for the other days of the world, others have a sovereignty in appearance even if it is not real.

It was also said that the predicate of the subject is the time expression (*al-ẓarf*), and *al-ḥaqq* is an adjective of *al-mulk*. The meaning is: the enduring sovereignty belonging to the Most Merciful is exclusive on this day.

﴿وكانَ يَوْمًا عَلى الكافِرِينَ عَسِيرًا﴾ ("and it is a difficult day for the disbelievers"). That is: this day, although sovereignty on it belongs to Allah alone, is severe for the disbelievers, because of what befalls them on it and the punishment they receive after the reckoning is established. As for the believers, it is easy and not difficult, because of the honour and the great glad tidings they receive on it.

**[Verse] "And the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands"** (﴿ويَوْمَ يَعَضُّ الظّالِمُ عَلى يَدَيْهِ﴾). The time expression is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning "remember" (*wa-dhkur*), just as the first time expression, namely "the day the sky is split open," is governed by this same omitted verb. The apparent meaning is that the biting here is literal, and there is no obstacle to that nor any reason to interpret it otherwise.

It was also said that it is a metaphor for rage and regret. The intended "wrongdoer" is every wrongdoer who comes to that place and arrives at that station. The fact that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion does not preclude this. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion.

**[Verse] "He says, 'Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger'"** (﴿يَقُولُ يالَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا﴾). *Yaqūlu* (يَقُولُ) is in a position of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The content of the speech is: "Oh, I wish..." (*yā laytanī*). The addressee is omitted: "O people, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger." *Sabīlan* (سَبِيلًا) means a path, which is the path of truth; he would have walked on it until he was freed from these misleading matters. The intended meaning is following the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he brought.

**[Verse] "Oh woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend"** (﴿ياوَيْلَتى لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أتَّخِذْ فُلانًا خَلِيلًا﴾). This is a supplication against himself, invoking woe and perdition, for having taken as a close friend a disbeliever who misled him in the world. *Fulān* (فُلانٌ) is a substitute term for proper names.

Al-Naysābūrī said: Some scholars of the Arabic language claimed that the use of *fulān* is not established in eloquent speech except as a quotation. One does not say "So-and-so came to me," but one says "Zayd said: So-and-so came to me," because it is the name of the word which is the name-marker. Thus it occurs in the speech of Allah. It was said that *fulān* is a substitute for the proper name of a male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for the proper name of a female who has intellect. It was also said that it is a substitute for an indefinite male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for an indefinite female who has intellect. As for *al-fulān* and *al-fulānah*, they are substitutes for non-rational beings. *Fulu* (فُلُ) is restricted to the vocative except in cases of necessity, as in the words of the poet:

*"Fī lajjatin amsik fulānan ʿan Fulī"*
("In a deep sea, hold back so-and-so from such-and-such.")

And his saying:

*"Ḥaddithānī ʿan fulānin wa-Fulī"*
("Tell me about so-and-so and such-and-such.")

*Fulu* is not a shortened form (*murakhkhamah*) of *fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Abū Ḥayyān claimed that Ibn ʿUṣfūr and Ibn Mālik both made *fulān* a substitute for the proper name of one who has intellect.

Al-Ḥasan read *yā wayltī* (يا ويْلَتِي) with a clear *yā* (ي), and al-Dūrī read it with *imālah* (the vowel-raising of *alif*). Abū ʿAlī said: Abandoning *imālah* is better, because the original of this word is *yā*, then the *kasrah* was changed to a *fatḥah* and the *yā* to a *tā* (ت), fleeing from the *yā*. So whoever uses *imālah* returns to what was fled from.

**[Verse] "He has led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me"** (﴿لَقَدْ أضَلَّنِي عَنِ الذِّكْرِ بَعْدَ إذْ جاءَنِي﴾). That is: by Allah, this one whom I took as a close friend has indeed led me astray from the Qur'an, or from the admonition, or from the word of testimony, or from all of these, after it had come to me, and I had come under its influence and been able to receive it.

**[Verse] "And Satan is ever a deserter of man"** (﴿وكانَ الشَّيْطانُ لِلْإنْسانِ خَذُولًا﴾). *Al-khadhl* (الخَذْلُ) is abandoning help. From it comes the deserting (*khudhlān*) of Iblīs toward the polytheists, since they take him as an ally, then he abandons them when they call on him for help. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. It is possible that it is part of the speech of Allah, or part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that he called his friend "Satan" after having made him one who misleads. Or it is possible that by "Satan" he means Iblīs, because he is the one who made him patient toward keeping company with misleaders.

**[Verse] "And the Messenger says, 'My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned'"** (﴿وقالَ الرَّسُولُ يارَبِّ إنَّ قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا هَذا القُرْآنَ مَهْجُورًا﴾). This is conjoined to ﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("And those who do not expect to meet Us say") [al-Furqān: 21]. The meaning is: my people have taken this Qur'an, which I brought to them, which You commanded me to convey and sent me with, as something abandoned, left aside. They did not believe in it, nor did they accept it in any way.

It was also said that it derives from *hajara* (هَجَرَ), meaning to talk nonsense (*hadhā*). The meaning would then be that they took it as nonsensical talk and delirium. It was also said that the meaning of *mahjūran* (مَهْجُورًا) is "abandoned in it" (*mahjūran fīhi*), and then the preposition was omitted. Their abandonment of it is their saying: "It is sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients." This statement is what the Messenger (ﷺ) will say on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that it is a quotation of his saying (ﷺ) in the world.

**[Verse] "And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals"** (﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾). (p-1040) This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, has made for every one of the prophets who call to Allah an enemy from among the criminals of his people who opposes him. So do not despair, O Muhammad, for this is the practice of the prophets before you. Be patient as they were patient.

**[Verse] "And your Lord is sufficient as a guide and a helper"** (﴿وكَفى بِرَبِّكَ هادِيًا ونَصِيرًا﴾). The exegetes said: the *bāʾ* is superfluous (*zāʾidah*), meaning "Your Lord is sufficient." *Naṣīran* (نَصِيرًا) and *hādiyan* (هادِيًا) are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*), or as specifications (*tamyīz*). That is: He guides His servants to the interests of religion and of the world, and He helps them against their enemies.

**[Verse] "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"** (﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ القُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً واحِدَةً﴾). This is among their proposals and their obstinate demands. That is: Why did Allah not send down this Qur'an to us in one single installment, not divided into portions?

There is disagreement about who said this statement. It was said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was said that they are the Jews, who said: "Why did you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down?" This is a false claim and an untenable assertion, because those books were also sent down in portions, just as the Qur'an was, but they are obstinate, or ignorant, not knowing the manner in which the books of Allah, glorified is He, were sent down to His prophets.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it"). That is: We sent down the Qur'an in this way, in portions. The *kāf* (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is an indication of what is understood from their speech. That is: like that dispersed sending down which they criticized and proposed the opposite of, We sent it down so that We might strengthen your heart by this manner of sending down. For sending it down in portions, installment by installment, according to events, is closer to your memorizing it and your understanding of its meanings, and that is among the greatest causes of strengthening. The *lām* (ل) is connected to the omitted verb which we have assumed.

Abū Ḥātim said: Al-Akhfash said that it is the answer to an omitted oath. He said: This is a weak opinion. ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read *li-yuthabbita* (لِيُثَبِّتَ) with the third-person masculine, meaning Allah, glorified is He. It was also said that this word, namely *kadhālika* (كَذَلِكَ), is part of the speech of the polytheists, and the meaning is "like that," i.e., like the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. Thus one pauses at His saying "like that," then one begins with His saying ﴿لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("that We may strengthen your heart by it"), with the meaning: We sent it down to you in portions for this purpose. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is better and more excellent. Al-Naḥḥās said: The sending down of the Qur'an in installments was among the signs of prophethood, because they did not ask him about anything without being answered about it, and this could only come from a prophet. So that was a strengthening of his heart and of their hearts.

**[Verse] "And We have arranged it in gradual arrangement"** (﴿ورَتَّلْناهُ تَرْتِيلًا﴾). This is conjoined to the omitted verb. That is: thus We sent it down and arranged it in arrangement (*tartīlan*). The meaning of *tartīl* (التَّرْتِيل) is that one verse follows another. This was said by al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. It was also said that the meaning is that He made it clear with clarification. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās. Mujāhid said: some of it following some of it. Al-Suddī said: We distinguished it with distinction. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I know of *tartīl* only as verification and clarification.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned that they are refuted at every time, and their claim is rejected in every way and in every state. He said:

**[Verse] "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation"** (﴿ولا يَأْتُونَكَ بِمَثَلٍ إلّا جِئْناكَ بِالحَقِّ وأحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا﴾). That is: the polytheists do not come to you, O Muhammad, with any example (*mathal*) of their examples, among which are their obstinate proposals, except that We come to you, in response to their example, with the true answer, established, which nullifies what they brought of the example, crushes it, and repels it.

Thus the intended meaning of "example" here is the question and the proposal, and the intended meaning of "truth" is its answer, which cuts off its pretext, nullifies its doubt, and eradicates its root.

The meaning of *aḥsana tafsīran* (أحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا) is: We bring you the best explanation. So *aḥsana tafsīran* is conjoined to *al-ḥaqq*. The exception in His saying ﴿إلّا جِئْناكَ﴾ ("except that We bring you") is an incomplete exception (*mufarragh*), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. That is: they do not come to you with any example except in a state of Our coming to you with that.

Then He threatened these ignorant people and blamed them, saying:

**[Verse] "Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell"** (﴿الَّذِينَ يُحْشَرُونَ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ إلى جَهَنَّمَ﴾). That is: they will be gathered while upon their faces. The relative clause (*al-mawṣūl*) is the subject, and its predicate is *ulāʾika* (أُولَئِكَ, "those"). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who..." It is permissible to put it in the accusative as a dispraise.

The meaning of "gathered upon their faces" is that they will be dragged upon them to Hell.

**[Verse] "Those are worse in place"** (﴿أُولَئِكَ شَرٌّ مَكانًا﴾). That is: worse in station and in final destination.

**[Verse] "And more astray in way"** (﴿وأضَلُّ سَبِيلًا﴾). That is: more mistaken in path. That is because they have already become people of the Fire.

The exegesis of a verse like this has already been given in Surat Subḥān (al-Isrāʾ). It has been said that this is connected to His saying: ﴿أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا وأحْسَنُ مَقِيلًا﴾ ("The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place and finer in place of repose") [al-Furqān: 24].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verse 25–34 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent﴾. He said: Allah will gather the creation on the Day of Resurrection in one plain: the jinn, the humans, the animals, the beasts of prey, the birds, and all of creation. Then the lowest heaven will be split open, and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those on the earth of jinn, humans and all of creation. They will surround the jinn, the humans and all of creation. The people of the earth will say: "Is our Lord among you?" They will say: "No." Then the second heaven will be split open, and the same will be mentioned, and so on for each heaven until the seventh heaven. In each heaven there will be more than in the heaven before it. Then our Lord will descend in a shade of clouds, and around Him will be the Karubiyyun (the cherubim), who are more numerous than the inhabitants of the seven heavens, and the humans, and the jinn, and all of creation. They have horns like the joints of cucumbers, and they are beneath the Throne. They have a loud sound of glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), and sanctification of Allah, the Exalted. The distance between the sole of the foot of one of them and his ankle is a five-hundred-year journey; from his knee to his thigh is a five-hundred-year journey; from his thigh to his collarbone is a five-hundred-year journey; and what is above that is a five-hundred-year journey.

Its chain according to Ibn Jarir is thus: He said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, al-Hajjaj ibn Mubarak ibn Fudala narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, that he heard Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it with a chain thus: He said: Muhammad ibn ʿAmmar ibn al-Harith Mamul narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn Zayd, with it.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il narrated it with a chain. al-Suyuti said: it is sahih (sound) through the route of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: that Abu Muʿayt used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah without harming him, and he was a forbearing man. But the rest of the Quraysh, when they sat with him, would harm him. Abu Muʿayt had a close friend who was absent from him in Syria. The Quraysh said: "Abu Muʿayt has become a Sabian (has left his religion)." His friend arrived from Syria at night and said to his wife: "What has Muhammad done of what he was upon?" She said: "He has become more intense in his affair." He said: "What has my friend Abu Muʿayt done?" She said: "He has become a Sabian." So he spent a night of ill omen. When morning came, Abu Muʿayt came to him and greeted him, but he did not return the greeting. He said: "Why do you not return my greeting?" He said: "How can I return your greeting when you have turned away?" He said: "Has Quraysh really done this?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what will relieve their hearts if I do it?" He said: "Go to him in his gathering, spit in his face, and insult him with the most vile insult you know." He did so, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not respond except by wiping his face of the spittle. Then he turned to him and said: "If I find you outside the mountains of Makkah, I will strike your neck, patiently (ṣabran)." When the Day of Badr came and his companions went out, he refused to go out. His companions said to him: "Come out with us." He said: "This man promised me that if he found me outside the mountains of Makkah, he would strike my neck patiently." They said: "You have a red camel that cannot be overtaken; if there is defeat, you can fly on it." So he went out with them. When Allah defeated the polytheists and his camel carried him over rough ground, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took him captive, along with seventy men from Quraysh. Abu Muʿayt was brought before him, and he said: "Will you kill me from among these?" He said: "Yes, for what you spat in my face." So Allah revealed concerning Abu Muʿayt: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾ up to His words: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾.

Abu Nuʿaym narrated this story through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned that the friend of Abu Muʿayt was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾, that he said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, and they are the two friends in Hell."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, that he said: "The enemy of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Abu Jahl, and the enemy of Musa was Qarun, and Qarun was the cousin of Musa."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The polytheists said: "If Muhammad were a prophet as he claims, why would his Lord not send down the Qur'an all at once? It descends upon him one verse or two verses, one surah or two surahs." So Allah revealed in answer to what they said on His Prophet: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ up to ﴿and most misguided in way﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ that he said: "So that We may firm up your heart with it and bind your heart." ﴿And We have recited it in measured recitation﴾: he said: "We have made it come in installments (tarsil), one thing after another." ﴿And they bring you no example except that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾: he said: "If We had sent down the Qur'an all at once, then they asked you, you would not have had an answer for them. But We hold it back from you, so when they ask you, you answer."

(p-1039)

**[Verse] "And the day the sky is split open with clouds"** (﴿ويَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السَّماءُ بِالغَمامِ﴾). Here Allah, glorified is He, describes some of the events of the Day of Resurrection. *Tashaqqaq* means to split open or to be opened up. ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Waththáb, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr read *tashaqqaq* with a light *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ). Its underlying form is *tatashaqqaq* (تَتَشَقَّقُ). The rest read it with a doubled *shīn* (تَشَقَّقُ), by assimilation (*idghām*). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second. The meaning of "split open with the clouds" is that the sky splits open to release the clouds.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "The sky splits open while clouds are over it, just as you say: 'The prince rode out with his weapons (*bi-silāḥihi*),' meaning, 'with his weapons upon him,' and 'He went out in his clothes (*bi-thiyābihi*),' meaning, 'with his clothes upon him.'" The basis of what he said is that *bāʾ* (ب) and *ʿan* (عن) are interchangeable, as when you say: "I shot with the bow (*bi-l-qaws*)" and "I shot from the bow (*ʿan al-qaws*)."

It is related that the sky splits open to release a thin white cloud. It was also said that the sky splits open with the cloud that lies between it and the people.

The meaning is that the clouds split open when the sky splits open. It was also said that the sky splits open for the descent of the angels, as Allah, glorified is He, says after this: ﴿ونُزِّلَ المَلائِكَةُ تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("and the angels are sent down, a descent"). It was also said that the *bāʾ* in *bi-l-ghamām* (بِالغَمامِ) is causal (*sababiyyah*), meaning "because of the cloud," i.e., because of its emerging from it, as if the cloud were that by which the sky is split open. It was also said that the *bāʾ* is connected to an omitted element, meaning "accompanied by the cloud" (*mutalabbisah bi-l-ghamām*).

Ibn Kathīr read ﴿ونُنْزِلُ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ ("and We send down the angels") with a light *zāy*, from *al-inzāl* (الإنزال), with a *nūn* after it, a silent *nūn*, and a light *zāy* with a *kasrah*, as the imperfect of *anzala*. *Al-malāʾikata* (الملائكة) is in the accusative as the object.

The remaining canonical readers read ﴿ونُزِّلَ﴾ ("and [the angels] are sent down") with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn* and a *kasrah* on the doubled *zāy*, as a past passive. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read *nazzala* (نَزَّلَ) with doubling, as a past active, whose subject is Allah, glorified is He. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read *anzala al-malāʾikata* (أنْزَلَ المَلائِكَةَ). It is also related from him that he read *tanazzalati al-malāʾikatu* (تَنَزَّلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ). Other readings have been transmitted as irregular (*shādhdh*).

The emphasis on this verb with the verbal noun ﴿تَنْزِيلًا﴾ ("a descent") indicates that this descent is of a strange kind and of a wondrous manner. The scholars said: "This is a descent of good pleasure and mercy, not a descent of wrath and punishment."

**[Verse] "Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful"** (﴿المُلْكُ يَوْمَئِذٍ الحَقُّ لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾). *Al-mulk* (المُلْكُ) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) is an adjective of it, and *li-l-raḥmān* (لِلرَّحْمَنِ) is the predicate (*khabar*). This is what al-Zajjāj said. That is: the enduring sovereignty that does not cease belongs to the Most Merciful on that day, because sovereignty that passes away and ends is not sovereignty in reality. The benefit of restricting it by the time expression is that this sovereignty belongs to Him, glorified is He, exclusively on this day. As for the other days of the world, others have a sovereignty in appearance even if it is not real.

It was also said that the predicate of the subject is the time expression (*al-ẓarf*), and *al-ḥaqq* is an adjective of *al-mulk*. The meaning is: the enduring sovereignty belonging to the Most Merciful is exclusive on this day.

﴿وكانَ يَوْمًا عَلى الكافِرِينَ عَسِيرًا﴾ ("and it is a difficult day for the disbelievers"). That is: this day, although sovereignty on it belongs to Allah alone, is severe for the disbelievers, because of what befalls them on it and the punishment they receive after the reckoning is established. As for the believers, it is easy and not difficult, because of the honour and the great glad tidings they receive on it.

**[Verse] "And the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands"** (﴿ويَوْمَ يَعَضُّ الظّالِمُ عَلى يَدَيْهِ﴾). The time expression is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning "remember" (*wa-dhkur*), just as the first time expression, namely "the day the sky is split open," is governed by this same omitted verb. The apparent meaning is that the biting here is literal, and there is no obstacle to that nor any reason to interpret it otherwise.

It was also said that it is a metaphor for rage and regret. The intended "wrongdoer" is every wrongdoer who comes to that place and arrives at that station. The fact that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion does not preclude this. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion.

**[Verse] "He says, 'Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger'"** (﴿يَقُولُ يالَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا﴾). *Yaqūlu* (يَقُولُ) is in a position of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The content of the speech is: "Oh, I wish..." (*yā laytanī*). The addressee is omitted: "O people, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger." *Sabīlan* (سَبِيلًا) means a path, which is the path of truth; he would have walked on it until he was freed from these misleading matters. The intended meaning is following the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he brought.

**[Verse] "Oh woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend"** (﴿ياوَيْلَتى لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أتَّخِذْ فُلانًا خَلِيلًا﴾). This is a supplication against himself, invoking woe and perdition, for having taken as a close friend a disbeliever who misled him in the world. *Fulān* (فُلانٌ) is a substitute term for proper names.

Al-Naysābūrī said: Some scholars of the Arabic language claimed that the use of *fulān* is not established in eloquent speech except as a quotation. One does not say "So-and-so came to me," but one says "Zayd said: So-and-so came to me," because it is the name of the word which is the name-marker. Thus it occurs in the speech of Allah. It was said that *fulān* is a substitute for the proper name of a male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for the proper name of a female who has intellect. It was also said that it is a substitute for an indefinite male who has intellect, and *fulānah* for an indefinite female who has intellect. As for *al-fulān* and *al-fulānah*, they are substitutes for non-rational beings. *Fulu* (فُلُ) is restricted to the vocative except in cases of necessity, as in the words of the poet:

*"Fī lajjatin amsik fulānan ʿan Fulī"*
("In a deep sea, hold back so-and-so from such-and-such.")

And his saying:

*"Ḥaddithānī ʿan fulānin wa-Fulī"*
("Tell me about so-and-so and such-and-such.")

*Fulu* is not a shortened form (*murakhkhamah*) of *fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Abū Ḥayyān claimed that Ibn ʿUṣfūr and Ibn Mālik both made *fulān* a substitute for the proper name of one who has intellect.

Al-Ḥasan read *yā wayltī* (يا ويْلَتِي) with a clear *yā* (ي), and al-Dūrī read it with *imālah* (the vowel-raising of *alif*). Abū ʿAlī said: Abandoning *imālah* is better, because the original of this word is *yā*, then the *kasrah* was changed to a *fatḥah* and the *yā* to a *tā* (ت), fleeing from the *yā*. So whoever uses *imālah* returns to what was fled from.

**[Verse] "He has led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me"** (﴿لَقَدْ أضَلَّنِي عَنِ الذِّكْرِ بَعْدَ إذْ جاءَنِي﴾). That is: by Allah, this one whom I took as a close friend has indeed led me astray from the Qur'an, or from the admonition, or from the word of testimony, or from all of these, after it had come to me, and I had come under its influence and been able to receive it.

**[Verse] "And Satan is ever a deserter of man"** (﴿وكانَ الشَّيْطانُ لِلْإنْسانِ خَذُولًا﴾). *Al-khadhl* (الخَذْلُ) is abandoning help. From it comes the deserting (*khudhlān*) of Iblīs toward the polytheists, since they take him as an ally, then he abandons them when they call on him for help. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. It is possible that it is part of the speech of Allah, or part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that he called his friend "Satan" after having made him one who misleads. Or it is possible that by "Satan" he means Iblīs, because he is the one who made him patient toward keeping company with misleaders.

**[Verse] "And the Messenger says, 'My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned'"** (﴿وقالَ الرَّسُولُ يارَبِّ إنَّ قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا هَذا القُرْآنَ مَهْجُورًا﴾). This is conjoined to ﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("And those who do not expect to meet Us say") [al-Furqān: 21]. The meaning is: my people have taken this Qur'an, which I brought to them, which You commanded me to convey and sent me with, as something abandoned, left aside. They did not believe in it, nor did they accept it in any way.

It was also said that it derives from *hajara* (هَجَرَ), meaning to talk nonsense (*hadhā*). The meaning would then be that they took it as nonsensical talk and delirium. It was also said that the meaning of *mahjūran* (مَهْجُورًا) is "abandoned in it" (*mahjūran fīhi*), and then the preposition was omitted. Their abandonment of it is their saying: "It is sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients." This statement is what the Messenger (ﷺ) will say on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that it is a quotation of his saying (ﷺ) in the world.

**[Verse] "And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals"** (﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾). (p-1040) This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, has made for every one of the prophets who call to Allah an enemy from among the criminals of his people who opposes him. So do not despair, O Muhammad, for this is the practice of the prophets before you. Be patient as they were patient.

**[Verse] "And your Lord is sufficient as a guide and a helper"** (﴿وكَفى بِرَبِّكَ هادِيًا ونَصِيرًا﴾). The exegetes said: the *bāʾ* is superfluous (*zāʾidah*), meaning "Your Lord is sufficient." *Naṣīran* (نَصِيرًا) and *hādiyan* (هادِيًا) are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*), or as specifications (*tamyīz*). That is: He guides His servants to the interests of religion and of the world, and He helps them against their enemies.

**[Verse] "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"** (﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ القُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً واحِدَةً﴾). This is among their proposals and their obstinate demands. That is: Why did Allah not send down this Qur'an to us in one single installment, not divided into portions?

There is disagreement about who said this statement. It was said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was said that they are the Jews, who said: "Why did you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down?" This is a false claim and an untenable assertion, because those books were also sent down in portions, just as the Qur'an was, but they are obstinate, or ignorant, not knowing the manner in which the books of Allah, glorified is He, were sent down to His prophets.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it"). That is: We sent down the Qur'an in this way, in portions. The *kāf* (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is an indication of what is understood from their speech. That is: like that dispersed sending down which they criticized and proposed the opposite of, We sent it down so that We might strengthen your heart by this manner of sending down. For sending it down in portions, installment by installment, according to events, is closer to your memorizing it and your understanding of its meanings, and that is among the greatest causes of strengthening. The *lām* (ل) is connected to the omitted verb which we have assumed.

Abū Ḥātim said: Al-Akhfash said that it is the answer to an omitted oath. He said: This is a weak opinion. ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read *li-yuthabbita* (لِيُثَبِّتَ) with the third-person masculine, meaning Allah, glorified is He. It was also said that this word, namely *kadhālika* (كَذَلِكَ), is part of the speech of the polytheists, and the meaning is "like that," i.e., like the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. Thus one pauses at His saying "like that," then one begins with His saying ﴿لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾ ("that We may strengthen your heart by it"), with the meaning: We sent it down to you in portions for this purpose. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is better and more excellent. Al-Naḥḥās said: The sending down of the Qur'an in installments was among the signs of prophethood, because they did not ask him about anything without being answered about it, and this could only come from a prophet. So that was a strengthening of his heart and of their hearts.

**[Verse] "And We have arranged it in gradual arrangement"** (﴿ورَتَّلْناهُ تَرْتِيلًا﴾). This is conjoined to the omitted verb. That is: thus We sent it down and arranged it in arrangement (*tartīlan*). The meaning of *tartīl* (التَّرْتِيل) is that one verse follows another. This was said by al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. It was also said that the meaning is that He made it clear with clarification. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās. Mujāhid said: some of it following some of it. Al-Suddī said: We distinguished it with distinction. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I know of *tartīl* only as verification and clarification.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned that they are refuted at every time, and their claim is rejected in every way and in every state. He said:

**[Verse] "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation"** (﴿ولا يَأْتُونَكَ بِمَثَلٍ إلّا جِئْناكَ بِالحَقِّ وأحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا﴾).
