Then he would come to that well, lift that stone, and Allah would help him to lift it. He would lower his food and drink down to him, then replace the stone as it was. He continued like this for as long as Allah willed. Then one day he went out to gather firewood as he always did. He gathered his wood, bound his bundle, and finished with it. When he wanted to lift it, he was overcome by drowsiness, lay down and slept, and Allah struck upon his ears for years while he slept. Then he got up, stretched, turned onto his other side, and lay down, and Allah struck upon his ears for another seven years. Then he got up, lifted his bundle, and he did not think except that he had slept a single hour of the day. He came to the town and sold his bundle, then bought food and drink as he used to do. Then he went to the pit in its place where he had been, and searched for it but did not find it, for his people had come to have no need of it (وقد كان بدا لقومه فيه بد). So they brought him out, and they believed in him and affirmed him. The Prophet would ask them about that black man: 'What became of him?' They would say, 'We do not know,' until that Prophet died. Then Allah awakened the black man from his sleep after that. Indeed, that black man is the first to enter Paradise."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir after narrating it: "It contains strangeness and irregularity, and perhaps there is an interpolation (idraj) in it." End of quotation. This hadith is also mursal (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zurara ibn Awfa, who said: "The qarn (generation) is one hundred and twenty years." These same narrators also narrated from Qatada, who said: "The qarn is seventy years." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Salama, who said: "The qarn is one hundred years." It has also been reported with a marfu' attribution (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)) that he said: "The qarn is one hundred years," and [it is reported that he] said: "fifty years," and said: "The qarn is forty years."

I do not think any of that is authentic, since the term qarn has been applied to a group of people, as in the sound hadith: "The best of generations (qurun) is my generation."

Al-Hakim, in his book al-Kuna, narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached Ma'd ibn Adnan, he would stop and say: 'The genealogists have lied.'" Then [Ibn Abbas] said: Allah said: ﴿And generations in between, many﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And they had certainly passed by the town﴾ that it is Sodom, the town of Lot, which was rained upon with the evil rain, meaning stones.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Have you seen one who takes as his god his own desire?﴾ that he said: "A man used to worship a white stone for a period of time in the pre-Islamic era. When he found a stone more beautiful than it, he would cast it away and worship the other. So Allah revealed the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated regarding the verse that he said: "That disbeliever does not desire anything except that he follows it."

The lam in His words ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: "By Allah, We certainly gave Moses the Torah." Allah, exalted is He, mentioned a portion of the stories of the earlier peoples to console the Messenger (ﷺ), since the denial of prophets by their peoples is a habit of those who associate partners with Allah. This is not specific to Muhammad (ﷺ). Harun is in apposition (*ʿaṭf al-bayān*, an explanatory appositive). It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by *qaṭʿ* (a shift from apposition to an independent accusative). And *wazīran* is the second object. It has also been said that it is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), and that the second object is elsewhere, but the first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-wazīr* in the language is the one to whom one returns and by whose opinion one acts. *Al-wazar* is that which one takes refuge in, and from it comes ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11]. The explanation of *al-wazīr* has already been given in Surah Ta-Ha. Being a *wazīr* does not contradict prophethood, for prophets were sent in the same era, and they were commanded to support one another. Harun was Moses' *wazīr* at the beginning of the matter.

Because they were both prophets, they were addressed: ﴿Go to the people who denied Our signs﴾. These were Pharaoh and his people, and the signs are the nine that were mentioned earlier. Even though they had not denied them at the time Allah commanded Moses and Harun to go, but the denial occurred afterward, this past tense carries the meaning of the future, in the usual manner of Allah's reports. The meaning is: "Go to the people who will deny Our signs."

It has been said that they were described as deniers when the matter was narrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to show the reason for their deserving punishment.

It has been said that the intended meaning may be: "to the people whose condition came to be that they denied."

It has been said that the intended meaning of describing them as deniers at the time of sending is that they were deniers of the divine signs, and the intended meaning is not the signs of the message.

Al-Qushayri said: His saying, exalted is He, in another place ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24], does not contradict this, because when two are commanded, each one is commanded.

It is possible to say that the singling out of Moses for address in some places is because he was the principal in the message, and the joining of them in address is because both were sent together.

﴿So We destroyed them with destruction﴾. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "So they went to them, and they denied both of them, so We destroyed them." That is, We annihilated them as a consequence of that denial, with a great annihilation.

It has been said that the intended meaning of *tadmīr* (destruction) here is the judgment of it, because it did not occur immediately after Moses and Harun were sent to them, but after a period of time.

﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾. There are several views on the accusative of *qawm* (people). It is conjoined to the *hāʾ* and *mīm* in *dammarnāhum* (We destroyed them). Or it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning "remember." Or by a hidden verb explained by what follows, which is *aghraqnāhum* (We drowned them), meaning: "We drowned the people of Noah, We drowned them." Al-Farra' said that it is in the accusative governed by *aghraqnāhum* mentioned after it, without any hidden estimated verb explained by what follows. Al-Nahhas refuted this, saying that *aghraqnā* does not transitively take two objects so as to govern the attached pronoun and "the people of Noah." The meaning of ﴿when they denied the messengers﴾ is that they denied Noah and denied those before him among the messengers of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever denies one prophet has denied all the prophets. Their drowning was by the flood, as was mentioned earlier in Surah Hud. ﴿And We made them a sign for the people﴾: that is, We made their drowning, or their story, (p-1042) a sign for the people, that is, a lesson for all people in general, by which everyone who witnesses it and hears its report is admonished. ﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾: the intended wrongdoers are the people of Noah specifically. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is everyone who followed their path in denial. ﴿A painful punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Hereafter. The accusative of *ʿādan* (ʿĀd) is by conjunction to "the people of Noah." It has been said that it is by the place of "the wrongdoers." It has been said that it is the object of *jaʿalnāhum* (We made them). And Thamud is conjoined to ʿĀd. The story of ʿĀd and Thamud has been mentioned earlier.

﴿And the companions of the *Rass*﴾. *Al-Rass* in Arabic speech is a well that is not lined with stone, and its plural is *risās*. So said Abu ʿUbaydah, and from it is the poet's verse:

*They are travelling to their land, the Tanabilah, who dig out the rass wells.*

Al-Suddi said: it is a well in Antioch, in which they killed Habib the carpenter, and they were named after it. He is the companion of Ya-Sin who said ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 20]. Likewise said Muqatil, ʿIkrimah, and others.

It has been said: they are a people in Adharbayjan who killed their prophets, so their trees and crops dried up, and they died of hunger and thirst.

It has been said: they used to worship trees. It has been said: they used to worship idols, so Allah sent Shuʿayb to them, and they denied him and harmed him.

It has been said: they are a people to whom Allah sent a prophet, and they devoured him. It has been said: they are the People of the Trench.

It has been said: the *Rass* is the abandoned well mentioned earlier, and its companions are its people.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon) it is said: *al-Rass* is the name of a well that belonged to the remnant of Thamud. It has been said: *al-Rass* is water and palm trees belonging to the Banu Asad. It has been said: it is the accumulated snow in the mountains.

*Al-Rass* is also the name of a valley, and from it comes the verse of Zuhayr:

*They departed at dawn and became dusky at the pre-dawn, so they were for the valley of al-Rass like the hand to the mouth.*

*Al-Rass* also means reconciliation between people and corruption between them, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (*al-aḍdād*).

It has been said: they are the companions of Hanzalah ibn Safwan, and they are the ones Allah tested with the bird known as the *ʿanqāʾ* (phoenix).

﴿And generations between that, many﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it. *Qurūn* is the plural of *qarn* (generation), meaning people of generations. A *qarn* is one hundred years. It has been said: one hundred and twenty. It has been said: a *qarn* is forty years. The reference in His words "between that" is to the nations mentioned earlier. A speaker may mention various things and then refer to them with "that."

﴿And to each We struck examples﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning "and We warned each, We struck examples for them, and We clarified the proof for them, and We did not strike for them false examples as these disbelievers do." He made it accusative by an implied verb explained by what follows, because *ḥadhdharnā*, *dhakkarnā* and *andhharnā* (We warned, We reminded, We admonished) have the sense of *ḍarabnā* (We struck). It is also permissible that it is conjoined to what precedes, and the *tanwīn* (nunation) is a replacement for the omitted genitive noun, which is "the nations," meaning: "every nation, We struck examples for them." As for the second *kullan*, it is accusative by the verb that follows it. *Al-Tatbīr* is destruction by punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: everything that you break and crumble, you have *tabbartahu*. Al-Mu'arrij and al-Akhfash said: the meaning of ﴿We destroyed with destruction﴾ is "We annihilated with annihilation," where the *tāʾ* and *bāʾ* have replaced the *dāl* and *mīm*.

﴿And they certainly passed by the town which was rained upon with an evil rain﴾. This is a resumed sentence explaining their witnessing the traces of the destruction of some nations.

The meaning: "And they certainly passed by," that is, the polytheists of Makkah, "by the town of the people of Lut, which was rained upon with an evil rain," that is, it was destroyed by the stones with which they were rained upon. The accusative of *maṭar* (rain) is as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or as a second object, since the meaning is "I gave it and I bestowed upon it the evil rain," or as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a rain like the evil rain." Abu al-Samal read *al-sūʾ* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. The explanation of *al-sūʾ* has already been given in *Barāʾah* (Surah al-Tawbah).

﴿Did they not used to see it?﴾ The interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, meaning: they used to see the mentioned town when they travelled to Syria for trade, for they used to pass by it. The *fāʾ* is for conjunction to an implied element, meaning: "they did not look at it, so they did not see it." ﴿Rather, they used not to expect resurrection﴾. He, exalted is He, turned from what preceded regarding their not seeing those traces to their not expecting resurrection, which entails that they did not expect recompense. It is also possible that the meaning of *yarjūna* (they expect) is *yakhāfūna* (they fear).

﴿And when they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. That is: they take you only as a mockery, that is, one who is mocked at. He restricted their treatment of him to taking him in mockery. So the answer to *idhā* (when) is ﴿they take you﴾. It has been said that the answer is omitted, and it is "they say: Is this the one...?" On this view, the clause ﴿they take you only in mockery﴾ is parenthetical. The first view is preferable.

The clause ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause with an implied "saying," meaning: "saying, Is this...?" The demonstrative indicates their belittling of him and their mockery of him. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "Allah sent him." *Rasūlan* (as a messenger) is accusative as a circumstantial element, meaning "sent." The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is the relative clause. Its relative clause is:

﴿They almost led us astray from our gods﴾. That is, they said: "He almost led us astray: he would have turned us away from our gods, so that we would abandon their worship." The *in* here is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah*), and the pronoun of the matter is omitted, meaning: "indeed he almost turned us away from them."

﴿Had we not been steadfast in them﴾: that is, we restrained ourselves in their worship.

Then Allah, exalted is He, responded to them, saying: ﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in way﴾. That is: when they see the punishment of the Day of Resurrection that they deserve and merit because of their disbelief, who is further astray in path, that is, farther from the truth and guidance: they or the believers?

Then He, exalted is He, clarified for them that they have no basis for what they went to except imitation and following desire. So He said, marvelling at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿Have you seen one who has taken his desire as his god?﴾. He placed the second object first for emphasis, as you say, "I knew him departing, Zayd," meaning: he obeyed his desire with an obedience like the obedience to a god. That is: look at him, O Muhammad, and be amazed at him.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that he does not desire anything except that he follows it.

﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾. The interrogative is for denial and remoteness, meaning: "Would you then be a keeper over him and a guarantor, until you bring him back to faith and remove him from disbelief?" You are not able to do that and cannot manage it. Guidance and misguidance are not left to your will; you are only to deliver. It has been said that this verse is abrogated (*mansūkhah*, subject to *naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of fighting.

Then He, exalted is He, moved from the first denial to another denial, and said: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand?﴾. That is: do you think that most of them hear what you recite to them of the verses of the Qur'an and of the admonitions, or understand the meanings of that and comprehend it, so that you would be concerned for their affair and hope for their faith? They are not like that. Rather, they are like (p-1043) one who neither hears nor understands.

Then He, exalted is He, clarified their condition and cut off the hope of you regarding them, and said: ﴿They are not but like livestock﴾. That is: in benefiting from what they hear, they are only like beasts that are deprived of understanding and reason, so do not hope for them. For the benefit of hearing and understanding is lost in them, even though they hear what is said to them and understand what is recited to them. But because they did not benefit from that, they were like one who lacks it.

Then He, exalted is He, turned from judging them as being like livestock to something above that, and said: ﴿Rather, they are more astray in way﴾. That is: more astray in path than livestock. Muqatil said: beasts know their Lord and are guided to their pastures and submit to their owners, but these do not submit and do not know their Lord who created them and provided for them. It has been said: they were more astray than livestock because there is no reckoning for livestock and no punishment for them. It has also been said: they were more astray because beasts, when they do not understand the validity of monotheism and prophethood, do not believe in the falsity of that, unlike these, for they believed in falsehood out of obstinacy, arrogance, fanaticism and rejection of the truth.

And ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made with him his brother Harun as a minister﴾, that he said: "a helper and a support." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿So We destroyed them with destruction﴾, that he said: "We annihilated them with punishment."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, saying: "*al-Rass* is a town of Thamud." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, saying: "*al-Rass* is a well in Adharbayjan." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he asked Kaʿb about the companions of the *Rass*, and he said: "The companion of Ya-Sin, who said ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 20], and his people threw him into a well with stones."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 35–44 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of mankind to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection will be the black slave. That is because Allah sent a prophet to the people of a town, and none of its people believed in him except that black man. Then the people of the town went out to the Prophet, dug a well for him, threw him into it, and then sealed it over with a huge rock. That slave would go and gather firewood, carrying it on his back, then bring his firewood and sell it, and with it buy food and drink. Then he would come to that well, lift that stone, and Allah would help him to lift it. He would lower his food and drink down to him, then replace the stone as it was. He continued like this for as long as Allah willed. Then one day he went out to gather firewood as he always did. He gathered his wood, bound his bundle, and finished with it. When he wanted to lift it, he was overcome by drowsiness, lay down and slept, and Allah struck upon his ears for years while he slept. Then he got up, stretched, turned onto his other side, and lay down, and Allah struck upon his ears for another seven years. Then he got up, lifted his bundle, and he did not think except that he had slept a single hour of the day. He came to the town and sold his bundle, then bought food and drink as he used to do. Then he went to the pit in its place where he had been, and searched for it but did not find it, for his people had come to have no need of it (وقد كان بدا لقومه فيه بد). So they brought him out, and they believed in him and affirmed him. The Prophet would ask them about that black man: 'What became of him?' They would say, 'We do not know,' until that Prophet died. Then Allah awakened the black man from his sleep after that. Indeed, that black man is the first to enter Paradise."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir after narrating it: "It contains strangeness and irregularity, and perhaps there is an interpolation (idraj) in it." End of quotation. This hadith is also mursal (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zurara ibn Awfa, who said: "The qarn (generation) is one hundred and twenty years." These same narrators also narrated from Qatada, who said: "The qarn is seventy years." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Salama, who said: "The qarn is one hundred years." It has also been reported with a marfu' attribution (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)) that he said: "The qarn is one hundred years," and [it is reported that he] said: "fifty years," and said: "The qarn is forty years."

I do not think any of that is authentic, since the term qarn has been applied to a group of people, as in the sound hadith: "The best of generations (qurun) is my generation."

Al-Hakim, in his book al-Kuna, narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached Ma'd ibn Adnan, he would stop and say: 'The genealogists have lied.'" Then [Ibn Abbas] said: Allah said: ﴿And generations in between, many﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And they had certainly passed by the town﴾ that it is Sodom, the town of Lot, which was rained upon with the evil rain, meaning stones.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Have you seen one who takes as his god his own desire?﴾ that he said: "A man used to worship a white stone for a period of time in the pre-Islamic era. When he found a stone more beautiful than it, he would cast it away and worship the other. So Allah revealed the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated regarding the verse that he said: "That disbeliever does not desire anything except that he follows it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 45–60 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted finished mentioning the ignorance and misguidance of the ignorant, He followed it with a portion of the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), together with what they contain of great bounty. The first of them is the argument from the state of the shadow. He said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shadow?﴾ This seeing (ru'yah) is either visual, and the meaning is "Have you not looked at the handiwork of your Lord," or "Have you not looked at the shadow, how your Lord extended it." Or it is of the heart, in the sense of knowledge, since the shadow is changing, and everything changing is originated, and for every originated thing there is an originator.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Alam tara" means "Did you not know," and this is seeing of the heart. He said: this speech is on the (reversed) order, and the sense is: "Have you not considered the shadow, how your Lord extended it," meaning the shadow from the time of dawn until the sun rises, which is a shadow with no sun in it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said that it is from the setting of the sun until its rising.

(p-1044) Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-zill (shade) is in the morning, and al-fay' (shade after noon) is in the evening, because it returns after the sun passes its zenith. It was called fay' because it "returned" (fa'a) from the east toward the west.

Humayd ibn Thawr said, describing an acacia tree and using it as a metaphor for a woman:
"Neither does the shade bear the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shade after noon taste the chill of the evening."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-zill is what the sun has erased, and al-fay' is what has erased the sun. Abu 'Ubaydah related from Ru'bah that he said: "Whatever the sun has been upon and then left, is fay' and zill; and whatever the sun has not been upon, is zill." End of quotation.

The reality of the shade is that it is an intermediate matter between pure light and pure darkness. This intermediate state is more balanced than the two extremes, because pure darkness is disliked by the nature and repulsive to the senses, while complete light, because of its intensity, dazzles the sense of sight and harms through heat. For this reason the Garden was described with it, in His saying: ﴿and an extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]. The clause ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾ is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. That is: if He willed, He would have prevented the sun from rising. The first (interpretation) is preferable.

Expressing "stillness" as residence and settledness is permissible, and from it comes the saying: "So-and-so dwelt (sakana) in such-and-such a land," when he resided there and settled in it.

His saying ﴿Then We made the sun over it a guide﴾ is conjoined to His saying "extended the shade" and falls under its ruling. That is: We made it (the sun) a sign by which its states are used as a proof for His states, because the shade follows it as a guide follows on the road, in that it grows with it and diminishes, extends and contracts.

His saying ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ is also conjoined to "extended" and falls under its ruling. The meaning: Then We withdrew that extended shade and erased it, as the sun's rays gradually reached its place, until that shading came to nothing and vanished. It was also said: the intended meaning in the verse is its withdrawal at the Hour, by the withdrawal of its causes, which are the luminous bodies. The first is preferable.

The meaning is that the shade remains in this atmosphere from the rising of dawn until the sun rises. When the sun rises, the shade is withdrawn, and behind it in this atmosphere are the sun's rays, so it shines upon the earth and upon things until its setting. When it sets, there is no shade there, but only the remnant of the daylight's light. Some people said: He withdrew it by the setting of the sun, because if the sun has not set, shade still remains in it, and its disappearance is only complete with the coming of night and the entry of darkness upon it.

It was also said: the meaning is: Then We drew in the sun's light into the shade with a gentle drawing, and the meaning of "to Us" is that its return is to Him, the Exalted, just as its coming into being is from Him, a gentle drawing, that is, gradually, little by little, according to the rising of the sun. It was said: "gently" (yasiran) means "swiftly." It was said: the meaning is "easily upon Us," that is, its withdrawal is easy for Us and not difficult.

﴿And He is the One who made the night for you as a garment﴾: He, the Exalted, likened what is covered by the darkness of night to a concealing garment. Ibn Jarir said: He described the night with a garment as a comparison, in that it conceals things and covers them. The lam (in "for you") is connected to "made" (ja'ala). ﴿and sleep as rest (subat)﴾: that is, and He made sleep "subat," that is, a rest for you, because you are cut off from occupations. The root of subat is stretching out. It is said: the woman "sabatat" her hair, meaning she loosed it and let it down; and a man is "masbut," meaning of stretched-out build.

It was also said: sleep is called subat because it occurs by stretching out, and in stretching out there is the meaning of rest. It was also said: al-sabt is cutting off, so sleep is a cutting off from occupations, and from it comes the "sabt" of the Jews, because they were cut off from occupations.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-subat is sleep, which is to be cut off from movement while the spirit is in the body, that is: He made your sleep a rest for you.

Al-Khalil said: al-subat is heavy sleep, that is: He made your sleep heavy so that the repose and rest would be complete. ﴿and made the day a resurrection (nushur)﴾: that is, a time of rising from that subat. He likened wakefulness to life, just as He likened sleep to subat, which resembles death. In al-Kashshaf it is said that subat is death, and it is deduced from this that "resurrection" is in opposition to it.

﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as heralds of His mercy﴾: it is read al-rih (the wind, singular), and it is read bushran (as glad tidings), with the single ba' and with nun. The tafsir of this verse has been fully discussed before in al-A'raf. ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water (ma'an tahuran)﴾: that is, by which one purifies oneself, just as one says "wudu'" (ablution) for the water with which one performs ablution.

Al-Azhari said: al-tahur in the language is the pure and purifying (thing), and al-tuhur is that by which one purifies oneself. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-tahur, with a fatha on the ta', is the noun, as is al-wada' and al-waqud, and with a damma it is the verbal noun. This is what is known in the language. The majority have held that al-tahur is the pure and purifying, and this is supported by its being a form of intensification.

It is related from Abu Hanifah that he said: al-tahur is the pure, and he cited for that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord gives them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21], meaning pure. From it comes the saying of the poet:
"O my two companions, is there in a glance, after repentance, a remedy by which I may heal my heart from my transgression?
Toward plump-buttocked, tender gazelles, whose sweet front teeth and saliva are pure."
So he described the saliva as tahur, and it is not purifying. Tha'lab preferred the first view, and it is the stronger, because of what al-Azhari related from the people of the language earlier.

As for the poet's description of saliva as tahur, it is by way of exaggeration. In any case, the Shari'ah has come with the ruling that water is pure in itself and purifying to others. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He sends down upon you from the sky water to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Water was created pure (tahuran)."

Then He mentioned the cause of the sending down. He said: ﴿That We may give life thereby﴾: that is, by the water sent down from the sky, to a land (baldatan) dead (maytan). He described the land (baldah) as maytan, and it is an adjective of the masculine form because it is in the sense of al-balad (the land, masculine).

Al-Zajjaj said: by "al-balad" he meant the place, and by "giving life" here is meant the bringing forth of vegetation from the place in which there is no vegetation. ﴿and that We give it to drink, to cattle and to many people (anasiyya kathiran)﴾: that is, We give that water to drink. Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in one narration from them, and Abu Hayyan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah, read nasqiyahu with a fatha on the nun, and the rest read it with a damma. The min in "mimma khalaqna" is for the beginning (of the extent), and it is connected to nusqiyahu. It is permissible for it to be connected to something omitted, as a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-an'am (cattle) has already been discussed. Al-anasi is the plural of insan (human) according to the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said it is the plural of insi (human, relative adjective). Al-Farra' has another opinion: that it is the plural of insan, and the original is "anasin," like sarhan and sarahin, and bustan and basatin, so they made the ba' a substitute for the nun.

﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember﴾: the pronoun in "sarrafnahu" (We have distributed it)

(p-1045) The majority held that it refers to the signs mentioned, that is: We repeated the states of shading, and the mention of the formation of clouds and the sending down of rain in the Qur'an and in all the heavenly books, so that they might reflect and take heed. ﴿But most people refused except disbelief (kufuran) and denial of it.﴾ Others said it refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the rain, that is: We distributed the rain among them in the different lands, so We increase in some lands and decrease in others. It was also said the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, whose mention occurred at the beginning of the surah where He said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. And His saying ﴿He has indeed led me astray from the reminder after it had come to me﴾ [al-Furqan: 29], and His saying ﴿Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30]. The meaning: We have certainly repeated this Qur'an by sending down its verses among people, that they might remember by it and take heed of what is in it, but most of them refused ﴿except disbelief (kufur)﴾ in it. It was also said it refers to the wind. As for the return of the pronoun to the rain, its meaning has been differed upon. It was said: what we mentioned. It was also said: We distributed it among them as heavy rain, drizzle, light rain and fine mist. It was also said: its distribution is the diversification of benefit from it in drinking, watering, cultivation and purification.

'Ikrimah said: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿But most people refused except disbelief﴾ is their saying: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (naw')."

'Ikrimah read sarafnahu with a light (unstressed) form, and the rest read it with the intensive form.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read liyadhdhakaru with a light dhal from dhikr (remembrance), and the rest read it with the intensive form from tadhakkur (reflection).

﴿And had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner (nadhiran)﴾: that is, a messenger who warns them, just as We divided the rain among them. But We did not do that; rather We appointed one warner, and he is you, O Muhammad. So respond to that with thankfulness for the blessing.

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they call you to of following their gods. Rather, strive in the call and be steadfast in it. The pronoun in His saying ﴿and strive against them with it, a great striving (jihadan kabiran)﴾ refers to the Qur'an, that is: strive against them with the Qur'an, and recite to them what it contains of thunderbolts, admonitions, commands and prohibitions.

It was said: the pronoun refers to Islam. It was said: with the sword. The first is preferable. This surah is Meccan, and the command to fight came only after the Hijrah. It was also said: the pronoun refers to abandoning obedience, understood from His saying ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾. It was also said: the pronoun refers to what His saying ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾ indicates, because if He, the Exalted, had raised a warner in every town, then each warner would only have struggled against the town to which he was sent. But when He limited Himself to one warner for all the towns, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ), then all forms of striving gathered upon him, so his striving became great, grew mighty, and comprised every kind of striving. The distance in these two views is not hidden.

Then He mentioned a fourth proof for tawhid, and said: ﴿And He is the One who released the two seas (maraja al-bahrayn)﴾. Maraja means: left free, mixed, and let loose. It is said: "I released the animal (marajtu al-dabbah) and I let it loose (amrajtuha)," when I let it go to pasture and left it free to go wherever it wished. Mujahid said: He let them loose, and one of them flows into the other.

Ibn 'Arafah said: He mixed them, so they meet. It is said: "I mixed it (marajtuhu)" when I blended it, and "al-din and al-amr marija" means it became mixed and disordered, and from it comes His saying ﴿in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5]. Al-Azhari said: ﴿maraja al-bahrayn﴾ means "He left them between them," as one says "the animal released (maraja)" when I let it graze. Tha'lab said: al-maraj is making to run, so His saying ﴿maraja al-bahrayn﴾ means He made them run. Al-Akhfash said: some people say "amraja al-bahrayn," like maraja; fa'ala and af'ala have the same meaning.

﴿This one is sweet, pleasant to drink (furat)﴾: al-furat is the one extremely sweet. This clause is a resumed statement, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "How did He let them loose?" So it was said: "This is sweet and this is salty." It is also permissible that it is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

It is said that sweet water is called *furat* because it "breaks" thirst (*yafrutu al-ʿatash*), meaning it cuts through and breaks it. ﴿And this is salty, bitter﴾: that is, intensely salty. This is the meaning of *ujaj* (*ujaj*, intensely brackish). It is also said that *ujaj* means intensely hot, or intensely bitter. Talha read *milh* (مَلِحٌ) with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *lam*.

﴿And He placed between them a barrier (*barzakh*) and a forbidding partition (*hijran mahjuran*)﴾: the *barzakh* is the barrier and separator which Allah, by His power, placed between them, separating them and preventing them from mixing (*al-tamaruj*). The meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is a concealed cover that is kept hidden, preventing one of them from mixing with the other. So the *barzakh* is the barrier, and the *hajr* is the preventing.

It is also said that the meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is what has preceded, that it is a word that one seeking refuge says, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says this word to it. It is also said: a limit that is fixed. It is also said: what is meant by the sweet sea is the great rivers such as the Nile, the Euphrates and the Jayhun, and what is meant by the salty sea is the well-known seas, and the *barzakh* between them is the land that intervenes.

It is also said: the meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is "forbidden and prohibited", that this salty water should not become sweet through the sweet, or that this sweet water should not become salty through the salty. A similar verse is His saying, glorified is He, in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side. Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾ [al-Rahman: 19–20]. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned a state among the conditions of the creation of man and of water, saying: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage﴾. What is meant by "water" here is the water of the sperm-drop (*nutfah*), that is, He created a human from the water of the sperm-drop and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage. It is also said: what is meant by "water" is water in general, which is meant in His saying: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30]. What is meant by *nasab* (lineage) is the relationship within which marriage is not permitted.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the derivation of *sihr* (marriage relation, *ṣihr*) is from *ṣahartu al-shayʾ*, when you mix a thing. Marriages were called *ṣihr* because of the mixing of people through them. It is also said: *ṣihr* is the kinship of marriage. The kinship of the wife are the *akhtan* (her male relatives by marriage), and the kinship of the husband are the *aḥmā'* (his female relatives by marriage), and *aṣhār* (in-laws) includes both. This is what al-Asma'i said.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: *nasab* consists of seven categories of kinship, which His saying gathers: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. From here up to His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] is prohibition through *ṣihr*, which is the close association that resembles kinship. Allah prohibited seven categories by lineage and seven by *ṣihr*. The aforementioned verse includes six of them, and the seventh is His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Zajjaj and others made nursing (*al-riḍaʿ*) part of lineage, and this is supported by his saying (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace): "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing."

﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾: that is, of perfect and great power. Among His overwhelming power is the creation of man and His division of him into the two categories mentioned (p-1046).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾, that he said: after dawn and before the sun rises.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him with the wording: "Have you not considered that when you pray the dawn prayer, there is a shade between the rising of the sun and its setting? Then Allah sends the sun upon it as a guide, and it withdraws the shade."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding the verse, that he said: the extension of the shade is what is between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun. ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾: he said: permanently. ﴿Then We made the sun its guide﴾: he says: the rising of the sun. ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us, a gradual withdrawal﴾: he said: swiftly.

The compilers of the Sunan (*Ahl al-Sunan*) and Ahmad and others transmitted from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, shall we perform ablution from the well of Bud'a? It is a well into which menstrual rags, dog meat and filth are thrown. He said: Indeed, water is pure (*ṭahūr*), nothing makes it impure."

There is a lengthy discussion concerning the chain of this hadith, which we have fully covered in our commentary on al-Muntaqa.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "There is no year with less rain than another year, but Allah diverts it wherever He wills." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember﴾, and so on.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And strive against them with it﴾ that he said: with the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding ﴿And it is He who released the two seas﴾, that it means He mixed one of them with the other, yet the sweet does not corrupt the salty and the salty does not corrupt the sweet.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿and a forbidding partition﴾, that he said: He kept one of them apart from the other by His command and decree.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughira, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab was asked about ﴿lineage and marriage﴾, and he said: "I think you know what lineage is. As for marriage, it is the in-laws and the companions."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 45–60 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted finished mentioning the ignorance and misguidance of the ignorant, He followed it with a portion of the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), together with what they contain of great bounty. The first of them is the argument from the state of the shadow. He said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shadow?﴾ This seeing (ru'yah) is either visual, and the meaning is "Have you not looked at the handiwork of your Lord," or "Have you not looked at the shadow, how your Lord extended it." Or it is of the heart, in the sense of knowledge, since the shadow is changing, and everything changing is originated, and for every originated thing there is an originator.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Alam tara" means "Did you not know," and this is seeing of the heart. He said: this speech is on the (reversed) order, and the sense is: "Have you not considered the shadow, how your Lord extended it," meaning the shadow from the time of dawn until the sun rises, which is a shadow with no sun in it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said that it is from the setting of the sun until its rising.

(p-1044) Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-zill (shade) is in the morning, and al-fay' (shade after noon) is in the evening, because it returns after the sun passes its zenith. It was called fay' because it "returned" (fa'a) from the east toward the west.

Humayd ibn Thawr said, describing an acacia tree and using it as a metaphor for a woman:
"Neither does the shade bear the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shade after noon taste the chill of the evening."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-zill is what the sun has erased, and al-fay' is what has erased the sun. Abu 'Ubaydah related from Ru'bah that he said: "Whatever the sun has been upon and then left, is fay' and zill; and whatever the sun has not been upon, is zill." End of quotation.

The reality of the shade is that it is an intermediate matter between pure light and pure darkness. This intermediate state is more balanced than the two extremes, because pure darkness is disliked by the nature and repulsive to the senses, while complete light, because of its intensity, dazzles the sense of sight and harms through heat. For this reason the Garden was described with it, in His saying: ﴿and an extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]. The clause ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾ is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. That is: if He willed, He would have prevented the sun from rising. The first (interpretation) is preferable.

Expressing "stillness" as residence and settledness is permissible, and from it comes the saying: "So-and-so dwelt (sakana) in such-and-such a land," when he resided there and settled in it.

His saying ﴿Then We made the sun over it a guide﴾ is conjoined to His saying "extended the shade" and falls under its ruling. That is: We made it (the sun) a sign by which its states are used as a proof for His states, because the shade follows it as a guide follows on the road, in that it grows with it and diminishes, extends and contracts.

His saying ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ is also conjoined to "extended" and falls under its ruling. The meaning: Then We withdrew that extended shade and erased it, as the sun's rays gradually reached its place, until that shading came to nothing and vanished. It was also said: the intended meaning in the verse is its withdrawal at the Hour, by the withdrawal of its causes, which are the luminous bodies. The first is preferable.

The meaning is that the shade remains in this atmosphere from the rising of dawn until the sun rises. When the sun rises, the shade is withdrawn, and behind it in this atmosphere are the sun's rays, so it shines upon the earth and upon things until its setting. When it sets, there is no shade there, but only the remnant of the daylight's light. Some people said: He withdrew it by the setting of the sun, because if the sun has not set, shade still remains in it, and its disappearance is only complete with the coming of night and the entry of darkness upon it.

It was also said: the meaning is: Then We drew in the sun's light into the shade with a gentle drawing, and the meaning of "to Us" is that its return is to Him, the Exalted, just as its coming into being is from Him, a gentle drawing, that is, gradually, little by little, according to the rising of the sun. It was said: "gently" (yasiran) means "swiftly." It was said: the meaning is "easily upon Us," that is, its withdrawal is easy for Us and not difficult.

﴿And He is the One who made the night for you as a garment﴾: He, the Exalted, likened what is covered by the darkness of night to a concealing garment. Ibn Jarir said: He described the night with a garment as a comparison, in that it conceals things and covers them. The lam (in "for you") is connected to "made" (ja'ala). ﴿and sleep as rest (subat)﴾: that is, and He made sleep "subat," that is, a rest for you, because you are cut off from occupations. The root of subat is stretching out. It is said: the woman "sabatat" her hair, meaning she loosed it and let it down; and a man is "masbut," meaning of stretched-out build.

It was also said: sleep is called subat because it occurs by stretching out, and in stretching out there is the meaning of rest. It was also said: al-sabt is cutting off, so sleep is a cutting off from occupations, and from it comes the "sabt" of the Jews, because they were cut off from occupations.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-subat is sleep, which is to be cut off from movement while the spirit is in the body, that is: He made your sleep a rest for you.

Al-Khalil said: al-subat is heavy sleep, that is: He made your sleep heavy so that the repose and rest would be complete. ﴿and made the day a resurrection (nushur)﴾: that is, a time of rising from that subat. He likened wakefulness to life, just as He likened sleep to subat, which resembles death. In al-Kashshaf it is said that subat is death, and it is deduced from this that "resurrection" is in opposition to it.

﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as heralds of His mercy﴾: it is read al-rih (the wind, singular), and it is read bushran (as glad tidings), with the single ba' and with nun. The tafsir of this verse has been fully discussed before in al-A'raf. ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water (ma'an tahuran)﴾: that is, by which one purifies oneself, just as one says "wudu'" (ablution) for the water with which one performs ablution.

Al-Azhari said: al-tahur in the language is the pure and purifying (thing), and al-tuhur is that by which one purifies oneself. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-tahur, with a fatha on the ta', is the noun, as is al-wada' and al-waqud, and with a damma it is the verbal noun. This is what is known in the language. The majority have held that al-tahur is the pure and purifying, and this is supported by its being a form of intensification.

It is related from Abu Hanifah that he said: al-tahur is the pure, and he cited for that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord gives them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21], meaning pure. From it comes the saying of the poet:

﴿And He placed between them a barrier (*barzakh*) and a forbidding partition (*hijran mahjuran*)﴾: the *barzakh* is the barrier and separator which Allah, by His power, placed between them, separating them and preventing them from mixing (*al-tamaruj*). The meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is a concealed cover that is kept hidden, preventing one of them from mixing with the other. So the *barzakh* is the barrier, and the *hajr* is the preventing.

It is also said that the meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is what has preceded, that it is a word that one seeking refuge says, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says this word to it. It is also said: a limit that is fixed. It is also said: what is meant by the sweet sea is the great rivers such as the Nile, the Euphrates and the Jayhun, and what is meant by the salty sea is the well-known seas, and the *barzakh* between them is the land that intervenes.

It is also said: the meaning of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ is "forbidden and prohibited", that this salty water should not become sweet through the sweet, or that this sweet water should not become salty through the salty. A similar verse is His saying, glorified is He, in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side. Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾ [al-Rahman: 19–20]. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned a state among the conditions of the creation of man and of water, saying: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage﴾. What is meant by "water" here is the water of the sperm-drop (*nutfah*), that is, He created a human from the water of the sperm-drop and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage. It is also said: what is meant by "water" is water in general, which is meant in His saying: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30]. What is meant by *nasab* (lineage) is the relationship within which marriage is not permitted.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the derivation of *sihr* (marriage relation, *ṣihr*) is from *ṣahartu al-shayʾ*, when you mix a thing. Marriages were called *ṣihr* because of the mixing of people through them. It is also said: *ṣihr* is the kinship of marriage. The kinship of the wife are the *akhtan* (her male relatives by marriage), and the kinship of the husband are the *aḥmā'* (his female relatives by marriage), and *aṣhār* (in-laws) includes both. This is what al-Asma'i said.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: *nasab* consists of seven categories of kinship, which His saying gathers: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. From here up to His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] is prohibition through *ṣihr*, which is the close association that resembles kinship. Allah prohibited seven categories by lineage and seven by *ṣihr*. The aforementioned verse includes six of them, and the seventh is His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Zajjaj and others made nursing (*al-riḍaʿ*) part of lineage, and this is supported by his saying (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace): "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing."

﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾: that is, of perfect and great power. Among His overwhelming power is the creation of man and His division of him into the two categories mentioned (p-1046).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾, that he said: after dawn and before the sun rises.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him with the wording: "Have you not considered that when you pray the dawn prayer, there is a shade between the rising of the sun and its setting? Then Allah sends the sun upon it as a guide, and it withdraws the shade."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding the verse, that he said: the extension of the shade is what is between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun. ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾: he said: permanently. ﴿Then We made the sun its guide﴾: he says: the rising of the sun. ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us, a gradual withdrawal﴾: he said: swiftly.

The compilers of the Sunan (*Ahl al-Sunan*) and Ahmad and others transmitted from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, shall we perform ablution from the well of Bud'a? It is a well into which menstrual rags, dog meat and filth are thrown. He said: Indeed, water is pure (*ṭahūr*), nothing makes it impure."

There is a lengthy discussion concerning the chain of this hadith, which we have fully covered in our commentary on al-Muntaqa.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "There is no year with less rain than another year, but Allah diverts it wherever He wills." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember﴾, and so on.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And strive against them with it﴾ that he said: with the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding ﴿And it is He who released the two seas﴾, that it means He mixed one of them with the other, yet the sweet does not corrupt the salty and the salty does not corrupt the sweet.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿and a forbidding partition﴾, that he said: He kept one of them apart from the other by His command and decree.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughira, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab was asked about ﴿lineage and marriage﴾, and he said: "I think you know what lineage is. As for marriage, it is the in-laws and the companions."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 45–60 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted finished mentioning the ignorance and misguidance of the ignorant, He followed it with a portion of the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), together with what they contain of great bounty. The first of them is the argument from the state of the shadow. He said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shadow?﴾ This seeing (ru'yah) is either visual, and the meaning is "Have you not looked at the handiwork of your Lord," or "Have you not looked at the shadow, how your Lord extended it." Or it is of the heart, in the sense of knowledge, since the shadow is changing, and everything changing is originated, and for every originated thing there is an originator.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Alam tara" means "Did you not know," and this is seeing of the heart. He said: this speech is on the (reversed) order, and the sense is: "Have you not considered the shadow, how your Lord extended it," meaning the shadow from the time of dawn until the sun rises, which is a shadow with no sun in it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said that it is from the setting of the sun until its rising.

(p-1044) Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-zill (shade) is in the morning, and al-fay' (shade after noon) is in the evening, because it returns after the sun passes its zenith. It was called fay' because it "returned" (fa'a) from the east toward the west.

Humayd ibn Thawr said, describing an acacia tree and using it as a metaphor for a woman:
"Neither does the shade bear the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shade after noon taste the chill of the evening."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-zill is what the sun has erased, and al-fay' is what has erased the sun. Abu 'Ubaydah related from Ru'bah that he said: "Whatever the sun has been upon and then left, is fay' and zill; and whatever the sun has not been upon, is zill." End of quotation.

The reality of the shade is that it is an intermediate matter between pure light and pure darkness. This intermediate state is more balanced than the two extremes, because pure darkness is disliked by the nature and repulsive to the senses, while complete light, because of its intensity, dazzles the sense of sight and harms through heat. For this reason the Garden was described with it, in His saying: ﴿and an extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]. The clause ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾ is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. That is: if He willed, He would have prevented the sun from rising. The first (interpretation) is preferable.

Expressing "stillness" as residence and settledness is permissible, and from it comes the saying: "So-and-so dwelt (sakana) in such-and-such a land," when he resided there and settled in it.

His saying ﴿Then We made the sun over it a guide﴾ is conjoined to His saying "extended the shade" and falls under its ruling. That is: We made it (the sun) a sign by which its states are used as a proof for His states, because the shade follows it as a guide follows on the road, in that it grows with it and diminishes, extends and contracts.

His saying ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ is also conjoined to "extended" and falls under its ruling. The meaning: Then We withdrew that extended shade and erased it, as the sun's rays gradually reached its place, until that shading came to nothing and vanished. It was also said: the intended meaning in the verse is its withdrawal at the Hour, by the withdrawal of its causes, which are the luminous bodies. The first is preferable.

The meaning is that the shade remains in this atmosphere from the rising of dawn until the sun rises. When the sun rises, the shade is withdrawn, and behind it in this atmosphere are the sun's rays, so it shines upon the earth and upon things until its setting. When it sets, there is no shade there, but only the remnant of the daylight's light. Some people said: He withdrew it by the setting of the sun, because if the sun has not set, shade still remains in it, and its disappearance is only complete with the coming of night and the entry of darkness upon it.

It was also said: the meaning is: Then We drew in the sun's light into the shade with a gentle drawing, and the meaning of "to Us" is that its return is to Him, the Exalted, just as its coming into being is from Him, a gentle drawing, that is, gradually, little by little, according to the rising of the sun. It was said: "gently" (yasiran) means "swiftly." It was said: the meaning is "easily upon Us," that is, its withdrawal is easy for Us and not difficult.

﴿And He is the One who made the night for you as a garment﴾: He, the Exalted, likened what is covered by the darkness of night to a concealing garment. Ibn Jarir said: He described the night with a garment as a comparison, in that it conceals things and covers them. The lam (in "for you") is connected to "made" (ja'ala). ﴿and sleep as rest (subat)﴾: that is, and He made sleep "subat," that is, a rest for you, because you are cut off from occupations. The root of subat is stretching out. It is said: the woman "sabatat" her hair, meaning she loosed it and let it down; and a man is "masbut," meaning of stretched-out build.

It was also said: sleep is called subat because it occurs by stretching out, and in stretching out there is the meaning of rest. It was also said: al-sabt is cutting off, so sleep is a cutting off from occupations, and from it comes the "sabt" of the Jews, because they were cut off from occupations.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-subat is sleep, which is to be cut off from movement while the spirit is in the body, that is: He made your sleep a rest for you.

Al-Khalil said: al-subat is heavy sleep, that is: He made your sleep heavy so that the repose and rest would be complete. ﴿and made the day a resurrection (nushur)﴾: that is, a time of rising from that subat. He likened wakefulness to life, just as He likened sleep to subat, which resembles death. In al-Kashshaf it is said that subat is death, and it is deduced from this that "resurrection" is in opposition to it.

Al-Azhari said: al-tahur in the language is the pure and purifying (thing), and al-tuhur is that by which one purifies oneself. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-tahur, with a fatha on the ta', is the noun, as is al-wada' and al-waqud, and with a damma it is the verbal noun. This is what is known in the language. The majority have held that al-tahur is the pure and purifying, and this is supported by its being a form of intensification.

It is related from Abu Hanifah that he said: al-tahur is the pure, and he cited for that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord gives them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21], meaning pure. From it comes the saying of the poet:
"O my two companions, is there in a glance, after repentance, a remedy by which I may heal my heart from my transgression?
Toward plump-buttocked, tender gazelles, whose sweet front teeth and saliva are pure."
So he described the saliva as tahur, and it is not purifying. Tha'lab preferred the first view, and it is the stronger, because of what al-Azhari related from the people of the language earlier.

As for the poet's description of saliva as tahur, it is by way of exaggeration. In any case, the Shari'ah has come with the ruling that water is pure in itself and purifying to others. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He sends down upon you from the sky water to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Water was created pure (tahuran)."

He described the land (baldah) as maytan, and it is an adjective of the masculine form because it is in the sense of al-balad (the land, masculine).

Al-Zajjaj said: by "al-balad" he meant the place, and by "giving life" here is meant the bringing forth of vegetation from the place in which there is no vegetation. ﴿and that We give it to drink, to cattle and to many people (anasiyya kathiran)﴾: that is, We give that water to drink. Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in one narration from them, and Abu Hayyan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah, read nasqiyahu with a fatha on the nun, and the rest read it with a damma. The min in "mimma khalaqna" is for the beginning (of the extent), and it is connected to nusqiyahu. It is permissible for it to be connected to something omitted, as a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-an'am (cattle) has already been discussed. Al-anasi is the plural of insan (human) according to the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said it is the plural of insi (human, relative adjective). Al-Farra' has another opinion: that it is the plural of insan, and the original is "anasin," like sarhan and sarahin, and bustan and basatin, so they made the ba' a substitute for the nun.

﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember﴾: the pronoun in "sarrafnahu" (We have distributed it)

(p-1045) The majority held that it refers to the signs mentioned, that is: We repeated the states of shading, and the mention of the formation of clouds and the sending down of rain in the Qur'an and in all the heavenly books, so that they might reflect and take heed. ﴿But most people refused except disbelief (kufuran) and denial of it.﴾ Others said it refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the rain, that is: We distributed the rain among them in the different lands, so We increase in some lands and decrease in others. It was also said the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, whose mention occurred at the beginning of the surah where He said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. And His saying ﴿He has indeed led me astray from the reminder after it had come to me﴾ [al-Furqan: 29], and His saying ﴿Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30]. The meaning: We have certainly repeated this Qur'an by sending down its verses among people, that they might remember by it and take heed of what is in it, but most of them refused ﴿except disbelief (kufur)﴾ in it. It was also said it refers to the wind. As for the return of the pronoun to the rain, its meaning has been differed upon. It was said: what we mentioned. It was also said: We distributed it among them as heavy rain, drizzle, light rain and fine mist. It was also said: its distribution is the diversification of benefit from it in drinking, watering, cultivation and purification.

'Ikrimah said: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿But most people refused except disbelief﴾ is their saying: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (naw')."

'Ikrimah read sarafnahu with a light (unstressed) form, and the rest read it with the intensive form.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read liyadhdhakaru with a light dhal from dhikr (remembrance), and the rest read it with the intensive form from tadhakkur (reflection).

﴿And had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner (nadhiran)﴾: that is, a messenger who warns them, just as We divided the rain among them. But We did not do that; rather We appointed one warner, and he is you, O Muhammad. So respond to that with thankfulness for the blessing.

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they call you to of following their gods. Rather, strive in the call and be steadfast in it. The pronoun in His saying ﴿and strive against them with it, a great striving (jihadan kabiran)﴾ refers to the Qur'an, that is: strive against them with the Qur'an, and recite to them what it contains of thunderbolts, admonitions, commands and prohibitions.

It was said: the pronoun refers to Islam. It was said: with the sword. The first is preferable. This surah is Meccan, and the command to fight came only after the Hijrah. It was also said: the pronoun refers to abandoning obedience, understood from His saying ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾. It was also said: the pronoun refers to what His saying ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾ indicates, because if He, the Exalted, had raised a warner in every town, then each warner would only have struggled against the town to which he was sent. But when He limited Himself to one warner for all the towns, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ), then all forms of striving gathered upon him, so his striving became great, grew mighty, and comprised every kind of striving. The distance in these two views is not hidden.

Mujahid said: He let them loose, and one of them flows into the other.

Ibn 'Arafah said: He mixed them, so they meet. Al-Akhfash said: some people say "amraja al-bahrayn," like maraja; fa'ala and af'ala have the same meaning.

﴿This one is sweet, pleasant to drink (furat)﴾: al-furat is the one extremely sweet. This clause is a resumed statement, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "How did He let them loose?" So it was said: "This is sweet and this is salty."
