Al-Nahhas said: among the best of what has been said about the meaning of the verse is: whoever spends in other than the obedience of Allah is extravagant; whoever withholds from the obedience of Allah is stingy; and whoever spends in the obedience of Allah is moderate (*qawām*). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it is the one who does not go hungry or naked, and does not spend (excessively) such that people say, "He has been extravagant."

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "Those are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They would not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty; rather they wanted from food only what would ward off their hunger and strengthen them for the worship of Allah, and from clothing only what would cover their nakedness and protect them from heat and cold."

Abu Ubayda said: "They did not exceed what is reasonable, nor were they stingy," like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29].

Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿and between that is a *qiwām*﴾ with a *kasrah* on the *qāf*, while the rest read it with a *fatḥah*. It has been said that both have the same meaning. It has also been said: *al-qiwām* with a *kasrah* is what a thing is sustained by and remains steadfast upon, while with a *fatḥah* it means justice and uprightness; this was said by Tha'lab.

It has been said: with a *fatḥah*, it means justice between two things; with a *kasrah*, it is what sustains a thing, which is neither in excess nor deficient.

It has been said: with a *kasrah*, it means sufficiency and the appropriate measure. The subject of *kāna* is implied in it, meaning: their expenditure was between that. *Bayna* is built on the *fatḥah* because it is one of the adverbs of place that are *mabni* on the *fatḥah*.

Al-Nahhas said: "I do not know what the reason for this is, because when *bayna* is in a position of *raf'* (nominative), it is inflected."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the disbeliever is an aide against his Lord﴾, that it refers to Abu al-Hakam, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the words ﴿Say, "I do not ask of you any reward for it"﴾, that he said: "Say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to; it is only a thing from the goods of this world."

Al-Khatib narrated in *Kitab al-Nujum* from him as well, concerning the words ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾, that he said: "They are these twelve constellations: first Aries, then Taurus, then Gemini, then Cancer, then Leo, then Virgo, then Libra, then Scorpio, then Sagittarius, then Capricorn, then Aquarius, then Pisces."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, that he said: "(One is) white and (the other) black."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well, saying: "Whatever of the night a person has missed of doing (good) he can make up during the day, and whatever of the day he has missed he can make up at night."

Al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that 'Umar prolonged the Duha prayer, and it was said to him: "You have done today something you did not used to do." He said: "Some of my daily portion (*wird*) remained for me, so I wanted to complete it," or he said: "to fulfill it," and he recited this verse: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, that he said: "They are the believers ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾," he said: "with obedience, chastity and humility."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Hawnan*: with knowledge and forbearance."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning the words ﴿Indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment﴾, that he said: "The lasting one."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, that he said: "They are the believers who are not extravagant, spending in disobedience to Allah, and who are not stingy, withholding the rights of Allah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah (the Exalted) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), He returned to mentioning the disgraceful acts of the disbelievers and the shameful aspects of their conduct, so He said: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what neither benefits them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harms them﴾ if they abandon it. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a supporter (zahir) against his Lord﴾. The word ẓahīr means one who backs or supports, that is, one who aids against his Lord through shirk (associating partners with God) and hostility. Backing against the Lord is backing against His Messenger or against His religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: Because he follows Satan and helps him in disobeying Allah, since their worship of idols is an aid to Satan.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever contemptible (hayyin) and humiliated against his Lord﴾, from the saying of the Arabs, "I cast him behind (ẓahartu bihi)," meaning, "I made him behind your back, so you do not pay attention to him." From this is His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (ẓihriyyan)﴾ [Hud: 92], meaning, "as something insignificant." From this too is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Badr, let not my need be cast behind your back, lest its answer fail me."

It was also said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever powerful against his Lord﴾, meaning the one he worships, which is the idol, is strong and dominant, doing with him whatever it wills, since inanimate matter has no power to harm or benefit. It is permissible for ẓahīr to be a plural, like His saying: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporting host (ẓahīr)﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The meaning then is that some disbelievers support others against the Messenger of Allah or against a religion. The intended meaning of "the disbeliever" here is the category, and this does not conflict with the fact that the cause of revelation was a specific disbeliever, as it is said it was Abu Jahl.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, meaning a bringer of good tidings to the believers of Paradise and a warner to the disbelievers of the Fire.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "I do not ask you for any wage for the Qur'an," or for conveying the message, which is indicated by "sent." The exception in His saying: ﴿except for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning, "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It was also said that it is connected (muttaṣil).

The meaning, according to the connected reading, is: "except for whoever wills to draw near to Him, the Exalted, through obedience," and He framed this in the form of a wage, insofar as it is something intended to be obtained.

When the Exalted explained that the disbelievers are backing one another against the Messenger of Allah, and commanded him not to seek any wage from them at all, He commanded him to rely upon Him in warding off harms and bringing about benefits.

So He said: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾. He specified the attribute of life to indicate that the living one is the one in whom trust is placed for matters of benefit, and that lasting life belongs to Allah alone, the Exalted, and not to living beings whose lives come to an end, for when they die, whoever relies upon them is lost. Tawakkul (reliance) is the servant's dependence upon Allah in all affairs. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾, meaning, declare Him free of the attributes of deficiency. It was also said: The meaning of sabbiḥ (glorify) is pray (ṣalli), since prayer is called tasbih. ﴿And He is sufficient as one aware of the sins of His servants﴾, meaning, "He is sufficient for you." This is an expression used for emphasis, like your saying: "Allah is sufficient as a Lord." Khabīr means one who is informed of matters to such a degree that nothing of them is hidden from Him.

Then He increased the emphasis and said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Aʿraf. The relative pronoun (alladhī) is in the genitive position as an attribute of al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living). He said baynihumā ("between them," dual) and did not say baynahunna (feminine plural), because He meant the two categories, just as al-Quṭāmī said:

"Does it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have been split apart, separated?"

If it is objected that this implies the creation of the Throne came after the creation of the heavens and the earth, as thumma (then) indicates, the reply is: The word thumma did not enter upon the creation of the Throne, but upon its elevation above the heavens and the earth. Al-Raḥmān is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is a second attribute of al-Ḥayy. The majority read it with the nominative. It was also said that it may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in istawā, or that it may be a subject whose predicate is the clause, meaning: "then ask," according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, as in the verse of the poet:

"A speaker said: Khawlān, so marry their girls."

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read al-Raḥmāni in the genitive as an attribute of al-Ḥayy or of the relative pronoun.

﴿So ask about Him, one who is aware (khabīran)﴾. The pronoun in bihi refers to what was mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth and the establishment upon the Throne. The meaning is: ask about the details of these matters which were mentioned in summary.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: The bāʾ (in bihi) has the meaning of ʿan (about), meaning, "ask about Him," like His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will occur﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 1], and the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Would that you had asked the horses, daughter of Malik, if you are ignorant of what you do not know."

Imru' al-Qays also said:

"So if you ask me about women, I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."

The intended meaning of "the Aware" is Allah, the Exalted, because no one knows the details of those created things except Him. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "If you met so-and-so, the lion would meet you because of it," meaning, "the lion would meet you by your meeting with it." So khabīran is in the accusative either as an object or as a circumstantial emphatic accusative (ḥāl muʾakkida). Abu al-Baqāʾ considered the circumstantial reading weak, saying: "It is weak for khabīran to be a circumstantial accusative of the subject of isʾal (ask), because the Aware is only asked in the manner of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿And it is the truth confirming﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91; Fatir: 31]." He said: "It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial accusative of al-Raḥmān if you make it nominative with istawā."

Ibn Jarir said: It is permissible for the bāʾ in bihi to be extra (zāʾida). The meaning is: "ask Him while He is Aware."

It was said: His saying "bihi" functions as an oath, like His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 1]. The first of these interpretations is the closest of them.

Then the Exalted informed about them that they were ignorant of the meaning of al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ The exegetes said: They said, "We do not know al-Raḥmān except the Raḥmān of Yamamah," meaning Musaylima. Al-Zajjaj said: Al-Raḥmān is one of the names of Allah. When they heard it, they denied it and said, "And what is al-Raḥmān?" ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ The interrogative is for denial, meaning: We will not prostrate to the Most Merciful whom you command us to prostrate to. Whoever reads with the yāʾ (taḥtiyya, third person) means: "Shall we prostrate to what Muhammad commands us to prostrate to?"

The people of Medina and Basra read ﴿what you command us﴾ with the tāʾ (second person). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Al-Aʿmash, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read it with the yāʾ. Abu ʿUbayd said: They mean al-Raḥmān. Al-Nahhas said: It is not necessary to interpret the Kufans' reading with this distant interpretation. Rather, the better interpretation is that the meaning for them is "prostrate to what the Prophet (ﷺ) commands," and the reading then becomes this, though the first is clearer.

﴿And it increased them in aversion﴾, meaning: the command to prostrate increased them in aversion from the religion and distance from it. It was also said: the mention of al-Raḥmān increased them in distance from faith. Muqatil said this, but the first is preferable.

Then the Exalted mentioned what, if they had reflected upon it, would have made them know the obligation of prostrating to al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burūj)﴾. The intended meaning of burūj is the constellations of the stars, meaning their twelve stations. It was said: they are the large stars, but the first is preferable. They were called burūj, which are lofty palaces, because they are for the planets like lofty dwellings for those who reside in them. The derivation of burj is from tabarruj (display), which means appearance. ﴿And placed therein a lamp (sirājan)﴾, meaning the sun. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]. The majority read sirājan in the singular. Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read surujan in the plural, meaning the great blazing stars. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

Al-Zajjaj said: In explaining the reading of Hamza and al-Kisaʾi, they meant the sun and the planets. ﴿And a luminous moon (qamaran munīran)﴾, meaning it gives light to the earth when it rises. Al-Aʿmash read qumran with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. This is a weak, anomalous (shādhdh) reading.

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession (khilfatan)﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: Khilfa means everything that comes after something else. The night is khilfa for the day and the day is khilfa for the night, because each of them succeeds the other and comes after it. From this is the khilfa of plants, which is a leaf that emerges after the first leaf in summer. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"In them the gazelles and the wild cattle walk in succession, and their young rise up from every resting place."

Al-Farra said in explaining the verse: It means one goes and another comes. Mujahid said: Khilfa is from khilaf (difference): this is white and that is black. It was also said: they alternate in light and darkness, and in increase and decrease.

It was also said: It is of the figure of omitting the modified noun, meaning: He made the night and the day possessors of succession, that is, difference.

﴿For whoever wills to remember (yadhdhakkara)﴾. Hamza read it lightened (yadhkura), and the majority read it with shadda (yadhdhakkara). So the first reading is from dhikr (remembrance) of Allah, and the second reading is from tadhakkur (remembering, reflecting) of Him. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read yatadhakkaru. The meaning of the verse is that the one who remembers and takes heed, when he looks at the alternation of night and day, knows that in their transition from state to state there must be an agent of change.

﴿Or wills gratitude (shukūran)﴾, meaning, wills to thank Allah for the great blessings and abundant kindnesses that He deposited in the night and the day. Al-Farra said: yudhakkiru and yatadhakkaru come with one meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) it is: "and they remember what is in it" (wa-yadhkurū mā fīhi).

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾. This is a new sentence brought to explain the righteous servants of Allah, the Exalted. "And the servants of the Most Merciful" is the subject, and its predicate is the relative clause with its complement. Hawn is a verbal noun, and it means tranquility and dignity.

A group of exegetes went to the view that hawnan is connected to yamshūna, meaning they walk upon the earth walking in humility. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It seems that this should be interpreted as meaning that the character of the one who walks is "humble" appropriate to his walk. As for the meaning being the attribute of walking alone, it is false, because many a man walks humbly and gently while being a sly wolf. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to walk with a forward lean in his stride, as if he were walking downhill.

﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. The Exalted mentioned that they bear what comes to them of harm from the people of ignorance and folly, so they do not respond to ignorance with ignorance, nor do they engage in foolishness with the foolish.

Al-Nahhas said: This "peace" is not from greeting (taslīm) but from being free of something (tasallum). The Arabs say salāman, meaning "a disavowal from you," that is, "innocence from you." It is in the accusative in one of two ways: either it is a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning "they say: we make peace, peace," and this is according to Sibawayh's view, or it is an object, meaning "they say this word." Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred this.

Mujahid said: The meaning of salāman is "rightness (sadād)," meaning he says to the ignorant a statement that repels him with gentleness and softness.

Sibawayh said: The Muslims were not commanded on that day to greet the polytheists, but this is according to his saying: "[We say] a greeting from you, and there is no good or evil between us and you."

Al-Mubarrad said: It should have been said that the Muslims were not commanded that day to fight them, then they were commanded to fight them.

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: Sibawayh erred in this and expressed it badly.

Al-Nahhas said: We know of no statement by Sibawayh concerning abrogation (naskh) and the abrogated except in this verse, for he said at the end of his statement, "then the verse of the sword abrogated it."

I say: This is how a man's speech is when he speaks without knowledge and walks without following the proper path. The Muslims were not commanded to greet the polytheists, nor were they forbidden from it. Rather, they were commanded to pardon and to observe a beautiful avoidance (al-hajr al-jamīl), so there is no need to claim abrogation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-Khalil told me: "I came to Abu Rabi'a al-A'rabi, who was among the most knowledgeable people I had seen. He was on a roof, so we greeted him, and he returned our greeting and said to us: *istawū* ("Stand level" / "Rise up"). We remained bewildered and did not know what he meant. A Bedouin beside him said to us: 'He told you to get up.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿Then He rose over the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]." He said: "So we climbed up to him, and he said: 'Would you like some leavened bread and warm milk?' We said: 'We have just left,' so he said: '*Salaman*' ('Peace'). We did not know what he meant, so the Bedouin said: 'He has greeted you with *mutarakah*, a parting that has neither good nor evil in it.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'﴾."

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. *Al-baytutah* (spending the night) is that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep. Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever the night overtakes has spent the night, whether he sleeps or does not sleep, as one says: 'So-and-so spent the night anxious.'" The meaning is: they spend the night before their Lord prostrating on their faces and standing on their feet. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"So we spent the night standing at the head of our horse, / it wrestles with us over its own self, and we wrestle with it."*

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment"﴾. That is: despite their obedience, they are fearful, anxious and afraid of His punishment. *Al-gharam* means the constant, enduring (torment). From it comes the word *al-gharim* (the creditor/debtor), because of his persistence in demanding. It is said: "So-and-so is *mughram* with such-and-such," meaning he is persistently attached to it and devoted to it. This is its meaning in the language of the Arabs, as mentioned by Ibn al-A'rabi, Ibn Arafa and others. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"If He punishes, it will be a lasting torment; / and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-gharam* is the most severe punishment. Abu Ubayda said: it is destruction. Ibn Zayd said: it is evil.

The clause ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a dwelling place and a station﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it. The predicate being specified is omitted, meaning "it" (Hell). The accusative of *mustaqarran* is either a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, indicating a state) or a *tamyiz* (specificative accusative, clarifying a noun), and likewise *muqaman*. It has been said that both are synonyms, and one was joined to the other only because their wording differs. It has also been said that they differ in meaning: *mustaqarr* is for the disobedient, who will be taken out (of Hell), while *muqam* is for the disbelievers, who will remain forever. *Sā'at* is among the verbs of blame, like *bi'sat*. It is possible that this is from the words of Allah, glorified is He, and it is also possible that it is a quotation of their words.

Then He described them, glorified is He, by moderation in spending, saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, 'Asim and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *yaqtarū* with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, from *qatara yaqturu* like *qa'ada yaq'udu*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*, which is a well-known and good dialect. The people of Madinah, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Abu Ubayda said: it is said *qatara al-rajulu 'alā 'iyālihi yaqturu*, *yaqturu qatran*, and *aqtara yuqtiru iqtāran*; the meaning of all of them is restricting expenditure.

Al-Nahhas said: among the best of what has been said about the meaning of the verse is: whoever spends in other than the obedience of Allah is extravagant; whoever withholds from the obedience of Allah is stingy; and whoever spends in the obedience of Allah is moderate (*qawām*). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it is the one who does not go hungry or naked, and does not spend (excessively) such that people say, "He has been extravagant."

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "Those are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They would not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty; rather they wanted from food only what would ward off their hunger and strengthen them for the worship of Allah, and from clothing only what would cover their nakedness and protect them from heat and cold."

Abu Ubayda said: "They did not exceed what is reasonable, nor were they stingy," like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29].

Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿and between that is a *qiwām*﴾ with a *kasrah* on the *qāf*, while the rest read it with a *fatḥah*. It has been said that both have the same meaning. It has also been said: *al-qiwām* with a *kasrah* is what a thing is sustained by and remains steadfast upon, while with a *fatḥah* it means justice and uprightness; this was said by Tha'lab.

It has been said: with a *fatḥah*, it means justice between two things; with a *kasrah*, it is what sustains a thing, which is neither in excess nor deficient.

It has been said: with a *kasrah*, it means sufficiency and the appropriate measure. The subject of *kāna* is implied in it, meaning: their expenditure was between that. *Bayna* is built on the *fatḥah* because it is one of the adverbs of place that are *mabni* on the *fatḥah*.

Al-Nahhas said: "I do not know what the reason for this is, because when *bayna* is in a position of *raf'* (nominative), it is inflected."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the disbeliever is an aide against his Lord﴾, that it refers to Abu al-Hakam, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the words ﴿Say, "I do not ask of you any reward for it"﴾, that he said: "Say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to; it is only a thing from the goods of this world."

Al-Khatib narrated in *Kitab al-Nujum* from him as well, concerning the words ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾, that he said: "They are these twelve constellations: first Aries, then Taurus, then Gemini, then Cancer, then Leo, then Virgo, then Libra, then Scorpio, then Sagittarius, then Capricorn, then Aquarius, then Pisces."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, that he said: "(One is) white and (the other) black."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well, saying: "Whatever of the night a person has missed of doing (good) he can make up during the day, and whatever of the day he has missed he can make up at night."

Al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that 'Umar prolonged the Duha prayer, and it was said to him: "You have done today something you did not used to do." He said: "Some of my daily portion (*wird*) remained for me, so I wanted to complete it," or he said: "to fulfill it," and he recited this verse: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, that he said: "They are the believers ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾," he said: "with obedience, chastity and humility."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Hawnan*: with knowledge and forbearance."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning the words ﴿Indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment﴾, that he said: "The lasting one."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, that he said: "They are the believers who are not extravagant, spending in disobedience to Allah, and who are not stingy, withholding the rights of Allah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah (the Exalted) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), He returned to mentioning the disgraceful acts of the disbelievers and the shameful aspects of their conduct, so He said: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what neither benefits them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harms them﴾ if they abandon it. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a supporter (zahir) against his Lord﴾. The word ẓahīr means one who backs or supports, that is, one who aids against his Lord through shirk (associating partners with God) and hostility. Backing against the Lord is backing against His Messenger or against His religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: Because he follows Satan and helps him in disobeying Allah, since their worship of idols is an aid to Satan.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever contemptible (hayyin) and humiliated against his Lord﴾, from the saying of the Arabs, "I cast him behind (ẓahartu bihi)," meaning, "I made him behind your back, so you do not pay attention to him." From this is His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (ẓihriyyan)﴾ [Hud: 92], meaning, "as something insignificant." From this too is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Badr, let not my need be cast behind your back, lest its answer fail me."

It was also said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever powerful against his Lord﴾, meaning the one he worships, which is the idol, is strong and dominant, doing with him whatever it wills, since inanimate matter has no power to harm or benefit. It is permissible for ẓahīr to be a plural, like His saying: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporting host (ẓahīr)﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The meaning then is that some disbelievers support others against the Messenger of Allah or against a religion. The intended meaning of "the disbeliever" here is the category, and this does not conflict with the fact that the cause of revelation was a specific disbeliever, as it is said it was Abu Jahl.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, meaning a bringer of good tidings to the believers of Paradise and a warner to the disbelievers of the Fire.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "I do not ask you for any wage for the Qur'an," or for conveying the message, which is indicated by "sent." The exception in His saying: ﴿except for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning, "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It was also said that it is connected (muttaṣil).

The meaning, according to the connected reading, is: "except for whoever wills to draw near to Him, the Exalted, through obedience," and He framed this in the form of a wage, insofar as it is something intended to be obtained.

When the Exalted explained that the disbelievers are backing one another against the Messenger of Allah, and commanded him not to seek any wage from them at all, He commanded him to rely upon Him in warding off harms and bringing about benefits.

So He said: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾. He specified the attribute of life to indicate that the living one is the one in whom trust is placed for matters of benefit, and that lasting life belongs to Allah alone, the Exalted, and not to living beings whose lives come to an end, for when they die, whoever relies upon them is lost. Tawakkul (reliance) is the servant's dependence upon Allah in all affairs. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾, meaning, declare Him free of the attributes of deficiency. It was also said: The meaning of sabbiḥ (glorify) is pray (ṣalli), since prayer is called tasbih. ﴿And He is sufficient as one aware of the sins of His servants﴾, meaning, "He is sufficient for you." This is an expression used for emphasis, like your saying: "Allah is sufficient as a Lord." Khabīr means one who is informed of matters to such a degree that nothing of them is hidden from Him.

Then He increased the emphasis and said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Aʿraf. The relative pronoun (alladhī) is in the genitive position as an attribute of al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living). He said baynihumā ("between them," dual) and did not say baynahunna (feminine plural), because He meant the two categories, just as al-Quṭāmī said:

"Does it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have been split apart, separated?"

If it is objected that this implies the creation of the Throne came after the creation of the heavens and the earth, as thumma (then) indicates, the reply is: The word thumma did not enter upon the creation of the Throne, but upon its elevation above the heavens and the earth. Al-Raḥmān is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is a second attribute of al-Ḥayy. The majority read it with the nominative. It was also said that it may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in istawā, or that it may be a subject whose predicate is the clause, meaning: "then ask," according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, as in the verse of the poet:

"A speaker said: Khawlān, so marry their girls."

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read al-Raḥmāni in the genitive as an attribute of al-Ḥayy or of the relative pronoun.

﴿So ask about Him, one who is aware (khabīran)﴾. The pronoun in bihi refers to what was mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth and the establishment upon the Throne. The meaning is: ask about the details of these matters which were mentioned in summary.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: The bāʾ (in bihi) has the meaning of ʿan (about), meaning, "ask about Him," like His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will occur﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 1], and the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Would that you had asked the horses, daughter of Malik, if you are ignorant of what you do not know."

Imru' al-Qays also said:

"So if you ask me about women, I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."

The intended meaning of "the Aware" is Allah, the Exalted, because no one knows the details of those created things except Him. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "If you met so-and-so, the lion would meet you because of it," meaning, "the lion would meet you by your meeting with it." So khabīran is in the accusative either as an object or as a circumstantial emphatic accusative (ḥāl muʾakkida). Abu al-Baqāʾ considered the circumstantial reading weak, saying: "It is weak for khabīran to be a circumstantial accusative of the subject of isʾal (ask), because the Aware is only asked in the manner of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿And it is the truth confirming﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91; Fatir: 31]." He said: "It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial accusative of al-Raḥmān if you make it nominative with istawā."

Ibn Jarir said: It is permissible for the bāʾ in bihi to be extra (zāʾida). The meaning is: "ask Him while He is Aware."

It was said: His saying "bihi" functions as an oath, like His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 1]. The first of these interpretations is the closest of them.

Then the Exalted informed about them that they were ignorant of the meaning of al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ The exegetes said: They said, "We do not know al-Raḥmān except the Raḥmān of Yamamah," meaning Musaylima. Al-Zajjaj said: Al-Raḥmān is one of the names of Allah. When they heard it, they denied it and said, "And what is al-Raḥmān?" ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ The interrogative is for denial, meaning: We will not prostrate to the Most Merciful whom you command us to prostrate to. Whoever reads with the yāʾ (taḥtiyya, third person) means: "Shall we prostrate to what Muhammad commands us to prostrate to?"

The people of Medina and Basra read ﴿what you command us﴾ with the tāʾ (second person). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Al-Aʿmash, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read it with the yāʾ. Abu ʿUbayd said: They mean al-Raḥmān. Al-Nahhas said: It is not necessary to interpret the Kufans' reading with this distant interpretation. Rather, the better interpretation is that the meaning for them is "prostrate to what the Prophet (ﷺ) commands," and the reading then becomes this, though the first is clearer.

﴿And it increased them in aversion﴾, meaning: the command to prostrate increased them in aversion from the religion and distance from it. It was also said: the mention of al-Raḥmān increased them in distance from faith. Muqatil said this, but the first is preferable.

Then the Exalted mentioned what, if they had reflected upon it, would have made them know the obligation of prostrating to al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burūj)﴾. The intended meaning of burūj is the constellations of the stars, meaning their twelve stations. It was said: they are the large stars, but the first is preferable. They were called burūj, which are lofty palaces, because they are for the planets like lofty dwellings for those who reside in them. The derivation of burj is from tabarruj (display), which means appearance. ﴿And placed therein a lamp (sirājan)﴾, meaning the sun. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]. The majority read sirājan in the singular. Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read surujan in the plural, meaning the great blazing stars. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

Al-Zajjaj said: In explaining the reading of Hamza and al-Kisaʾi, they meant the sun and the planets. ﴿And a luminous moon (qamaran munīran)﴾, meaning it gives light to the earth when it rises. Al-Aʿmash read qumran with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. This is a weak, anomalous (shādhdh) reading.

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession (khilfatan)﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: Khilfa means everything that comes after something else. The night is khilfa for the day and the day is khilfa for the night, because each of them succeeds the other and comes after it. From this is the khilfa of plants, which is a leaf that emerges after the first leaf in summer. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"In them the gazelles and the wild cattle walk in succession, and their young rise up from every resting place."

Al-Farra said in explaining the verse: It means one goes and another comes. Mujahid said: Khilfa is from khilaf (difference): this is white and that is black. It was also said: they alternate in light and darkness, and in increase and decrease.

It was also said: It is of the figure of omitting the modified noun, meaning: He made the night and the day possessors of succession, that is, difference.

﴿For whoever wills to remember (yadhdhakkara)﴾. Hamza read it lightened (yadhkura), and the majority read it with shadda (yadhdhakkara). So the first reading is from dhikr (remembrance) of Allah, and the second reading is from tadhakkur (remembering, reflecting) of Him. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read yatadhakkaru. The meaning of the verse is that the one who remembers and takes heed, when he looks at the alternation of night and day, knows that in their transition from state to state there must be an agent of change.

﴿Or wills gratitude (shukūran)﴾, meaning, wills to thank Allah for the great blessings and abundant kindnesses that He deposited in the night and the day. Al-Farra said: yudhakkiru and yatadhakkaru come with one meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) it is: "and they remember what is in it" (wa-yadhkurū mā fīhi).

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾. This is a new sentence brought to explain the righteous servants of Allah, the Exalted. "And the servants of the Most Merciful" is the subject, and its predicate is the relative clause with its complement. Hawn is a verbal noun, and it means tranquility and dignity.

A group of exegetes went to the view that hawnan is connected to yamshūna, meaning they walk upon the earth walking in humility. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It seems that this should be interpreted as meaning that the character of the one who walks is "humble" appropriate to his walk. As for the meaning being the attribute of walking alone, it is false, because many a man walks humbly and gently while being a sly wolf. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to walk with a forward lean in his stride, as if he were walking downhill.

﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. The Exalted mentioned that they bear what comes to them of harm from the people of ignorance and folly, so they do not respond to ignorance with ignorance, nor do they engage in foolishness with the foolish.

Al-Nahhas said: This "peace" is not from greeting (taslīm) but from being free of something (tasallum). The Arabs say salāman, meaning "a disavowal from you," that is, "innocence from you." It is in the accusative in one of two ways: either it is a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning "they say: we make peace, peace," and this is according to Sibawayh's view, or it is an object, meaning "they say this word." Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred this.

Mujahid said: The meaning of salāman is "rightness (sadād)," meaning he says to the ignorant a statement that repels him with gentleness and softness.

Sibawayh said: The Muslims were not commanded on that day to greet the polytheists, but this is according to his saying: "[We say] a greeting from you, and there is no good or evil between us and you."

Al-Mubarrad said: It should have been said that the Muslims were not commanded that day to fight them, then they were commanded to fight them.

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: Sibawayh erred in this and expressed it badly.

Al-Nahhas said: We know of no statement by Sibawayh concerning abrogation (naskh) and the abrogated except in this verse, for he said at the end of his statement, "then the verse of the sword abrogated it."

I say: This is how a man's speech is when he speaks without knowledge and walks without following the proper path. The Muslims were not commanded to greet the polytheists, nor were they forbidden from it. Rather, they were commanded to pardon and to observe a beautiful avoidance (al-hajr al-jamīl), so there is no need to claim abrogation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-Khalil told me: "I came to Abu Rabi'a al-A'rabi, who was among the most knowledgeable people I had seen. He was on a roof, so we greeted him, and he returned our greeting and said to us: *istawū* ("Stand level" / "Rise up"). We remained bewildered and did not know what he meant. A Bedouin beside him said to us: 'He told you to get up.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿Then He rose over the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]." He said: "So we climbed up to him, and he said: 'Would you like some leavened bread and warm milk?' We said: 'We have just left,' so he said: '*Salaman*' ('Peace'). We did not know what he meant, so the Bedouin said: 'He has greeted you with *mutarakah*, a parting that has neither good nor evil in it.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'﴾."

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. *Al-baytutah* (spending the night) is that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep. Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever the night overtakes has spent the night, whether he sleeps or does not sleep, as one says: 'So-and-so spent the night anxious.'" The meaning is: they spend the night before their Lord prostrating on their faces and standing on their feet. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"So we spent the night standing at the head of our horse, / it wrestles with us over its own self, and we wrestle with it."*

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment"﴾. That is: despite their obedience, they are fearful, anxious and afraid of His punishment. *Al-gharam* means the constant, enduring (torment). From it comes the word *al-gharim* (the creditor/debtor), because of his persistence in demanding. It is said: "So-and-so is *mughram* with such-and-such," meaning he is persistently attached to it and devoted to it. This is its meaning in the language of the Arabs, as mentioned by Ibn al-A'rabi, Ibn Arafa and others. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"If He punishes, it will be a lasting torment; / and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-gharam* is the most severe punishment. Abu Ubayda said: it is destruction. Ibn Zayd said: it is evil.

The clause ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a dwelling place and a station﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it. The predicate being specified is omitted, meaning "it" (Hell). The accusative of *mustaqarran* is either a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, indicating a state) or a *tamyiz* (specificative accusative, clarifying a noun), and likewise *muqaman*. It has been said that both are synonyms, and one was joined to the other only because their wording differs. It has also been said that they differ in meaning: *mustaqarr* is for the disobedient, who will be taken out (of Hell), while *muqam* is for the disbelievers, who will remain forever. *Sā'at* is among the verbs of blame, like *bi'sat*. It is possible that this is from the words of Allah, glorified is He, and it is also possible that it is a quotation of their words.

Then He described them, glorified is He, by moderation in spending, saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, 'Asim and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *yaqtarū* with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, from *qatara yaqturu* like *qa'ada yaq'udu*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*, which is a well-known and good dialect. The people of Madinah, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Abu Ubayda said: it is said *qatara al-rajulu 'alā 'iyālihi yaqturu*, *yaqturu qatran*, and *aqtara yuqtiru iqtāran*; the meaning of all of them is restricting expenditure.

Al-Nahhas said: among the best of what has been said about the meaning of the verse is: whoever spends in other than the obedience of Allah is extravagant; whoever withholds from the obedience of Allah is stingy; and whoever spends in the obedience of Allah is moderate (*qawām*). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it is the one who does not go hungry or naked, and does not spend (excessively) such that people say, "He has been extravagant."

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "Those are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They would not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty; rather they wanted from food only what would ward off their hunger and strengthen them for the worship of Allah, and from clothing only what would cover their nakedness and protect them from heat and cold."

Abu Ubayda said: "They did not exceed what is reasonable, nor were they stingy," like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29].

Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿and between that is a *qiwām*﴾ with a *kasrah* on the *qāf*, while the rest read it with a *fatḥah*. It has been said that both have the same meaning. It has also been said: *al-qiwām* with a *kasrah* is what a thing is sustained by and remains steadfast upon, while with a *fatḥah* it means justice and uprightness; this was said by Tha'lab.

It has been said: with a *fatḥah*, it means justice between two things; with a *kasrah*, it is what sustains a thing, which is neither in excess nor deficient.

It has been said: with a *kasrah*, it means sufficiency and the appropriate measure. The subject of *kāna* is implied in it, meaning: their expenditure was between that. *Bayna* is built on the *fatḥah* because it is one of the adverbs of place that are *mabni* on the *fatḥah*.

Al-Nahhas said: "I do not know what the reason for this is, because when *bayna* is in a position of *raf'* (nominative), it is inflected."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the disbeliever is an aide against his Lord﴾, that it refers to Abu al-Hakam, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the words ﴿Say, "I do not ask of you any reward for it"﴾, that he said: "Say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to; it is only a thing from the goods of this world."

Al-Khatib narrated in *Kitab al-Nujum* from him as well, concerning the words ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾, that he said: "They are these twelve constellations: first Aries, then Taurus, then Gemini, then Cancer, then Leo, then Virgo, then Libra, then Scorpio, then Sagittarius, then Capricorn, then Aquarius, then Pisces."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, that he said: "(One is) white and (the other) black."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well, saying: "Whatever of the night a person has missed of doing (good) he can make up during the day, and whatever of the day he has missed he can make up at night."

Al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that 'Umar prolonged the Duha prayer, and it was said to him: "You have done today something you did not used to do." He said: "Some of my daily portion (*wird*) remained for me, so I wanted to complete it," or he said: "to fulfill it," and he recited this verse: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, that he said: "They are the believers ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾," he said: "with obedience, chastity and humility."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Hawnan*: with knowledge and forbearance."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning the words ﴿Indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment﴾, that he said: "The lasting one."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, that he said: "They are the believers who are not extravagant, spending in disobedience to Allah, and who are not stingy, withholding the rights of Allah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah (the Exalted) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), He returned to mentioning the disgraceful acts of the disbelievers and the shameful aspects of their conduct, so He said: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what neither benefits them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harms them﴾ if they abandon it. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a supporter (zahir) against his Lord﴾. The word ẓahīr means one who backs or supports, that is, one who aids against his Lord through shirk (associating partners with God) and hostility. Backing against the Lord is backing against His Messenger or against His religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: Because he follows Satan and helps him in disobeying Allah, since their worship of idols is an aid to Satan.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever contemptible (hayyin) and humiliated against his Lord﴾, from the saying of the Arabs, "I cast him behind (ẓahartu bihi)," meaning, "I made him behind your back, so you do not pay attention to him." From this is His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (ẓihriyyan)﴾ [Hud: 92], meaning, "as something insignificant." From this too is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Badr, let not my need be cast behind your back, lest its answer fail me."

It was also said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever powerful against his Lord﴾, meaning the one he worships, which is the idol, is strong and dominant, doing with him whatever it wills, since inanimate matter has no power to harm or benefit. It is permissible for ẓahīr to be a plural, like His saying: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporting host (ẓahīr)﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The meaning then is that some disbelievers support others against the Messenger of Allah or against a religion. The intended meaning of "the disbeliever" here is the category, and this does not conflict with the fact that the cause of revelation was a specific disbeliever, as it is said it was Abu Jahl.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, meaning a bringer of good tidings to the believers of Paradise and a warner to the disbelievers of the Fire.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "I do not ask you for any wage for the Qur'an," or for conveying the message, which is indicated by "sent." The exception in His saying: ﴿except for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning, "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It was also said that it is connected (muttaṣil).

The meaning, according to the connected reading, is: "except for whoever wills to draw near to Him, the Exalted, through obedience," and He framed this in the form of a wage, insofar as it is something intended to be obtained.

When the Exalted explained that the disbelievers are backing one another against the Messenger of Allah, and commanded him not to seek any wage from them at all, He commanded him to rely upon Him in warding off harms and bringing about benefits.

So He said: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾. He specified the attribute of life to indicate that the living one is the one in whom trust is placed for matters of benefit, and that lasting life belongs to Allah alone, the Exalted, and not to living beings whose lives come to an end, for when they die, whoever relies upon them is lost. Tawakkul (reliance) is the servant's dependence upon Allah in all affairs. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾, meaning, declare Him free of the attributes of deficiency. It was also said: The meaning of sabbiḥ (glorify) is pray (ṣalli), since prayer is called tasbih. ﴿And He is sufficient as one aware of the sins of His servants﴾, meaning, "He is sufficient for you." This is an expression used for emphasis, like your saying: "Allah is sufficient as a Lord." Khabīr means one who is informed of matters to such a degree that nothing of them is hidden from Him.

Then He increased the emphasis and said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Aʿraf. The relative pronoun (alladhī) is in the genitive position as an attribute of al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living). He said baynihumā ("between them," dual) and did not say baynahunna (feminine plural), because He meant the two categories, just as al-Quṭāmī said:

"Does it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have been split apart, separated?"

If it is objected that this implies the creation of the Throne came after the creation of the heavens and the earth, as thumma (then) indicates, the reply is: The word thumma did not enter upon the creation of the Throne, but upon its elevation above the heavens and the earth. Al-Raḥmān is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is a second attribute of al-Ḥayy. The majority read it with the nominative. It was also said that it may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in istawā, or that it may be a subject whose predicate is the clause, meaning: "then ask," according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, as in the verse of the poet:

"A speaker said: Khawlān, so marry their girls."

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read al-Raḥmāni in the genitive as an attribute of al-Ḥayy or of the relative pronoun.

﴿So ask about Him, one who is aware (khabīran)﴾. The pronoun in bihi refers to what was mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth and the establishment upon the Throne. The meaning is: ask about the details of these matters which were mentioned in summary.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: The bāʾ (in bihi) has the meaning of ʿan (about), meaning, "ask about Him," like His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will occur﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 1], and the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Would that you had asked the horses, daughter of Malik, if you are ignorant of what you do not know."

Imru' al-Qays also said:

"So if you ask me about women, I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."

The intended meaning of "the Aware" is Allah, the Exalted, because no one knows the details of those created things except Him. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "If you met so-and-so, the lion would meet you because of it," meaning, "the lion would meet you by your meeting with it." So khabīran is in the accusative either as an object or as a circumstantial emphatic accusative (ḥāl muʾakkida). Abu al-Baqāʾ considered the circumstantial reading weak, saying: "It is weak for khabīran to be a circumstantial accusative of the subject of isʾal (ask), because the Aware is only asked in the manner of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿And it is the truth confirming﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91; Fatir: 31]." He said: "It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial accusative of al-Raḥmān if you make it nominative with istawā."

Ibn Jarir said: It is permissible for the bāʾ in bihi to be extra (zāʾida). The meaning is: "ask Him while He is Aware."

It was said: His saying "bihi" functions as an oath, like His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 1]. The first of these interpretations is the closest of them.

Then the Exalted informed about them that they were ignorant of the meaning of al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ The exegetes said: They said, "We do not know al-Raḥmān except the Raḥmān of Yamamah," meaning Musaylima. Al-Zajjaj said: Al-Raḥmān is one of the names of Allah. When they heard it, they denied it and said, "And what is al-Raḥmān?" ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ The interrogative is for denial, meaning: We will not prostrate to the Most Merciful whom you command us to prostrate to. Whoever reads with the yāʾ (taḥtiyya, third person) means: "Shall we prostrate to what Muhammad commands us to prostrate to?"

The people of Medina and Basra read ﴿what you command us﴾ with the tāʾ (second person). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Al-Aʿmash, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read it with the yāʾ. Abu ʿUbayd said: They mean al-Raḥmān. Al-Nahhas said: It is not necessary to interpret the Kufans' reading with this distant interpretation. Rather, the better interpretation is that the meaning for them is "prostrate to what the Prophet (ﷺ) commands," and the reading then becomes this, though the first is clearer.

﴿And it increased them in aversion﴾, meaning: the command to prostrate increased them in aversion from the religion and distance from it. It was also said: the mention of al-Raḥmān increased them in distance from faith. Muqatil said this, but the first is preferable.

Then the Exalted mentioned what, if they had reflected upon it, would have made them know the obligation of prostrating to al-Raḥmān. So He said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burūj)﴾. The intended meaning of burūj is the constellations of the stars, meaning their twelve stations. It was said: they are the large stars, but the first is preferable. They were called burūj, which are lofty palaces, because they are for the planets like lofty dwellings for those who reside in them. The derivation of burj is from tabarruj (display), which means appearance. ﴿And placed therein a lamp (sirājan)﴾, meaning the sun. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]. The majority read sirājan in the singular. Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read surujan in the plural, meaning the great blazing stars. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

Al-Zajjaj said: In explaining the reading of Hamza and al-Kisaʾi, they meant the sun and the planets. ﴿And a luminous moon (qamaran munīran)﴾, meaning it gives light to the earth when it rises. Al-Aʿmash read qumran with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. This is a weak, anomalous (shādhdh) reading.

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession (khilfatan)﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: Khilfa means everything that comes after something else. The night is khilfa for the day and the day is khilfa for the night, because each of them succeeds the other and comes after it. From this is the khilfa of plants, which is a leaf that emerges after the first leaf in summer. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"In them the gazelles and the wild cattle walk in succession, and their young rise up from every resting place."

Al-Farra said in explaining the verse: It means one goes and another comes. Mujahid said: Khilfa is from khilaf (difference): this is white and that is black. It was also said: they alternate in light and darkness, and in increase and decrease.

It was also said: It is of the figure of omitting the modified noun, meaning: He made the night and the day possessors of succession, that is, difference.

﴿For whoever wills to remember (yadhdhakkara)﴾. Hamza read it lightened (yadhkura), and the majority read it with shadda (yadhdhakkara). So the first reading is from dhikr (remembrance) of Allah, and the second reading is from tadhakkur (remembering, reflecting) of Him. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read yatadhakkaru. The meaning of the verse is that the one who remembers and takes heed, when he looks at the alternation of night and day, knows that in their transition from state to state there must be an agent of change.

﴿Or wills gratitude (shukūran)﴾, meaning, wills to thank Allah for the great blessings and abundant kindnesses that He deposited in the night and the day. Al-Farra said: yudhakkiru and yatadhakkaru come with one meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) it is: "and they remember what is in it" (wa-yadhkurū mā fīhi).

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾. This is a new sentence brought to explain the righteous servants of Allah, the Exalted. "And the servants of the Most Merciful" is the subject, and its predicate is the relative clause with its complement. Hawn is a verbal noun, and it means tranquility and dignity.

A group of exegetes went to the view that hawnan is connected to yamshūna, meaning they walk upon the earth walking in humility. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It seems that this should be interpreted as meaning that the character of the one who walks is "humble" appropriate to his walk. As for the meaning being the attribute of walking alone, it is false, because many a man walks humbly and gently while being a sly wolf. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to walk with a forward lean in his stride, as if he were walking downhill.

﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. The Exalted mentioned that they bear what comes to them of harm from the people of ignorance and folly, so they do not respond to ignorance with ignorance, nor do they engage in foolishness with the foolish.

Al-Nahhas said: This "peace" is not from greeting (taslīm) but from being free of something (tasallum). The Arabs say salāman, meaning "a disavowal from you," that is, "innocence from you." It is in the accusative in one of two ways: either it is a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning "they say: we make peace, peace," and this is according to Sibawayh's view, or it is an object, meaning "they say this word." Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred this.

Mujahid said: The meaning of salāman is "rightness (sadād)," meaning he says to the ignorant a statement that repels him with gentleness and softness.

Sibawayh said: The Muslims were not commanded on that day to greet the polytheists, but this is according to his saying: "[We say] a greeting from you, and there is no good or evil between us and you."

Al-Mubarrad said: It should have been said that the Muslims were not commanded that day to fight them, then they were commanded to fight them.

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: Sibawayh erred in this and expressed it badly.

Al-Nahhas said: We know of no statement by Sibawayh concerning abrogation (naskh) and the abrogated except in this verse, for he said at the end of his statement, "then the verse of the sword abrogated it."

I say: This is how a man's speech is when he speaks without knowledge and walks without following the proper path. The Muslims were not commanded to greet the polytheists, nor were they forbidden from it. Rather, they were commanded to pardon and to observe a beautiful avoidance (al-hajr al-jamīl), so there is no need to claim abrogation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-Khalil told me: "I came to Abu Rabi'a al-A'rabi, who was among the most knowledgeable people I had seen. He was on a roof, so we greeted him, and he returned our greeting and said to us: *istawū* ("Stand level" / "Rise up"). We remained bewildered and did not know what he meant. A Bedouin beside him said to us: 'He told you to get up.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿Then He rose over the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]." He said: "So we climbed up to him, and he said: 'Would you like some leavened bread and warm milk?' We said: 'We have just left,' so he said: '*Salaman*' ('Peace'). We did not know what he meant, so the Bedouin said: 'He has greeted you with *mutarakah*, a parting that has neither good nor evil in it.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the words of Allah: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'﴾."

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. *Al-baytutah* (spending the night) is that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep. Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever the night overtakes has spent the night, whether he sleeps or does not sleep, as one says: 'So-and-so spent the night anxious.'" The meaning is: they spend the night before their Lord prostrating on their faces and standing on their feet. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"So we spent the night standing at the head of our horse, / it wrestles with us over its own self, and we wrestle with it."*

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment"﴾. That is: despite their obedience, they are fearful, anxious and afraid of His punishment. *Al-gharam* means the constant, enduring (torment). From it comes the word *al-gharim* (the creditor/debtor), because of his persistence in demanding. It is said: "So-and-so is *mughram* with such-and-such," meaning he is persistently attached to it and devoted to it. This is its meaning in the language of the Arabs, as mentioned by Ibn al-A'rabi, Ibn Arafa and others. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"If He punishes, it will be a lasting torment; / and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-gharam* is the most severe punishment. Abu Ubayda said: it is destruction. Ibn Zayd said: it is evil.

The clause ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a dwelling place and a station﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it. The predicate being specified is omitted, meaning "it" (Hell). The accusative of *mustaqarran* is either a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, indicating a state) or a *tamyiz* (specificative accusative, clarifying a noun), and likewise *muqaman*. It has been said that both are synonyms, and one was joined to the other only because their wording differs. It has also been said that they differ in meaning: *mustaqarr* is for the disobedient, who will be taken out (of Hell), while *muqam* is for the disbelievers, who will remain forever. *Sā'at* is among the verbs of blame, like *bi'sat*. It is possible that this is from the words of Allah, glorified is He, and it is also possible that it is a quotation of their words.

Then He described them, glorified is He, by moderation in spending, saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, 'Asim and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *yaqtarū* with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, from *qatara yaqturu* like *qa'ada yaq'udu*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*, which is a well-known and good dialect. The people of Madinah, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'* and a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Abu Ubayda said: it is said *qatara al-rajulu 'alā 'iyālihi yaqturu*, *yaqturu qatran*, and *aqtara yuqtiru iqtāran*; the meaning of all of them is restricting expenditure.

Al-Nahhas said: among the best of what has been said about the meaning of the verse is: whoever spends in other than the obedience of Allah is extravagant; whoever withholds from the obedience of Allah is stingy; and whoever spends in the obedience of Allah is moderate (*qawām*). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it is the one who does not go hungry or naked, and does not spend (excessively) such that people say, "He has been extravagant."

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "Those are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They would not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty; rather they wanted from food only what would ward off their hunger and strengthen them for the worship of Allah, and from clothing only what would cover their nakedness and protect them from heat and cold."

Abu Ubayda said: "They did not exceed what is reasonable, nor were they stingy," like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29].

Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿and between that is a *qiwām*﴾ with a *kasrah* on the *qāf*, while the rest read it with a *fatḥah*. It has been said that both have the same meaning. It has also been said: *al-qiwām* with a *kasrah* is what a thing is sustained by and remains steadfast upon, while with a *fatḥah* it means justice and uprightness; this was said by Tha'lab.

It has been said: with a *fatḥah*, it means justice between two things; with a *kasrah*, it is what sustains a thing, which is neither in excess nor deficient.

It has been said: with a *kasrah*, it means sufficiency and the appropriate measure. The subject of *kāna* is implied in it, meaning: their expenditure was between that. *Bayna* is built on the *fatḥah* because it is one of the adverbs of place that are *mabni* on the *fatḥah*.

Al-Nahhas said: "I do not know what the reason for this is, because when *bayna* is in a position of *raf'* (nominative), it is inflected."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the disbeliever is an aide against his Lord﴾, that it refers to Abu al-Hakam, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the words ﴿Say, "I do not ask of you any reward for it"﴾, that he said: "Say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to; it is only a thing from the goods of this world."

Al-Khatib narrated in *Kitab al-Nujum* from him as well, concerning the words ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾, that he said: "They are these twelve constellations: first Aries, then Taurus, then Gemini, then Cancer, then Leo, then Virgo, then Libra, then Scorpio, then Sagittarius, then Capricorn, then Aquarius, then Pisces."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, that he said: "(One is) white and (the other) black."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well, saying: "Whatever of the night a person has missed of doing (good) he can make up during the day, and whatever of the day he has missed he can make up at night."

Al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that 'Umar prolonged the Duha prayer, and it was said to him: "You have done today something you did not used to do." He said: "Some of my daily portion (*wird*) remained for me, so I wanted to complete it," or he said: "to fulfill it," and he recited this verse: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, that he said: "They are the believers ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾," he said: "with obedience, chastity and humility."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Hawnan*: with knowledge and forbearance."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning the words ﴿Indeed, its punishment is a lasting torment﴾, that he said: "The lasting one."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, that he said: "They are the believers who are not extravagant, spending in disobedience to Allah, and who are not stingy, withholding the rights of Allah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 25, verses 61–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah (the Exalted) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), He returned to mentioning the disgraceful acts of the disbelievers and the shameful aspects of their conduct, so He said: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what neither benefits them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harms them﴾ if they abandon it. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a supporter (zahir) against his Lord﴾. The word ẓahīr means one who backs or supports, that is, one who aids against his Lord through shirk (associating partners with God) and hostility. Backing against the Lord is backing against His Messenger or against His religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: Because he follows Satan and helps him in disobeying Allah, since their worship of idols is an aid to Satan.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever contemptible (hayyin) and humiliated against his Lord﴾, from the saying of the Arabs, "I cast him behind (ẓahartu bihi)," meaning, "I made him behind your back, so you do not pay attention to him." From this is His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (ẓihriyyan)﴾ [Hud: 92], meaning, "as something insignificant." From this too is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Badr, let not my need be cast behind your back, lest its answer fail me."

It was also said: The meaning is, ﴿And the disbeliever is ever powerful against his Lord﴾, meaning the one he worships, which is the idol, is strong and dominant, doing with him whatever it wills, since inanimate matter has no power to harm or benefit. It is permissible for ẓahīr to be a plural, like His saying: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporting host (ẓahīr)﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The meaning then is that some disbelievers support others against the Messenger of Allah or against a religion. The intended meaning of "the disbeliever" here is the category, and this does not conflict with the fact that the cause of revelation was a specific disbeliever, as it is said it was Abu Jahl.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, meaning a bringer of good tidings to the believers of Paradise and a warner to the disbelievers of the Fire.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "I do not ask you for any wage for the Qur'an," or for conveying the message, which is indicated by "sent." The exception in His saying: ﴿except for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning, "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It was also said that it is connected (muttaṣil).

The meaning, according to the connected reading, is: "except for whoever wills to draw near to Him, the Exalted, through obedience," and He framed this in the form of a wage, insofar as it is something intended to be obtained.

When the Exalted explained that the disbelievers are backing one another against the Messenger of Allah, and commanded him not to seek any wage from them at all, He commanded him to rely upon Him in warding off harms and bringing about benefits.

So He said: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾. He specified the attribute of life to indicate that the living one is the one in whom trust is placed for matters of benefit, and that lasting life belongs to Allah alone, the Exalted, and not to living beings whose lives come to an end, for when they die, whoever relies upon them is lost. Tawakkul (reliance) is the servant's dependence upon Allah in all affairs. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾, meaning, declare Him free of the attributes of deficiency. It was also said: The meaning of sabbiḥ (glorify) is pray (ṣalli), since prayer is called tasbih. ﴿And He is sufficient as one aware of the sins of His servants﴾, meaning, "He is sufficient for you." This is an expression used for emphasis, like your saying: "Allah is sufficient as a Lord." Khabīr means one who is informed of matters to such a degree that nothing of them is hidden from Him.

Then He increased the emphasis and said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Aʿraf. The relative pronoun (alladhī) is in the genitive position as an attribute of al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living). He said baynihumā ("between them," dual) and did not say baynahunna (feminine plural), because He meant the two categories, just as al-Quṭāmī said:

"Does it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have been split apart, separated?"

If it is objected that this implies the creation of the Throne came after the creation of the heavens and the earth, as thumma (then) indicates, the reply is: The word thumma did not enter upon the creation of the Throne, but upon its elevation above the heavens and the earth. Al-Raḥmān is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is a second attribute of al-Ḥayy. The majority read it with the nominative. It was also said that it may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in istawā, or that it may be a subject whose predicate is the clause, meaning: "then ask," according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, as in the verse of the poet:

"A speaker said: Khawlān, so marry their girls."

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read al-Raḥmāni in the genitive as an attribute of al-Ḥayy or of the relative pronoun.

﴿So ask about Him, one who is aware (khabīran)﴾. The pronoun in bihi refers to what was mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth and the establishment upon the Throne. The meaning is: ask about the details of these matters which were mentioned in summary.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: The bāʾ (in bihi) has the meaning of ʿan (about), meaning, "ask about Him," like His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will occur﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 1], and the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Would that you had asked the horses, daughter of Malik, if you are ignorant of what you do not know."

Imru' al-Qays also said:

"So if you ask me about women, I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."

The intended meaning of "the Aware" is Allah, the Exalted, because no one knows the details of those created things except Him. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "If you met so-and-so, the lion would meet you because of it," meaning, "the lion would meet you by your meeting with it."
