"And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden" (25:68), i.e., He has forbidden its killing except by right, that is, by what makes souls deserving of being killed: disbelief after belief, or fornication after being chaste, or killing a soul without (another) soul. "And do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse" (25:68), i.e., they do not consider lawful the forbidden private parts without marriage or ownership by right hand. "And whoever does that" (25:68), i.e., anything of what has been mentioned, "will meet a penalty" (25:68) in the Hereafter. And athām (penalty) in the speech of the Arabs means punishment. Al-Farrā' said: Allah punished him with athām, yu'thimuhu, athāman and ithāman, i.e., He requited him with the requital of sin. ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid said: Athām is a valley in Hell which Allah made a punishment for the disbelievers. Al-Suddī said: It is a mountain in it. It was recited as yulaqqa with a damma on the yā' and a shadda on the qāf. Abū Muslim said: Athām and ithm are one and the same, and what is meant here is the requital of sins, so the name of the thing was applied to its requital.

al-Ḥasan recited "yalqa ayyāman" (plural of yawm), meaning hardships, and the Arabs express that by days. I do not think this reading is authentically transmitted from him. "The punishment will be doubled for him" (25:69). Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read yuḍāʿaf and yakhlud with jazm. Ibn Kathīr read yuḍaʿʿaf with the ʿayn shaddah, dropping the alif, with jazm. Ṭalḥah ibn Sulaymān read nuḍaʿʿif with a damma on the nūn, a kasra on the shaddah ʿayn, and jazm; this is the reading of Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah.

ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr, read both verbs with raf' as a resumptive (isti'nāf).

Ṭalḥah ibn Sulaymān read wa-takhlud with a fawqiyyah (second-person), addressing the disbeliever.

It is narrated from Abū ʿAmr that he read wa-yukhlad with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥah on the lām.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is an error in terms of transmission. The basis for jazm in yuḍāʿaf is that it is a substitute (badal) for yalqa, because the two are united in meaning. Similar to it is the poet's saying:

"Indeed, upon me is Allah's covenant that you pledge allegiance, / you will be taken unwillingly or come obediently."

The pronoun in His saying yakhlud fīhi refers to the doubled punishment, i.e., he will abide in the doubled punishment, humiliated, abased, despised.

"Except for one who repents and believes and does righteous work" (25:70). It was said that this is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil), and it was said that it is a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ).

Abū Ḥayyān said: Connection does not appear, because the excepted-from is judged as being one for whom the punishment is doubled, so the sense becomes: except one who repents, believes and does righteous work, so the punishment will not be doubled for him; but the negation of doubling does not necessitate the negation of punishment other than the doubled punishment.

He said: The preferable view in my opinion is that it is disconnected, i.e., but whoever repents.

Al-Qurṭubī said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception is general, covering the disbeliever and the fornicator. They differed concerning the Muslim murderer, and its explanation has preceded in al-Nisā' and al-Mā'idah.

The reference in His saying "those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds" (25:70) is to those previously mentioned. The meaning of replacing evil deeds with good deeds is that He erases their sins and establishes acts of obedience in their place.

al-Naḥḥās said: Among the best of what has been said about this is that in the place of a disbeliever a believer is written, and in the place of a disobedient one an obedient one. al-Ḥasan said: Some people say: the replacement is in the Hereafter, and that is not so; rather the replacement is in this world: Allah replaces for them faith in place of polytheism, sincerity in place of doubt, and chastity in place of immorality.

al-Zajjāj said: It does not make a good deed in place of an evil deed, but it makes repentance in place of the evil deed, and a good deed together with repentance.

It was said: Evil deeds are replaced by good deeds, and this was said by a group of the Companions and those after them.

It was said: Replacement is an expression for forgiveness, i.e., Allah forgives them those evil deeds, not that He replaces them with good deeds. It was said: What is meant by replacement is that He enables him to the opposites of what preceded from him. "And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (25:70). This sentence confirms what precedes it regarding the replacement.

"And whoever repents and does righteous work, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a turning" (25:71), i.e., whoever repents from what he committed and does a righteous deed after that, then indeed he turns back by that to Allah with a turning, i.e., he returns to Him with a sound, strong return.

al-Qaffāl said: It is possible that the first verse concerns those who repented from among the polytheists, which is why He said "except one who repents and believes." Then he joined to it "whoever repents" from among the Muslims, and followed his repentance with a righteous deed; he too has the ruling of those who repent.

It was said: (p-1050) whoever repents with his tongue but does not realize repentance through his deed, that repentance is not beneficial; rather, whoever repents and does righteous work, realizing his repentance by righteous deeds, is the one who turned to Allah with a turning, i.e., repented with true repentance, which is sincere (nasūḥ), and for this reason it was emphasized with the verbal noun. The meaning of the verse: whoever intends repentance and resolves upon it, let him turn to Allah; so the statement has the sense of a command. So it was said, lest the condition and the answer be identical, for one does not say of one who has repented "then indeed he turns back."

Then He, glorified is He, described these repenters who do righteous deeds, saying: "And those who do not witness falsehood" (25:72), i.e., they do not bear false testimony, or they do not attend falsehood. And zūr is lying and vanity, and they do not witness it. Most exegetes went to the second meaning.

al-Zajjāj said: Zūr in the language is lying, and there is no lie above associating partners with Allah.

al-Wāḥidī said: Most exegetes hold that zūr here means shirk.

The summary is that if yashhadūn is from shahādah (testimony), then there is an omitted genitive construction, i.e., they do not bear the testimony of falsehood; and if it is from shuhūd (attendance), as the majority went, then they differed about its meaning. Qatādah said: They do not assist the people of falsehood in their falsehood. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said: They do not attend idle play and singing. Ibn Jurayj said: Lying. It is also narrated from Mujāhid. The preferable view is not to restrict it to one kind of falsehood; rather what is meant is those who do not attend anything that truly qualifies as falsehood, whoever it may be. "And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity" (25:72), i.e., turning away from it, not inclining toward it. Laghw is every worthless thing of speech or deed.

al-Ḥasan said: Laghw is all sins. It was said: What is meant is they pass by people of idle talk; it is said: so-and-so is honored above what disgraces him, i.e., he keeps himself pure and honors himself from entering into idle talk and mixing with its people.

"And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord" (25:73), i.e., of the Qur'an, or of what in it is admonition and lesson, "do not fall upon them deaf and blind" (25:73), i.e., they do not fall upon them while being deaf and blind, but rather they bend over them hearing and seeing, and they benefit from them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning is that they do not neglect them, as if they were deaf who did not hear them and blind who did not see them.

Ibn Jarīr said: There is no falling down here; rather it is like saying "he sat weeping," though he was not sitting.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: It is as if the listener to the reminder is standing, so when he turns away from it, that is a falling, which is a collapse without order.

It was said the meaning is: when the verses of Allah are recited to them, their hearts tremble, so they fall down in prostration and weeping, and do not fall upon them deaf and blind.

al-Farrā' said: i.e., they did not remain in their former state as if they had not heard.

Al-Kashshāf said: It is not a negation of falling; rather it is an affirmation of it and a negation of deafness and blindness, and he meant that the negation is directed at the qualifier, not at the qualified.

"And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort of the eyes" (25:74). Min is either inceptive (ibtidā'iyyah) or explanatory (bayāniyyah).

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read wa-dhurriyyātinā in the plural. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ṭalḥah and ʿĪsā read wa-dhurriyyatinā in the singular. Dhurriyyah is used for the plural, as in His saying "offspring weak" (4:9), and for the singular, as in His saying "good offspring" (3:38). The accusative of qurrata aʿyun is as an object: it is said qarrat ʿaynuhu qurrah.

al-Zajjāj said: It is said: Allah comfort your eye, i.e., your heart meets what it loves.

al-Mufaḍḍal said: Regarding the comfort of the eye there are three opinions. The first is the coolness of her tears, because it is a sign of joy and laughter, just as its heat is a sign of sorrow and grief. The second is her sleep, because it occurs with a free mind and the departure of sorrow. The third is the attainment of contentment.

"And make us leaders for the righteous" (25:74), i.e., exemplars who are followed in goodness. He said imāman and did not say a'immah because it is intended as a collective noun, like His saying "then We bring you out as a child" (22:5). al-Farrā' said: He said imāman and did not say a'immah, just as He said of two "indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds" (26:16), meaning that it is from the singular which is intended as the plural.

al-Akhfash said: Imām is the plural of umm from amma yaummu, a plural on fi'āl, like ṣāḥib and ṣiḥāb, and qā'im and qiyām.

It was said: Imām is a verbal noun; it is said amma fulān fulānan imāman, like ṣiyām and qiyām.

It was said: They meant: make each one of us an imām. It was said: They meant: make us one imām, because our word is united. It was said: It is from inverted speech, and the meaning is: make the righteous an imām for us; and Mujāhid held this.

It was said: This supplication issues from them individually, and each one's expression during supplication is: make me an imām for the righteous; but the expressions of all were related in the first-person plural form for the sake of brevity, like His saying "O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous work" (23:51). In this, imāman remains as it is. And like what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

"O my blamers, do not increase my blame, / indeed the blamers are not trustworthy to me."

i.e., trustworthy ones. al-Qaffāl said: In my view, when imām is taken in the manner of a name, it is made singular, as if it were said: make us a proof for the righteous; and similarly bayyinah: it is said "these are the proof of so-and-so." al-Naysābūrī said: It was said in the verse that it indicates that religious leadership is something that should be sought and desired; the closer view is that they asked Allah to bring them in obedience to the level by which they are pointed to and followed.

The reference in His saying "those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for what they patiently endured" (25:75) is to those characterized by those qualities, and it is a subject whose predicate is what follows, and the sentences are resumptive.

It was said: "Those and what follows" is a predicate for His saying "and the servants of the Most Merciful." So said al-Zajjāj. The ghurfah is the lofty rank, and it is the highest and best of the stations of Paradise; originally it is for any elevated building, and the plural is ghuraf.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The ghurfah is Paradise. The bāʾ in "for what they patiently endured" is causal, and mā is verbal, i.e., they are rewarded the chamber because of their patience in the hardships of obligation. "And they will be met therein with greeting and peace" (25:75). Abū Bakr, al-Mufaḍḍal, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read yalqūna with a fatḥah on the yā', sukūn on the lām, and a light qāf. al-Farrā' chose this reading and said: because the Arabs say: so-and-so yulqī with greeting, peace and good, and seldom do they say yulqī. The rest read with a damma on the yā', fatḥah on the lām and a shaddah on the qāf, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading because of His saying "and He gave them radiance and joy" (76:11). The meaning is that they greet one another, and the Lord, glorified is He, sends peace to them. It was said: the tahiyyah is lasting survival and great dominion; it was said: it is (p-1051) in the sense of salām. It was said: the angels greet them and salute them. The apparent view is that this greeting and peace are from Allah, glorified is He, to them, and among that is His saying, glorified is He: "Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace" (33:44). It was said: the meaning of tahiyyah is the supplication for them for long life. The meaning of salām is the supplication for them for safety from calamities.

The accusative of *khalidina fīhā* is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: remaining therein without death. ﴿How excellent a dwelling-place and abode it is.﴾ That is, the chamber was excellent as a place of settling, where they would settle, and as an abode, where they would remain. This stands in contrast to His earlier words: ﴿Evil is it as a dwelling-place and abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 66].

﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.﴾ He, glorified is He, has made clear that He is free of need for the obedience of all of them, and that He imposed obligations upon them only so that they might benefit from the obligation. It is said: *mā ʿabaʾtu bi-fulān*, meaning "I did not care for so-and-so, and he has no worth in my sight." The root of *yaʿbaʾu* is from *al-ʿibʾ*, which means weight.

Al-Khalil said: *mā aʿbaʾu bi-fulān* means "I do not do anything with him," as if he considers him insignificant and contemptible, and claims that his existence and non-existence are equal. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿What weight would My Lord give you?﴾ He means: what weight would you have in His sight. *Al-ʿibʾ* is weight. The *mā* is either interrogative or negative. Al-Farrāʾ stated explicitly that it is interrogative. Ibn al-Shajarī said: "The true position in my view is that the place of *mā* is accusative, and the sense is: what weight does He give to you, meaning, what concern does He have for you." ﴿Were it not for your supplication﴾, meaning: were it not for your calling upon Him to worship Him. On this reading, the verbal noun *al-duʿāʾ* is annexed to its object, and this is the preference of al-Farrāʾ. Its subject is omitted, and the answer to *law lā* (were it not) is omitted, its implied sense being: were it not for your supplication, He would not care for you. This is supported by His words: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. The address is to all people, then He singled out the disbelievers from among them, saying: ﴿So you have denied﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "So the disbelievers have denied." In this reading there is clear evidence that the address is to all people.

It is also said that the verbal noun is annexed to its subject, meaning: were it not for your seeking refuge with Him in hardships.

It is also said that the meaning is: He would not care for you, meaning for the forgiveness of your sins, were it not for your calling upon the gods alongside Him.

Ibn Jinni related that Ibn ʿAbbās read in the same way as the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas related that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as both of them. Among those who said that the supplication is annexed to its subject were al-Qutaybi and al-Farisi, who said: the original is "were it not for your calling upon the gods along with Him."

Ibn Jinni related that Ibn ʿAbbās read in the same way as the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas related that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as both of them. Among those who said that the supplication is omitted, its implied sense on this reading being: were it not for your supplication, He would not punish you. The meaning of ﴿So you have denied﴾ on the first reading is: so you have denied what you were called to, and on the second reading: so you have denied monotheism.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So it will be a lasting penalty﴾, meaning: the consequence of denial will certainly cling to you. The majority of exegetes hold that what is meant here by *al-lizām* (the lasting penalty) is what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr. Another group said it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lizāman* means a decisive separation, meaning: it will be a decisive separation between you and the believers.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿So your denial will be a lasting penalty that clings to you, so you will not be granted repentance.﴾ Most reciters read the *lām* of *lizāman* with a kasra. Abu ʿUbayda cited, for Ṣakhr:

*Whether they escape the collapse of the earth,*
*they have indeed met their deaths, a lasting clinging.*

Ibn Jarir said: *lizāman* means a perpetual punishment and an annihilating destruction that joins some of you to others, like the words of Abu Dhuʾayb:

*So it overtook him with a stream of clinging rushing,*
*as a basin overflows with a scattered flood.*

He means by *al-lizām* that which follows one part of it another, and by *al-laffīf* the stones that fall from the collapsing rubble.

Abu Hatim related from Abu Zayd, who said: I heard Abu al-Simak reading *lizāman* with a fatha on the *lām*. Abu Jaʿfar said: it would be the verbal noun of *lazima* (to cling), but the kasra is preferable.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: Which sin is the greatest? He said: That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you. I said: Then which? He said: That you kill your child for fear that it will eat with you. I said: Then which? He said: That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So Allah revealed the confirmation of that: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾.

Al-Bukhari and others also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that some people among the polytheists had killed much and committed adultery much, then they came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "What you say and call to is indeed good, if you would inform us that there is an expiation for what we have done." So ﴿And those who do not invoke﴾ was revealed, the verse, and ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], the verse, was also revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr concerning His words ﴿will meet the penalty (athām)﴾ that he said: it is a valley in Hell.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, the verse, was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, and they said: There is not one of us who has not associated, killed and committed adultery. So Allah revealed ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse, saying to those who had committed this in polytheism. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿except those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. So Allah replaced for them disbelief with Islam, disobedience with obedience, denial with recognition, and ignorance with knowledge.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: We recited it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for years: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse, and whoever does that will meet the penalty (athām)﴾. Then ﴿except those who repent and believe﴾ was revealed. So I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at this, and at ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His words ﴿then Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ that he said: they are the believers who had been committing evil deeds before their faith, so Allah turned away from that and transformed them to good deeds, replacing their evil deeds with good deeds.

Ahmad, Hannad, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa al-Sifat* related from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: Present to him his minor sins. His minor sins will be presented to him, and his major sins will be kept away from him. It will be said: On such and such a day you did such and such. He will acknowledge it, not deny it, and he will be fearful of the major sins coming. It will be said: Give him for every evil deed he did a good deed." The hadiths concerning the expiation of evil deeds and their replacement with good deeds are numerous.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ (p-1052) that he said: *al-Zūr* was an idol in Medina around which they played every seven days, and the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they passed by it, passed by with dignity, not looking at it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning ﴿And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes﴾, that he said: they mean one who acts in obedience so that our eyes are gladdened by him in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And make us a leader for the righteous﴾: he said: leaders of guidance by whom people are guided, and do not make us leaders of misguidance. This is because He said of the people of happiness: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 73], and of the people of wretchedness: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas: 41].

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related from Sahl ibn Saʿd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿Those will be rewarded with the chamber﴾, that he said: The chamber is of red ruby, or green emerald, or white pearl, without any crack or flaw.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾, that he said: were it not for your faith. So Allah informed that He has no need of them if He had not created them as believers. Had He had a need of them, He would have made faith beloved to them as He made it beloved to the believers. ﴿So it will be a lasting penalty﴾: he said: death.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari related from him that he used to read: "So the disbelievers have denied; ﴿So it will be a lasting penalty﴾." ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he read it in this way.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related ﴿So it will be a lasting penalty﴾, he said: the killing on the day of Badr. In the two *Sahihs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is related from him that he said: Five have passed: the smoke, the moon, the seizing, the assault, and the lizam (the lasting penalty).
